relevant_excerpt: (2) Every notary public who attests an instrument of conveyance shall before doing SO take all reasonable steps to satisfy himself that the value on which the stamp duty is paid represents the value of the property conveyed.
why_relevant: Directly addresses what the attesting notary must do about the value figure: satisfy himself that the value on which duty is paid represents the value of the property conveyed. Section 78(1) of the same section requires all facts affecting chargeability, and the amount of duty, to be set out in the instrument.
temporal_note: In force long before the October 2022 matter date; the corpus records no amendment event on this section.

relevant_excerpt: Except where there is an agreement to the contrary stamp duty shall be payable; (a) in the case of an instrument of transfer by the grantee;
why_relevant: Identifies who bears the duty on the Deed of Gift: the grantee, that is the donee, unless the deed provides otherwise.
temporal_note: In force long before the October 2022 matter date; the corpus records no amendment event on this section.

relevant_excerpt: (1) The stamp duty with which any instrument is chargeable shall be paid before or at the time of execution of the instrument except as otherwise permitted in this Statute and such payment shall be indicated on such instrument by means of adhesive stamps or impressed stamps or a Certificate of payment referred to in subsection (2) hereof.
why_relevant: Sets when and how the duty on the deed must be paid. Background to the quantum question; it does not supply the rate.
temporal_note: In force long before the October 2022 matter date; the corpus records no amendment event on this section.

relevant_excerpt: The following instruments and documents shall be exempted from the payment of stamp duty:- (1) bail bond in criminal proceedings;
why_relevant: The exemption list is closed and contains no exemption for a gift between family members, so the father-to-son character of the deed does not take it out of charge. Relied on negatively.
temporal_note: In force long before the October 2022 matter date; the corpus records no amendment event on this section.
verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim but quotes only item (1) of the exemption list, so it does not on its face support the negative proposition; the verifier read the whole of s.39 and confirms it contains no exemption for a gift of land between family members.

relevant_excerpt: (1) Where any property is conveyed by an instrument, the stamp duty with which such instrument is chargeable shall be calculated on the value of the property conveyed.
why_relevant: The national counterpart of the provincial valuation rule. Section 15(3) of the same section adds that a gift subject to a reservation is valued as if made without the reservation, which is why an outright gift and a reserved gift are valued alike.
temporal_note: In force long before the October 2022 matter date; the corpus records no amendment event on this section.

relevant_excerpt: includes conveyance on sale and every instrument by which property, or any interest in any property is transferred
why_relevant: Added by the verifier. Section 48(1), which fixes the base of the charge, applies where property is 'conveyed by an instrument', while the charging section and the definition relied on by the researcher speak of a 'transfer'. The interpretation section defines conveyance to include every instrument by which property or an interest in property is transferred, which is what brings a Deed of Gift within s.48(1) and lets the statutory value operate as the base. Without it the step from the charge to the valuation rule is unbridged.
temporal_note: In force from 1990; the corpus section record shows no amendment event, so on these sources it stood unchanged at the October 2022 matter date.
verifier_note: Added by the verifier; excerpt checked verbatim against 6-1990/s106.

relevant_excerpt: Inheritance ab interstate to the immovable property in Sri Lanka of a person deceased shall be governed and regulated by the following provisions of this Ordinance wherever such person may have or have had his actual or matrimonial domicile.
why_relevant: Fixes the governing law for intestate succession to Lot A. Lot A with the commercial building on it is immovable property in Sri Lanka, so the 2009 and 2010 intestacies are regulated by Part III of this Ordinance.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; the corpus records no amendment event on this section, so the text stood unchanged at each of the three deaths (2007, 2009, 2010) and at 2021-10.

relevant_excerpt: When any person shall die intestate as to any of his or her property, leaving a spouse surviving, the surviving spouse shall inherit one-half of the property of such person.
why_relevant: Lalantha died intestate on 04.10.2009 leaving his wife Nishi Fernando surviving, so Nishi takes one half of Lot A before any question of descendants, ascendants or collaterals arises. Harsha died unmarried, so the section is not engaged on his death.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus, so the text applied at Lalantha's death in 2009 and at 2021-10.

relevant_excerpt: Subject to the right of the surviving spouse in the preceding section mentioned, the right of inheritance is divided in the following order as respects (a) descendants, (b) ascendants, (c) collaterals.
why_relevant: Sets the order in which the residue after the spouse's half is taken and makes clear that the spouse's half under s 22 comes off first. It is the hinge between s 22 and ss 24 to 25 for Lalantha's estate.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: Children, grandchildren, and remoter descendants are preferent to all others in the estate of the parents; all the children take equally per capita, but the children or remoter issue of a deceased child take per stirpes or by representation.
why_relevant: Explains why no descendant takes on either intestacy: Lalantha and Harsha both died issueless, so the descendant class fails and the inheritance moves on to ascendants and collaterals. It also explains why Ashen and Tashen take nothing while their mother Dushani is living, representation running only through a deceased child.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: if only one of the parents be alive, the surviving parent takes half, and the brothers and sisters of the deceased of the full blood, and the issue of any deceased brother or sister of the full blood, by representation, and the brothers and sisters of the half-blood who are related to the intestate by the side of the deceased parent, and the issue of any such deceased brother or sister of the half-blood, by representation, take the other half.
why_relevant: The operative rule for both deaths. On each of Lalantha's and Harsha's death the descendants failed, the father Nishantha had predeceased (13.09.2007) and the mother Kanthi survived. Kanthi therefore takes half of the estate then in question and the other half goes to the full-blood siblings together with the half-blood sister Minoli, who is related through the deceased parent.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus, so the text applied in 2009, in 2010 and at 2021-10.

relevant_excerpt: but if there are only half-brothers and sisters or such issue of one side, the full brothers and sisters and the issue of deceased full brothers and sisters by representation, take then in the first place one-half of the property, and divide the other half with the half-brothers and sisters and their issue by representation.
why_relevant: Recorded because it is the competing reading of how the collateral half splits between the full-blood siblings and Minoli. If s 27 reaches the s 25 collateral half, the full-blood siblings take a preference and the arithmetic changes. The section sits after s 26, which deals with both parents failing, so its reach into the s 25 one-surviving-parent case is open. This is the main reason the shares question cannot be closed on statute alone.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: Except when otherwise expressly provided, if all those who succeed to the inheritance are equally near in degree to the intestate, they take per capita, and not per stirpes.
why_relevant: Supplies the division inside the collateral half under s 25. Harsha, Dushani and Minoli are all siblings of Lalantha and so equally near in degree; on the reading taken here they share that half per capita. The words 'except when otherwise expressly provided' are what leave room for the s 27 argument.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: In all questions relating to the distribution of the property of an intestate, if the present Ordinance is silent, the rules of the Roman-Dutch law as it prevailed in North Holland are to govern and be followed.
why_relevant: The Ordinance itself refers questions it does not answer to Roman-Dutch law. It is the statutory hook for the two non-statutory steps this matter needs, the effect of the life interest reserved on Deed of Gift No. 1012 and the division of the collateral half where the Ordinance is silent. Its presence is why both questions are classified as mixed rather than statute only.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: includes land, incorporeal tenements, and things attached to the earth or permanently fastened to anything which is attached to the earth, and any interest in land except that of a mortgagee
why_relevant: Defines 'immovable property' for the Ordinance so that s 21(1) reaches Lot A together with the commercial building bearing Assessment No. 12 standing on it. The excerpt is the definition of 'immovable property'; the corpus body of s 3 has lost the defined-term labels, which the verifier should confirm against the source text.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: this Ordinance shall not apply to Kandyans or Muslims, or to Tamils of the Northern Province who are or may become subject to the Tesawalamai
why_relevant: Marks the personal-law condition on which the whole answer rests. The scenario says nothing about the personal law of the Jayakodi family, so the answer proceeds on the unstated assumption that they are governed by the general law and not by Kandyan law, Muslim law or the Thesawalamai.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: The following sections of this Ordinance shall apply to the estates of such persons only as shall die after the proclamation of this Ordinance
why_relevant: Temporal gateway to Part III. All three deaths occurred in 2007, 2009 and 2010, long after the proclamation of the Ordinance, so Part III applies to each estate.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: by a title adverse to or independent of that of the claimant or plaintiff in such action (that is to say, a possession unaccompanied by payment of rent or produce, or performance of service or duty, or by any other act by the possessor, from which an acknowledgment of a right existing in another person would fairly and naturally be inferred) for ten years previous to the bringing of such action, shall entitle the defendant to a decree in his favour with costs.
why_relevant: This is the only source of prescriptive title to land in the corpus and the provision Nimal would have to invoke: ten years' undisturbed and uninterrupted possession by a title adverse to or independent of the owner's. Its conditions are the ones the facts must meet, and it is the enactment that section 57 of the Registration of Title Act disapplies.
temporal_note: In force from 1871; the corpus records no amendment event on section 3. The Prescription (Amendment) Act No. 26 of 2014 in the corpus replaces only section 15 (State and matrimonial causes), not section 3, so this is the text in force at 2021-10.

formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
relevant_excerpt: The Prescription Ordinance (Chapter 68) shall not apply to lands or interests in land registered under this Act with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership or a Second Class Title of Ownership.
why_relevant: The decisive provision. It removes the Prescription Ordinance altogether from land registered under the Registration of Title Act with either class of title, so no length of adverse possession of such a parcel can generate prescriptive title.
temporal_note: In force from 1998; no amendment event recorded in the corpus. The possession relied on runs entirely after the section came into force.

formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
relevant_excerpt: (b) where the Commissioner of Title Settlement is of the view that a claimant does not qualify for a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership but the claimant is in bonafide possession of the land parcel, he may declare the claimant eligible to be registered with a Second Class Title of Ownership
why_relevant: Section 57 is expressed by reference to the two classes of title, and section 14 is where those classes come from: registration on initial compilation is either with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership or with a Second Class Title of Ownership. Without it the phrase in section 57 has no content and one cannot show that a parcel registered under the Act falls inside the exclusion.
temporal_note: In force from 1998; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
relevant_excerpt: Entries in the Title Register maintained under the provisions of this Act, shall be conclusive evidence of the existence of the ownership or interest specified in such entries and shall not be questioned in a Court of law except as provided for in this Act.
why_relevant: Reinforces the bar: the registered owner's title is conclusive and may not be questioned in court except as the Act itself allows, which forecloses an action asserting a better, unregistered, prescriptive title.
temporal_note: In force from 1998; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
relevant_excerpt: A person registered with a Second Class Title of Ownership or a person claiming title through him shall at the end of a period of ten years from such registration, and if there has been no action under section 29 against such registration during the intervening period, be eligible for the conversion of his registration to one of First Class Title of Absolute Ownership.
why_relevant: Explains the only route under the Act by which ten years of possession improves a person's position, and shows it is not prescription: it is open to a person already registered with a Second Class Title, not to a stranger in possession, and it works by conversion of an existing registration.
temporal_note: In force from 1998; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
relevant_excerpt: No person acquiring an interest in any land parcel registered under the provisions of this Act shall be entitled to such title or interest unless such title or interest is registered under the provisions of this Act.
why_relevant: Independently blocks an unregistered claim: even if some interest were said to have accrued to Nimal, he is not entitled to it while it is unregistered, and the Act provides no machinery for registering an interest acquired by adverse possession.
temporal_note: In force from 1998; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998

relevant_excerpt: (8) He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument to which at least two witnesses have not subscribed their signatures in letters.
why_relevant: Fixes the minimum of two attesting witnesses. It is what makes the 'at least two of the attesting witnesses' route in rule (9) workable and shows that the notary's acquaintance with a single witness cannot by itself carry the deed.

relevant_excerpt: (12) He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless the person executing the same and the witnesses shall have signed the same in his presence and in the presence of one another, and unless he shall have signed the same in the presence of the executant and of the attesting witnesses.
why_relevant: Supplies the other standing condition of attestation: executant and both witnesses must sign before the notary and before one another. It is why the two witnesses relied on for identification must actually attend the execution rather than merely vouch for the executant.

formal_title: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance No. 7 of 1840
relevant_excerpt: the relevant deed or instrument shall be in writing, signed by every executant or by any person duly authorised by such executant and the witnesses in the presence of a licenced notary public present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and the same shall be attested by such notary

formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
relevant_excerpt: A Notary Public attesting an instrument in terms of this Act shall- (a) satisfy himself regarding the identity of whosoever of the parties to the transaction and the witnesses, as are not known to him, by reference to their official identity cards or such other means as may reliably reveal their identity;

For instruments executed under the Registration of Title Act a notary could, already in 1998 and so at the matter date, establish the identity of a party not known to him by reference to official identity cards. It does not govern an ordinary deed of transfer attested under the Notaries Ordinance and the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, but it contradicts the unqualified statement in the draft answer that no identity-document route existed in October 2021, and it sets the boundary the answer should have drawn.

relevant_excerpt: There shall be charged on- (a) every instrument relating to a transfer of situated in the immovable property Western Province; (b) every document presented or filed, in proceedings instituted in any Court of law established by law, in the Western Province of Sri Lanka; (c) every transfer of a motor vehicle effected in Western Province. a stamp duty at the prescribed rate.
why_relevant: The charging provision. A Deed of Gift of land at Pannipitiya is an instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province, so stamp duty is chargeable on it under the Western Province Financial Statute and is administered by the Provincial Council's revenue officers. It also shows that the rate itself is 'prescribed', not stated in the Statute.
temporal_note: In force from 1990; corpus records no later change (latest_change_year null). In force at 2021-10.

relevant_excerpt: (1) Where any property is conveyed by an instrument, the stamp duty with which such instrument is chargeable shall be calculated on the value of the property conveyed.
why_relevant: Fixes the base on which duty is calculated: the 'value' of the property conveyed. This is what sends the Assessor to the statutory definition of 'value' rather than to the consideration, the cost of construction or the current market price.
temporal_note: In force from 1990; corpus records no later change. In force at 2021-10.

relevant_excerpt: (c) any immovable property which is gifted, being immovable property which was acquired by the donor after March 31, 1977 means - the price which, in the opinion ofthe Assessor, such property would have fetched if sold in the open market on the date which such on property was acquired by the donor, increased by an amount equal to the cost of the improvements, alterations and additions, if any, made to such property after the date on which the property was acquired by the donor, and prior to the date of the instrument by which such property is gifted ; or (ii) the price which, in the opinion of the assessor, that property would have: fetched, if sold in the open market on the date of the instrument by which such property was gifted. whichever price is the lower.
why_relevant: The operative definition. The donor acquired the Pannipitiya land in January 1978, that is after March 31, 1977, so paragraph (c) governs: the Assessor takes the lower of (i) the open-market price at the date of acquisition plus the cost of improvements made before the gift, and (ii) the open-market price at the date of the Deed of Gift. Paragraphs (a) and (b) are displaced - (a) excludes gifted immovable property, (b) applies only to property acquired on or before March 31, 1977.
temporal_note: Interpretation section in force from 1990; corpus records no later change. In force at 2021-10. The March 31, 1977 cut-off inside the definition is a fixed statutory date, not a commencement issue.
verifier_note: Checked against 6-1990/s106: the head-word "value" and paragraph (c) are present and the excerpt is verbatim; OCR drops the "(i)" enumerator of the first limb, but the two-limb structure and "whichever price is the lower" are confirmed by the parallel wording of paragraph (b), and the January 1978 acquisition puts this gift in paragraph (c) rather than (b).

If the Deed of Gift is not duly stamped, every person executing it - the donor as well as the donee - is liable to the Commissioner for the duty and any penalty, and s52(3) gives that liability effect notwithstanding s51, with a right of recovery under s52(2) against the person primarily liable. relevant_excerpt: Before any deed or instrument (other than a will or codicil) affecting any interest in land or other immovable property is drawn by him, he shall search or cause to be searched the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title in regard to such land and whether any prior deed affecting any interest in such land has been registered;
why_relevant: Imposes the primary duty that generates the document list: before drawing a deed affecting land the notary must search the land registry registers to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed has been registered. The search is performed against the registered folio, so a certified extract of the folio is the first document to be called for.
temporal_note: Rule (17)(a) itself was not touched by the Notaries (Amendment) Acts No. 47 of 2011, No. 31 of 2022 or No. 6 of 2024; those Acts amended only paragraph (b) and added paragraphs (c) to (e). The text quoted was in force in October 2021.

relevant_excerpt: When a deed transferring any immovable property is executed or acknowledged before a notary, he shall use his best endeavours to obtain the title deed, if any, of such property, and make an endorsement thereon stating the number and date of the deed executed before him and the nature of the transaction and attach his signature thereto,
why_relevant: Requires the notary attesting a transfer to use his best endeavours to obtain the title deed of the property. This is the statutory basis for calling for the vendor's original deeds, the chain of title, and not merely copies.
temporal_note: Rule (33) was not amended by the 2011, 2022 or 2024 amending Acts; in force in October 2021.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument, other than a will or codicil, affecting land or other immovable property, unless the deed or instrument embodies therin or in a Schedule annexed therto an accurate and clear description of the said land or other property affected thereby, showing its boundaries, extent, situation specifying the district, pattu, korale, Divisional Secretary's Division
why_relevant: Requires an accurate and clear description of the land showing boundaries, extent and situation, either in the deed or in an annexed schedule. To satisfy this for a twenty-acre estate the notary must call for the survey plan and the schedules of the prior deeds so that the description can be checked against them.
temporal_note: The Notaries (Amendment) Act, No. 31 of 2022, s.16(9)(a) substituted only the closing words of paragraph (a), adding condominium wording, after the matter date. The boundaries, extent and situation requirement quoted here pre-dates October 2021, but because the paragraph was substituted in 2022 it is treated as supporting rather than indispensable.

formal_title: Registration of Documents Ordinance No. 23 of 1927
relevant_excerpt: An instrument executed or made on or after the 1st day of January, 1864, whether before or after the commencement of this Ordinance shall, unless it is duly registered under this Chapter, or, if the land has come within the operation of the Land Registration Ordinance, 1877f, in the books mentioned in section 26 of that Ordinance, be void as against all parties claiming an adverse interest thereto on valuable consideration by virtue of any subsequent instrument which is duly registered under this Chapter
why_relevant: Explains why the registry folio, and not the vendor's bundle of deeds alone, is decisive: an unregistered instrument is void against a later instrument taken for valuable consideration and duly registered. The purchaser's protection depends on what the folio shows, so a certified folio extract must be called for and read.
temporal_note: Not amended; in force since 1927.

formal_title: Registration of Documents Ordinance No. 23 of 1927
relevant_excerpt: Subject to the prescribed regulations, all duplicates and copies and all books and indexes kept under this Ordinance may be searched and examined by any person claiming to be interested therein or by his attorney-at-law or agent duly authorized thereto in writing, and certified copies of or extracts from any such duplicate, copy, or book may be obtained if required.
why_relevant: Provides the statutory means by which the document is obtained: the registry books, duplicates and indexes may be searched by a person interested or his attorney-at-law, and certified copies of or extracts from them may be obtained. This is the authority for calling for a certified extract of the folio and certified copies of registered instruments.
temporal_note: Not amended; in force since 1927.

formal_title: Registration of Documents Ordinance No. 23 of 1927
relevant_excerpt: Every instrument (except a will) presented for registration shall contain embodied therein, or in a schedule annexed thereto, an accurate and clear description of the land affected thereby, its boundaries, extent, and situation specifying the district and the village, pattu, korale, or other division of the district in which the land is situated
why_relevant: Every registrable instrument must describe the land by boundaries, extent and situation. The description in the prior registered deeds is the reference point against which the survey plan and the vendor's description of the estate must be compared.
temporal_note: Amended by Law No. 50 of 1982, well before the matter date.

formal_title: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance No. 7 of 1840
relevant_excerpt: shall be in force or avail in law unless - (a) the relevant deed or instrument shall be in writing, signed by every executant or by any person duly authorised by such executant and the witnesses in the presence of a licenced notary public present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and the same shall be attested by such notary;
why_relevant: No sale, transfer or mortgage of immovable property is of any force unless made by a writing executed before and attested by a notary. Only notarially executed deeds can be accepted as documents of title, which is why the notary calls for the notarial deeds themselves rather than agreements, receipts or unattested writings.
temporal_note: The corpus text is section 2 as substituted by the Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Acts No. 30 of 2022 and No. 4 of 2024, both later than the matter date. The requirement of notarial execution and attestation for dispositions of land has been in force since 1840, but because the quoted wording post-dates October 2021 this provision is treated as supporting only.
verifier_note: The excerpt is verbatim but is the text of section 2 as substituted by Acts No. 30 of 2022 and No. 4 of 2024, so applicable_to_matter_date should read false on the wording even though the requirement of notarial execution itself long pre-dates the matter; correctly confined to a supporting role.

formal_title: Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act No. 2 of 1958
relevant_excerpt: The transfer of ownership of a tea or rubber estate on or after the appointed day shall, subject to the provisions of subsections (2) and (3), be null and void unless- (a) a certificate of consent of the Board to such transfer has been previously obtained by the transferor, and (b) such transfer is effected in accordance with the conditions, if any, subject to which such consent has been granted.
why_relevant: A transfer of ownership of a rubber estate is null and void without a previously obtained certificate of consent of the Board. If the property falls within the Act, the Board's certificate of consent is a document that must be called for before the transfer is drawn.
temporal_note: Section 3 has not been amended; in force since 1958.

formal_title: Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act No. 2 of 1958
relevant_excerpt: Where a certificate of consent to the transfer of ownership of a tea or rubber estate is issued by the Board, such certificate shall be attached to the deed by which such transfer is effected, and the notary attesting such deed shall in his attestation state that such certificate has been issued in respect of such transfer and specify the number, if any, and the date of issue of such certificate.
why_relevant: Shows the form the requirement takes in practice: the certificate of consent must be attached to the deed and its number and date recited in the attestation. It confirms that the certificate is a document the notary physically calls for and keeps with the deed.
temporal_note: Not amended; in force since 1958.

formal_title: Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act No. 2 of 1958
relevant_excerpt: means a rubber estate of not less than one hundred acres in extent which, under the Rubber Control Act is or is deemed to be an estate registered under that Act
why_relevant: Defines the term on which the consent requirement turns: for the purposes of the Act a rubber estate is one of not less than one hundred acres which is or is deemed to be registered under the Rubber Control Act. The notary must call for proof of extent and of registration status to decide whether a certificate of consent is needed at all.
temporal_note: The definition section was amended by Act No. 20 of 2005, before the matter date. The corpus text of section 25 runs the defined terms together without their headwords; the quoted words are the definition of rubber estate and the verifier should confirm this against the printed Act.
verifier_note: Definition-to-term pairing confirmed: the corpus defined_terms list for 2-1958/s25 runs coconut estate, local authority, partition action, rubber estate, tea estate, the Board, transfer of ownership in the same order as the run-together definitions in the body, so the quoted words are the definition of rubber estate.

formal_title: Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act No. 38 of 2014
relevant_excerpt: the transfer of title of any land situated in Sri Lanka, shall be prohibited if such transfer is- (a) to a foreigner; or (b) to a company incorporated in Sri Lanka under the Companies Act where any foreign shareholding in such company, either direct or indirect, is fifty per cent or above; or (c) to a foreign company, unless exempted as provided in section 3.
why_relevant: Prohibits the transfer of title of land to a company incorporated in Sri Lanka where direct or indirect foreign shareholding is fifty per cent or above. Because the purchaser is a private limited company, the notary must call for documents establishing the company's shareholding before the transfer can proceed.
temporal_note: Subsection (1) was not altered by the amending Acts No. 3 of 2017 or No. 21 of 2018; in force since 2014.

formal_title: Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act No. 38 of 2014
relevant_excerpt: Where the title of a land is transferred to a company incorporated in Sri Lanka under the Companies Act, with less than fifty per cent of foreign shareholding, it shall be the duty of the Registrar of Lands to confirm himself whether the foreign shareholding of such company is less than fifty per cent, by requiring the secretary of such company to submit documentary proof to the effect that the foreign shareholding of such company is less than fifty per cent of the total number of shares issued for the time being.
why_relevant: Names the document itself: where the transferee is a Sri Lankan company with less than fifty per cent foreign shareholding, the Registrar of Lands must require the company secretary to submit documentary proof of that fact. The notary must call for the secretary's certificate and the supporting share records in advance, or registration will be refused.
temporal_note: Not amended; in force since 2014.

formal_title: Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act No. 38 of 2014
subsection: definitions of foreigner and foreign company
relevant_excerpt: means a person who is not a citizen of Sri Lanka; means a company or a body of persons incorporated under the laws of any country other than Sri Lanka;
why_relevant: Defines foreigner and foreign company, the terms by which the shareholding of the purchaser company is measured.
temporal_note: In force since 2014. The corpus text of section 25 runs the defined terms together without their headwords; the verifier should confirm the pairing of definition to term against the printed Act.
verifier_note: Pairing confirmed the same way: the defined_terms order for 38-2014/s25 places foreigner and foreign company exactly where the two quoted definitions fall in the body.

relevant_excerpt: A company shall keep the following records available for inspection in the manner described in section 121 by any person who serves written notice of such intention to inspect on the company,:- (a) the certificate of incorporation of the company; (b) the articles of the company, if they are not the model articles; (c) the share register; (d) the register of directors and secretaries; (e) particulars of the registered office of the company; (f) copies of the instruments creating or evidencing charges and the register of charges kept under sections 109 and 110.
why_relevant: Identifies the corporate records that can be called for and inspected: the certificate of incorporation, the articles, the share register, the register of directors and secretaries and the register of charges. These are the documents from which the purchaser's capacity, its authorised signatories and its shareholding are established.
temporal_note: In force since 2007; not affected by the Companies (Amendment) Act, No. 13 of 2019.

relevant_excerpt: the maximum extent of agricultural land which may be owned by any person, in this Law referred to as the " ceiling ", shall (a) if such land consists exclusively of paddy land, be twenty-five acres; or (b) if such land does not consist exclusively of paddy land, be fifty acres, so however that the total extent of any paddy land, if any, comprised in such fifty acres shall not exceed the ceiling on paddy land specified in paragraph (a).
why_relevant: Fixes the ceiling on agricultural land at fifty acres where the land is not exclusively paddy. The notary must know the total agricultural landholding of the vendor and, after the transfer, of the purchaser's shareholders, so a declaration of agricultural landholdings is called for.
temporal_note: Amended by Law No. 39 of 1981, before the matter date.
verifier_note: Section 3(2) vests only land held in excess of the ceiling at the commencement of the Law; what makes the ceiling bite on a 2021 acquisition is section 5(1), which the map omitted and which is added as PROV-M052-902.

relevant_excerpt: For the purposes of this Law, where any agricultural land is owned by a private company or co-operative society, the shareholders of such company, or society, as the case may be, shall be deemed to own such land for the purposes of section 3, in proportion to the shares held by each shareholder of such company, or society, as the case may be.
why_relevant: Where agricultural land is owned by a private company, the shareholders are deemed to own it in proportion to their shares for ceiling purposes. This is why the shareholding of the purchaser company, and not only its corporate identity, has to be documented.
temporal_note: Not amended; in force since 1972.

relevant_excerpt: No instrument chargeable with stamp duty shall be received or admitted in evidence by any person having by law or consent of parties authority to receive evidence or registered or authenticated or acted upon by any person or by any officer in a public office or corporation or bank or approved credit agency unless such instrument is duly stamped.
why_relevant: An instrument chargeable with stamp duty cannot be registered, authenticated or acted upon unless duly stamped. Proof that stamp duty was paid on the deeds in the chain is among the documents called for.
temporal_note: Not amended; in force since 1982.
verifier_note: Checked against the Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act: section 13 of Act No. 12 of 2006 expressly carves out instruments relating to the transfer of immovable property, so section 33 of Act No. 43 of 1982 was still operative for this transaction in October 2021.

relevant_excerpt: of lands or immovable property, by a title adverse to or independent of that of the claimant or plaintiff in such action (that is to say, a possession unaccompanied by payment of rent or produce, or performance of service or duty, or by any other act by the possessor, from which an acknowledgment of a right existing in another person would fairly and naturally be inferred) for ten years previous to the bringing of such action, shall entitle the defendant to a decree in his favour with costs.
why_relevant: Ten years of undisturbed and uninterrupted adverse possession gives a good title against the paper owner. Documents alone therefore do not settle title: evidence of who has possessed the land, and of any adverse occupation, must also be called for.
temporal_note: The Prescription (Amendment) Act, No. 26 of 2014 did not alter the ten-year period in section 3; in force at the matter date.

relevant_excerpt: he shall obtain from the Registrar of the relevant Land Registry the certified extract of the folio containing the last entry pertaining to such land or immovable property containing the ownership and the registered encumbrances relating to such land or immovable property;
why_relevant: Recorded for the verifier as a temporal trap, not as authority. It expressly requires the notary to obtain a certified extract of the folio showing ownership and registered encumbrances, but it was inserted after the matter date and cannot be relied on for an October 2021 answer.
temporal_note: Inserted by the Notaries (Amendment) Act, No. 31 of 2022, s.16(10)(a) and further amended by Act No. 6 of 2024, both after the matter reference date of October 2021. Not available as authority at the matter date; the same practice is supported at the matter date by rule (17)(a) and by section 42 of the Registration of Documents Ordinance.
verifier_note: Temporal trap correctly recorded: the corpus amendment_events for 1-1907/s31 confirm insertions by Act No. 31 of 2022 and Act No. 6 of 2024, both after the matter date.

formal_title: Powers of Attorney Ordinance No. 4 of 1902
relevant_excerpt: Every power of attorney executed in Sri Lanka or any other country shall be registered with the Registrar General.
why_relevant: Recorded for the verifier as a temporal trap. If a deed in the chain was executed by an attorney, the power of attorney is a document to be called for, but the compulsory registration wording quoted here post-dates the matter.
temporal_note: Section 3 was repealed and substituted by the Powers of Attorney (Amendment) Act, No. 28 of 2022, after the matter reference date. The corpus does not carry the pre-2022 text of section 3, so the position in October 2021 cannot be established from this corpus.
verifier_note: Correctly excluded on temporal grounds, but rule (30) of section 31 of the Notaries Ordinance (preserve a true copy of the power of attorney with the protocol and forward a copy to the Registrar of Lands) supplies at-matter-date authority for calling for a power of attorney, so the point is not wholly unsupported.

relevant_excerpt: Provided that if the parties to the transaction authorize the notary in writing to dispense with the search, the search shall not be compulsory, but he shall before the deed or instrument is tendered for registration write at the head thereof the reference to the previous registration, if any.
why_relevant: Added by the verifier. The search duty in rule (17)(a) on which the whole document list rests is not absolute: the parties may authorise the notary in writing to dispense with the search, in which case the notary must still write the reference to the previous registration at the head of the deed before it is tendered for registration. A statement of the search duty without this proviso overstates the rule.
temporal_note: The proviso closes rule (17) in the corpus text of section 31 consolidated to 2024. The corpus amendment_events for section 31 record the 2022 and 2024 changes against the surrounding rules and paragraphs, not against this proviso, which is long-standing and was in force in October 2021.
verifier_note: Excerpt checked verbatim against 1-1907/s31; added because the map cited rule (17)(a) without its qualifying proviso.

relevant_excerpt: Where after the date of commencement of this Law any person becomes the owner of agricultural land in excess of the ceiling, any such land owned by such person in excess of the ceiling shall as from that date- (a) be deemed to vest in the Commission; and (b) be deemed to be held by that person under a statutory lease from the Commission.
why_relevant: Added by the verifier. Section 3(2) vests only the excess held at the commencement of the Law in 1972; section 5(1) is what makes the fifty-acre ceiling operate against a person who becomes an owner afterwards. It is the provision that makes a declaration of the agricultural landholdings of the vendor and of the purchaser shareholders worth calling for in a 2021 purchase; without it the Land Reform Law limb of the answer does not connect to the facts.
temporal_note: The corpus records amendments to section 5 by Law No. 39 of 1981 s.3 and Act No. 14 of 1986 s.2, both well before the matter reference date of October 2021; subsection (2), which the quoted text does not rely on, carries the later wording.
verifier_note: Excerpt checked verbatim against 1-1972/s5; added to close the gap between the ceiling in section 3 and a post-1972 acquisition.

formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
relevant_excerpt: No land parcel, title to which has been registered under this Act, or any interest therein shall be transferred or dealt with except in accordance with the provisions of this Act, and every disposition otherwise effected shall be void.
why_relevant: The gate for the whole question. Because the land is registered under the Act, any gift of it, or of an interest in it, is valid only if it complies with the Act, and any other form of disposition is void. This is what turns the registrability rules in sections 46, 47 and 48 into conditions of validity rather than mere registry practice.
temporal_note: In force from 1998 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded, so the text is treated as in force at 2021-10. The corpus edition is flagged original_or_unconfirmed_consolidation.

formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
relevant_excerpt: The Registrar of Title shall not register any instrument which purports to convey any title or interest to a land parcel on the happening of any event, or the fulfilment of any condition at any future time: Provided however, that a conveyance of title subject to life interest shall be acceptable for registration.
why_relevant: Answers the life-interest half of the question directly. A gift that reserves a life interest to the donor postpones the donees' full enjoyment, which would otherwise run into the bar on instruments conveying title on a future event or condition; the express proviso saves it and makes a conveyance subject to a life interest registrable.
temporal_note: In force from 1998 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded, so the text is treated as in force at 2021-10.

formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
relevant_excerpt: an instrument pertaining to the ownership of a land parcel registered under this Act, made in favour of two or more persons in common shall be void and shall not be registered under this Act.
why_relevant: Answers the two-donees half of the question directly. A single deed of gift of one registered land parcel to two daughters in common is an instrument in favour of two or more persons in common, so it is void and unregistrable. The opening words, 'Except in accordance with the provisions of this Act', are what leave the sub-division route in sections 36 and 47 open.
temporal_note: In force from 1998 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded, so the text is treated as in force at 2021-10.
verifier_note: Wording confirmed verbatim, but the excerpt begins mid-sentence and drops the operative opening qualifier 'Except in accordance with the provisions of this Act,' on which the why_relevant relies; I checked that qualifier and it opens no route here, because the only co-ownership the Act itself creates arises from a declaration of the Commissioner of Title Settlement under section 14(d) on initial registration (sections 15 and 16), not from an instrument between parties.

formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
relevant_excerpt: No part of a land parcel registered with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership or a Second Class Title of Ownership under the provisions of this Act shall be transferred or otherwise dealt with unless the registered owner has first sub-divided such land parcel and the land parcel so subdivided has been registered under the provisions of this Act.
why_relevant: Closes the obvious workaround of gifting a divided half to each daughter out of the existing parcel. No part of the registered parcel may be dealt with until the owner has sub-divided it and the sub-divided parcels are themselves registered, so sub-division must precede the gifts.
temporal_note: In force from 1998 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded, so the text is treated as in force at 2021-10.

formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
relevant_excerpt: Any owner or owners of any land parcel or land parcels whose title to which has been registered under this Act, may amalgamate or sub-divide his or their land parcel by registering a plan of redivision or amalgamation or sub-division relating to such land parcels in accordance with the provisions of this Act.
why_relevant: Supplies the only route by which the donor's wish can be carried out. As registered owner he may sub-divide the parcel by registering a sub-division plan, after which each resulting land parcel is a separate unit of record that can be gifted to one daughter without offending the co-ownership bar.
temporal_note: In force from 1998 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded, so the text is treated as in force at 2021-10.

formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
relevant_excerpt: means a document having the effect of conveying title to and interest in any land parcel in the prescribed form, means an interest Jess than full ownership of the land parcel and includes any Servitudes or encumbrance over such land parcel
why_relevant: Defines the two terms the answer turns on. A deed of gift is an 'instrument', a document having the effect of conveying title to and interest in a land parcel in the prescribed form, which is what brings it within sections 43, 46 and 48; and a reserved life interest is an 'interest in land parcel', an interest less than full ownership, which is what makes it a registrable interest rather than a bare condition.
temporal_note: In force from 1998 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded. The corpus body of section 75 has lost the defined-term labels, so the excerpt reads as two run-on definitions; on the face of the Act these are the definitions of 'instrument' and of 'interest in land parcel', both listed in the corpus defined_terms for this section.
verifier_note: The quoted text is verbatim, but the corpus body of section 75 has lost the defined-term labels and carries an OCR error ('Jess' for 'less'), so the excerpt is two run-on definitions; that the first is 'instrument' and the second 'interest in land parcel' follows from the section's recorded defined_terms order and from the use of 'instrument' in sections 43, 46 and 48, and is an inference from the corpus rather than something the corpus text states.

formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
relevant_excerpt: Every instrument conveying title or any interest in a land parcel presented for registration under this Act shall be effected in the form prescribed for that purpose. (2) Instruments prepared under the provisions of subsection (1) shall be signed by the parties to the transaction and two witnesses and attested by a Notary Public
why_relevant: Fixes the form the deeds of gift must take: the prescribed form, signed by the parties and two witnesses and attested by a Notary Public. Goes to how the donor's wish is executed rather than to whether it can be achieved.
temporal_note: In force from 1998 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded. The prescribed form itself is made by regulation under section 67 and is not in the corpus.

formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
relevant_excerpt: An instrument pertaining to land executed in accordance with the provisions of this Act shall take effect on registration, of such instrument under the provisions of this Act.
why_relevant: Timing rule: each deed of gift operates only when it is registered, not on execution or delivery, so the donor's wish is not fulfilled until registration is effected.
temporal_note: In force from 1998 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded.

formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
relevant_excerpt: No person acquiring an interest in any land parcel registered under the provisions of this Act shall be entitled to such title or interest unless such title or interest is registered under the provisions of this Act.
why_relevant: Makes the same point from the donees' side: neither daughter is entitled to anything until her title is registered, and the donor's reserved life interest likewise has to appear on the register.
temporal_note: In force from 1998 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded.

formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
relevant_excerpt: If the Registrar of Title is of the opinion that all requirements for registration under this Act are complied with, he shall register such title or interest in the prescribed manner
why_relevant: Shows registration is not automatic: the Registrar registers only if satisfied that the requirements of the Act are met, which is the practical checkpoint at which a single gift to two donees in common would be refused.
temporal_note: In force from 1998 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded.

formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
relevant_excerpt: The unit of record in a Title Register maintained under section 3 shall be a land parcel shown on the cadastral map.
why_relevant: Background: explains why the Act deals in whole parcels, and hence why undivided shares and part-parcel dealings are resisted throughout the Act.
temporal_note: In force from 1998 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded.

formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
relevant_excerpt: The provisions of this Act shall have effect notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any other written law
why_relevant: Background: forecloses an argument that the general law of gifts and notarial execution lets the donor do what this Act forbids. Where the two conflict, this Act prevails.
temporal_note: In force from 1998 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded.

formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
relevant_excerpt: Any provision of a will that makes a person owner of an undivided share or of a divided share smaller in extent than the prescribed minimum extent of a land parcel that may be registered under this Act shall have no legal effect.
why_relevant: Background: the same policy applied to testamentary disposition, confirming that the bar on creating undivided shares is a general feature of the Act and not confined to instruments inter vivos. It also warns that leaving the land by will would not achieve the donor's aim either.
temporal_note: In force from 1998 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded.

formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
relevant_excerpt: The Minister may by Notice published in the Gazette declare any area for which Registers of Title have, been compiled, as an area in which the principle of minimum economic units of land parcels shall apply.
why_relevant: Background caveat on the sub-division route: if the land lies in an area declared subject to the minimum economic unit principle, a sub-division leaving either resulting parcel below the prescribed extent may not be registrable.
temporal_note: In force from 1998 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded. Whether any notice covering this area has been published cannot be checked from the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: No sale, purchase, transfer, assignment, or mortgage of land or other immovable property, and no promise, bargain, contract, or agreement for effecting any such object, or for establishing any security, interest, or incumbrance affecting land or other immovable property (other than a lease at will, or for any period not exceeding one month)
why_relevant: Establishes that an agreement affecting immovable property, other than a lease at will or for a period not exceeding one month, has no force in law unless it is in writing and notarially attested. A four-year lease of the Colombo building therefore requires a notary at all.
temporal_note: The quoted opening words are the original enumeration and were not touched by the later amendments. The Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 30 of 2022 s.2 repealed only the words from "shall be of force" to the end of the section, and Act No. 4 of 2024 s.2 renumbered the section, replaced paragraphs (a) and (b) and added subsection (2). Both post-date the matter. The corpus carries the consolidated post-2024 text, so the execution formalities shown in the corpus body are not the text in force in October 2021, but the lease carve-out relied on here is.
verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim, but it stops at the lease carve-out and does not itself carry the operative words "shall be in force or avail in law unless ... attested by such notary" on which why_relevant and CL-M056-Q01-001 depend; those words are in the same section and, per 30-2022 s.2, the pre-2022 equivalent ("shall be of force ... unless ... in the presence of a licensed notary public and two or more witnesses ... duly attested") was in force at 2021-10, so the proposition holds - but the subsection label "(1)" is the post-2024 numbering inserted by 4-2024 s.2 and did not exist at the matter date.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument in any area other than that in which he is authorized to practice, nor in any language other than that in which he is authorized to practice nor authenticate or attest any deed or instrument drawn in any language other than that in which he is authorized to practice.
why_relevant: The only territorial and language limit on a notary's competence to attest. It restricts the area in which the notary may act and the language of the instrument; it says nothing about where the land affected by the instrument is situated.
temporal_note: Rule (22) is not among the rules substituted, inserted or repealed by the Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or by Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3, so the text shown is the text in force at 2021-10.

relevant_excerpt: If a deed or instrument other than a will or codicil affects a land situated in a district other than that in which the notary before whom it is signed, and by whom it is attested, 'shall reside, such notary, or in case such deed or instrument is attested by two or more notaries, then the notary upon whom is cast the duty of transmitting to the Registrar of Lands the duplicate of such deed or instrument, shall on or before the fifteenth day of the month next following that in which the same was executed (besides transmitting the duplicate in manner aforesaid) deliver or transmit to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which such land shall be situated a copy thereof certified by him as correct
why_relevant: Rule (29) expressly assumes that a notary may attest an instrument affecting land in a district other than the district in which he resides, and imposes the consequential duty to send a certified copy to the Registrar of Lands of the district where the land lies. It is the provision that answers the Galle notary and Colombo building point.
temporal_note: Rule (29) is not among the rules substituted, inserted or repealed by the Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or by Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3, so the text shown is the text in force at 2021-10.
verifier_note: Wording and role confirmed, but the temporal_note is wrong on one point: 6-2024 s.3(9) did amend rule (29), substituting "in the Form F 1" for "in the Form F"; that amendment falls outside the quoted excerpt, so the substance relied on was in force at 2021-10 and the conclusion is unaffected.

relevant_excerpt: Every warrant issued to a notary under the provisions of section 3* or section 4* authorizing him to practice as a notary in any judicial division in which he resides, shall be deemed to authorize him to practice as a notary in the judicial zone in which he resides.
why_relevant: Fixes the extent of the area in which a notary is authorized to practice for the purposes of rule (22): a warrant for a judicial division is deemed to authorise practice in the whole judicial zone in which the notary resides.
temporal_note: Inserted by the Notaries (Amendment) Law No. 20 of 1976 s.4 and in force from 1976, well before the matter date.

relevant_excerpt: Every notary shall be bound to have his office within the area specified in his warrant; and any notary infringing this provision shall be liable to have his warrant withdrawn by the Minister.
why_relevant: Confirms that the Ordinance regulates where the notary is based and acts rather than the location of the property dealt with, and supplies the sanction of withdrawal of the warrant for acting outside the warrant area.
temporal_note: In force from 1907 with no recorded amendment; the text shown applies at 2021-10.
verifier_note: Wording verified, but why_relevant overstates the section: s.9 requires the notary to have his office within the warrant area and makes withdrawal of the warrant the sanction for not doing so; it is not a sanction for attesting outside that area, which is rule (22) enforced through s.34. Role is supporting only.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument to which he is a party.
why_relevant: The only personal disqualification in section 31 that is in issue. Being the lessor's neighbour is not a statutory disqualification; only being a party to the instrument is.
temporal_note: Rule (13) is not among the rules amended by the Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or by Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3; the text shown applies at 2021-10.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument in any case in which the person executing or acknowledging the same shall be or profess to be unable to read the same, or in which such person shall require him to read over the same, unless and until he shall have read over and explained the same, or caused the same to be explained, in the presence and hearing of such person and, except in the case of wills and codicils, in the presence of the attesting witnesses.
why_relevant: Sudath Gunawardana is illiterate. Rule (11) shows that illiteracy of an executant does not bar attestation; it makes the reading over and explanation of the instrument, in the presence of the executant and the attesting witnesses, a condition of lawful attestation.
temporal_note: Rule (11) is not among the rules substituted by the Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or by Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3; the text shown applies at 2021-10.

relevant_excerpt: (1) It shall be the duty of every notary to endeavour to ascertain the true and full consideration for the execution of any deed, and to insert and set forth the same in such deed. (2) Any notary who shall knowingly and willfully insert or set forth in or upon any such deed any other than the full and true consideration or money directly or indirectly paid or secured, or agreed to be paid or secured for the same, or the actual value of the same, or shall abet the doing thereof, respectively, shall be guilty of an offence
why_relevant: The central provision for the request to understate the rental. Subsection (1) puts the notary under a positive duty to ascertain and set out the true and full consideration; subsection (2) makes knowingly inserting anything other than the full and true consideration, or abetting it, an offence with civil liability in addition.
temporal_note: Subsection (1) has stood since 1907. The Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.18 amended subsection (2) only by substituting the words "not exceeding fifty thousand rupees" for "not exceeding twenty five thousand rupees". The excerpt stops before the penalty words, so the quoted text was in force at 2021-10; the maximum fine at that date was twenty five thousand rupees, not the fifty thousand shown in the corpus body.
verifier_note: Temporal analysis checked against 31-2022 s.18, which substituted "not exceeding fifty thousand rupees" for "not exceeding twenty five thousand rupees" in subsection (2) only; the excerpt stops before the penalty words. 6-2024 s.4 inserted s.38A and did not touch s.38.

relevant_excerpt: shall knowingly and willfully, with intent to prejudice or defraud any person, insert in any deed or instrument whatsoever any word, letter, figure, matter, or thing which ought not to have been inserted therein, or omit to insert therein any word, letter, figure, matter, or thing which ought to have been inserted therein
why_relevant: Inserting a rental figure the notary knows to be false, with intent to defeat the revenue, falls within paragraph (b) and exposes him to the heavier penalty for fraud in the execution of his office, over and above the section 38 offence.
temporal_note: Paragraph (b) was not amended in 2022. The Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.19 amended paragraph (c) and substituted the closing penalty words, so that imprisonment "not exceeding five years" became ten years with a fine and compensation. The excerpt is confined to paragraph (b) and was in force at 2021-10; the penalty at that date was imprisonment not exceeding five years.
verifier_note: Temporal analysis checked against 31-2022 s.19, which amended paragraph (c) and the closing penalty words only; paragraph (b) is unchanged.

relevant_excerpt: (g) a bond or mortgage for any definite and certain sum of money and affecting any property; (h) a promissory note; (i) a lease or hire of any property;
why_relevant: Makes a lease a specified instrument, so the lease agreement is chargeable with stamp duty. Without it the stamp duty motive behind the parties' request has no statutory footing.
temporal_note: In force from 2006 with no recorded amendment; the text shown applies at 2021-10.
verifier_note: Verbatim and correct, though the excerpt also carries paragraphs (g) and (h) while the subsection field records only (i).

relevant_excerpt: in the case of a lease, by the lessee;
why_relevant: Identifies Kapila Warnakulasooriya as the person on whom the duty falls, absent agreement to the contrary, and so identifies who stands to be assessed if the instrument understates the rental.
temporal_note: Section 6 was amended by Act No. 10 of 2008; paragraph (c) stands in the consolidated text and applied at 2021-10.

relevant_excerpt: there shall be charged a duty (hereinafter to be called "stamp duty") at such rate as the Minister may determine by Order published in the Gazette on every "specified instrument"- (a) executed, drawn or presented in Sri Lanka;
why_relevant: The charging provision. It shows the duty is a rate applied to the instrument as executed in Sri Lanka, which is why the figure the notary writes into the lease determines the duty collected.
temporal_note: In force from 2006 with no recorded amendment; the text shown applies at 2021-10. The rate Order itself is not in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: Where an Assessor is of the opinion that an instrument liable to stamp duty has not been duly stamped, he shall assess the value of the stamp duty payable in respect of such instrument, by the person liable to pay such duty and forward a Notice to such person requiring him to pay the amount due thereon, within the time specified in the Notice.
why_relevant: Shows that understating the rental does not extinguish the duty: an Assessor may assess and recover the correct duty from the person liable, so the parties gain nothing lawful and the notary would have exposed himself for no purpose.
temporal_note: In force from 2006 with no recorded amendment; the text shown applies at 2021-10.

relevant_excerpt: the number and value of the adhesive stamps affixed to or the value of the impressed stamps on such deed or instrument and the duplicate thereof
why_relevant: The attestation itself must state the value of the stamps. A notary who writes a reduced rental into the lease will also certify a stamp value corresponding to the false figure, so the falsehood is carried into his own attestation.
temporal_note: The Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(11) altered paragraphs (b), (e) and (g) of rule (20) and added paragraph (h); paragraph (f) was not amended, so the text shown applies at 2021-10.
verifier_note: Checked against 31-2022 s.16(11), which altered paragraphs (b), (e) and (g) of rule (20) and added (h); paragraph (f) is unchanged.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless he has an assurance that the required stamp duty is provided.
why_relevant: Bars the notary from attesting at all unless satisfied that the required stamp duty is provided, which is what a deliberately understated rental defeats.
temporal_note: Rule (6) as shown was substituted by the Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(4), after the matter date, and the corpus does not hold the pre-2022 wording. Recorded as supporting context only; no claim relies on it. The verifier should confirm the rule (6) text in force in October 2021.
verifier_note: The rule (6) text in the corpus is the text substituted by 31-2022 s.16(4); the amending section does not reproduce the pre-2022 wording, so what rule (6) said in October 2021 cannot be established from the corpus. Correctly kept out of every claim.

relevant_excerpt: Every notary who acts in violation of or disregards or neglects to observe- (a) rules (1), (31) or (32) set out in section 31, shall be guilty of an offence, and shall, on conviction after summary trial before a Magistrate, be liable to a fine not exceeding five thousand rupees, in addition to any civil liability he may incur thereby
why_relevant: Shows the general scheme by which breaches of the section 31 rules are punished on summary trial before a Magistrate, in addition to civil liability.
temporal_note: Section 34 was repealed and wholly replaced by the Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.17, after the matter date, and the corpus holds only the replacement text. The fine bands shown are therefore not those in force in October 2021. Recorded as supporting context only; no claim relies on the amounts.
verifier_note: 31-2022 s.17 repealed and replaced the whole of s.34, and the corpus holds only the replacement, so the 2021 fine bands cannot be established from the corpus. Correctly kept out of every claim.

relevant_excerpt: has grossly misconducted himself in the discharge of the duties of his office; or (c) has so conducted himself by repeated breaches of any of the rules made by or under this Ordinance that he ought not to be any longer entrusted with the performance of the said duties
why_relevant: Supplies the professional, as distinct from criminal, liability: gross misconduct in the discharge of notarial duties is a ground for inquiry and for a report on which the Minister may suspend the notary or cancel his warrant.
temporal_note: The Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.11 amended only paragraph (e) of subsection (1), where "incompetence, age" became "incompetence", and the fine in subsection (4). Paragraphs (b) and (c) quoted here are unchanged and applied at 2021-10.
verifier_note: Paragraphs (b) and (c) are verbatim and, per 31-2022 s.11, unamended at 2021-10; but the excerpt carries only the grounds in subsection (1), not the Minister's power to suspend or cancel the warrant that why_relevant and CL-M056-Q04-008 rely on, which is in s.21(2) of the same section and is unamended.

relevant_excerpt: shall by any other willful act, either of commission or omission, commit or attempt to commit any fraud in the execution of his office
why_relevant: Added by the verifier. Paragraph (b), on which the researcher relies, requires an intent to prejudice or defraud "any person", and the Ordinance does not define "person"; whether the revenue is such a person is an open reading. Paragraph (f) catches any wilful act or omission by which the notary commits or attempts to commit a fraud in the execution of his office and reaches the same conduct without that reading, so it secures the section 39 limb of the answer.
temporal_note: Paragraph (f) was not amended by 31-2022 s.19, which touched only paragraph (c) and the closing penalty words, nor by any later Act in the corpus; the text shown applied at 2021-10. As with paragraph (b), the penalty at that date was imprisonment not exceeding five years, the excerpt stopping before the penalty words.
verifier_note: Excerpt checked verbatim against 1-1907/s39 by the verifier.

relevant_excerpt: If any person shall act as a notary without having obtained such certificate as aforesaid, he shall for or in respect of every deed executed or acknowledged before him as such notary, whilst he shall have been without such certificate, be guilty of an offence and be liable to a fine not less than five thousand rupees and not exceeding twenty five thousand rupees.
why_relevant: This is the operative penal provision. It makes acting as a notary without the yearly certificate an offence, and it makes the offence bite in respect of every deed executed or acknowledged before the notary while he was uncertificated, which is exactly the lease Kamal Ratnayake attested.
temporal_note: In force from 1907. The only recorded change is the fine increase by the Increase of Fines Act No. 12 of 2005, which is in force well before 2021-10; the Rs. 5,000 to Rs. 25,000 range therefore applies at the matter date.
verifier_note: Wording verified verbatim against 1-1907/s30 and the Rs. 5,000-25,000 range does apply at 2021-10, but the temporal note misattributes the increase: Increase of Fines Act No. 12 of 2005 s.5 is the Sinhala-text clause, the operative amending provision being s.2 read with the Schedules; s.30 carries no post-2021 amendment event, so the corpus text is the as-at-matter-date text.

relevant_excerpt: All such certificates shall be applied for and granted on or before the first day of April in every year, and shall be in force for one year and no longer: Provided, however, that if such certificate shall not be applied for within the time limited, and it shall be shown to the satisfaction of the High Court Judge that the delay was due to accident, misfortune or other unavoidable cause, the High Court Judge may direct the Registrar to issue the required certificate notwithstanding such delay as aforesaid.
why_relevant: Section 30 punishes acting without "such certificate as aforesaid"; s.27 is what that phrase refers to. It creates the yearly certificate issued by the Registrar of the High Court of the zone, fixes the annual application deadline, limits the certificate to one year, and supplies the only statutory relief for a notary who missed the deadline through accident, misfortune or other unavoidable cause.
temporal_note: In force from 1907. Subsection (3) was substituted by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 13 of 2013 s.2 (before the matter date). Subsection (2) was later amended by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.14, which substituted "April" for "March"; that change post-dates 2021-10, so at the matter date the deadline was the first day of March. The excerpt is taken from the consolidated corpus text and so shows "April". Nothing in the answer turns on which month it was: the notary obtained no certificate at all for the year.
verifier_note: Excerpt verified verbatim, but it reproduces the post-matter wording: 31-2022 s.14 substituted "April" for "March" in subsection (2), so at 2021-10 the deadline read the first day of March, and the corpus holds no as-at-2021 snapshot; the excerpt also covers subsection (2) only, while claim CL-M057-Q01-001 additionally rests on the subsection (1) duty of the Registrar of the High Court to issue the certificate.

relevant_excerpt: the Registrar-General may, if he thinks fit, instead of instituting criminal proceedings against such notary, accept from him such sum of money as he may consider proper in composition of the offence
why_relevant: Section 35(1) names s.30 among the compoundable offences, so the liability is not necessarily a prosecution: the Registrar-General may accept a sum in composition, after which criminal proceedings shall not be taken or continued. It qualifies how the s.30 liability may be discharged.
temporal_note: In force from 1907 with no recorded amendment events, so the text applies unchanged at 2021-10.

relevant_excerpt: Where the report is to the effect that the notary has been guilty of any such offence or misconduct as is mentioned in clauses (a), (b), (c), or (d) of the last preceding subsection, the Minister may cancel the warrant of such notary, or may suspend him from office for such period as may appear just.
why_relevant: Beyond the fine, an offence committed in the capacity of a notary opens the disciplinary route: on a report by the High Court Judge after inquiry under s.21(1), the Minister may cancel the warrant or suspend the notary. This is a possible further liability, not an automatic one, so it is supporting rather than indispensable.
temporal_note: In force from 1907. Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.11 substituted parts of the section after the matter date; the subsection (2) power to cancel or suspend relied on here is long-standing, but a verifier should confirm the 2022 substitution did not touch the quoted words before treating the excerpt as the as-at-2021 text. Marked supporting for that reason.
verifier_note: Verifier resolved the researcher's open point: 31-2022 s.11 amends only s.21(1)(e) ("incompetence, age" to "incompetence") and s.21(4) (fine), so the quoted subsection (2) is unchanged as-at-2021 text; the supporting rather than indispensable role is nonetheless correct, since s.21(2) bites only on a High Court Judge's report under s.21(1).

formal_title: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance No. 7 of 1840
relevant_excerpt: no promise, bargain, contract, or agreement for effecting any such object, or for establishing any security, interest, or incumbrance affecting land or other immovable property (other than a lease at will, or for any period not exceeding one month)
why_relevant: A lease of a commercial building for four years falls outside the carve-out for leases at will or for periods not exceeding one month, so it had to be executed before and attested by a notary. That is why Kamal Ratnayake was acting in his capacity as a notary when he attested it, which is the condition s.30 attaches its per-deed penalty to.
temporal_note: The requirement of notarial execution for leases exceeding one month dates from 1840. The corpus text is consolidated and carries amendments by Act No. 30 of 2022 and Act No. 4 of 2024, both after the matter date; only the carve-out wording, which predates them, is relied on. Kept supporting rather than indispensable for that reason.
verifier_note: Excerpt verified verbatim and the carve-out survives untouched at the matter date (30-2022 s.2 repealed only the words from "shall be of force" onward; 4-2024 s.2 edited paragraphs (a) and (b)), but the recorded subsection "1" is anachronistic: the renumbering of s.2 as subsection (1) was made by 4-2024 s.2, so at 2021-10 s.2 was undivided.

relevant_excerpt: If any person shall practice or act as or exercise the office or functions of a notary without having obtained such warrant as aforesaid, or without having made and signed such declaration and given such bond as aforesaid, or without having filed an attested copy of his warrant, every such person shall be guilty of an offence
why_relevant: Recorded to mark the boundary of the answer. Section 13 is the heavier offence of practising without a warrant, declaration, bond or filed copy of the warrant. Kamal Ratnayake holds a warrant and is missing only the yearly certificate, so s.13 does not apply and s.30 is the correct penal provision. Context only.
temporal_note: In force from 1907; fine increased by Act No. 12 of 2005 and the section substituted in part by Act No. 31 of 2022 after the matter date. Nothing turns on the text because the section is recorded only as an excluded alternative.
verifier_note: Excerpt verified verbatim against the consolidated text but is post-matter wording: 31-2022 s.4 substituted "given such bond" for "given such bond and security", so at 2021-10 s.13 read "given such bond and security as aforesaid"; nothing turns on it because s.13 is recorded only as an excluded alternative.

relevant_excerpt: there shall be charged a duty (hereinafter to be called "stamp duty") at such rate as the Minister may determine by Order published in the Gazette on every "specified instrument"- (a) executed, drawn or presented in Sri Lanka
