why_relevant: This is the charging section for the stamp duty payable on a mortgage bond executed in Sri Lanka in 2021. It also shows why the calculation cannot be completed on the corpus alone: the rate is not in the Act but in a Ministerial Order published in the Gazette, which is not in the corpus.
temporal_note: In force from 2006, no amendment event recorded on this section; in force at 2021-10. The rate Order made under it may have been varied before October 2021, and the corpus does not record those Orders.

relevant_excerpt: (g) a bond or mortgage for any definite and certain sum of money and affecting any property;
why_relevant: Defines 'specified instrument' for section 3 and brings a mortgage bond for a definite sum, affecting the Rajagiriya land, within the charge. Without this paragraph the charging section does not reach the instrument at all.
temporal_note: In force from 2006, no amendment event recorded on this section; in force at 2021-10.

relevant_excerpt: (e) in all other cases, by the person drawing, making or executing such instrument.
why_relevant: A mortgage is not one of the listed cases in paragraphs (a) to (ddd), so the residual paragraph (e) applies and the duty falls on the mortgagor who executes the bond, subject to any agreement to the contrary with the lender.
temporal_note: Section 6 was amended by Act No. 10 of 2008, before the matter date; the consolidated text in the corpus is the text in force at 2021-10.

relevant_excerpt: Stamp duty payable on any specified instrument relating to a mortgage or lease of any immovable property may be paid, prior to, or at the time of, the execution of the specified instrument, to a prescribed bank.
why_relevant: Sets the manner and time of payment for a mortgage of immovable property: payment to a prescribed bank before or at execution, with a bank certificate affixed to the instrument. Relevant to how the calculated sum would be paid, not to the amount.
temporal_note: Section 8 was substituted by Act No. 10 of 2008, before the matter date; the consolidated text in the corpus is the text in force at 2021-10.

relevant_excerpt: the Minister may from time to time by Order published in the Gazette specify the instruments, which shall be exempt from the payment of stamp duty.
why_relevant: Exemptions are also left to Gazette Order. Whether a mortgage bond securing a housing loan from the National Savings Bank was exempt or concessionary in October 2021 therefore cannot be settled on the corpus, which is a second reason the figure cannot be produced.
temporal_note: In force from 2006, no amendment event recorded; in force at 2021-10. The exemption Orders themselves are not in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: the provisions of the Stamp Duty Act, No. 43 of 1982, relating to the Imposition of Stamp Duty (other than any instrument relating to the transfer of immovable property, the transfer of motor vehicles or documents filed in Court), Exemptions and any other provision in the aforesaid Act, shall, in so far as the same are inconsistent with the provisions of this Act, have no operation
why_relevant: Explains why the 1982 Act is not the operative charging regime for a mortgage bond in 2021. The carve-out preserves the 1982 Act only for transfers of immovable property, motor vehicle transfers and court documents, none of which is a mortgage.
temporal_note: In force from 2006, no amendment event recorded; in force at 2021-10.

relevant_excerpt: All stamp duty payable to a Provincial Council in respect of documents and instruments referred to in List I of the Ninth Schedule to the Constitution, shall be paid to the respective Provincial Council within whose limits the instrument was executed or the property situated as the case may be
why_relevant: Directs where duty is paid when the instrument falls within the provincial list. Recorded because the land is at Rajagiriya, in the Western Province, so a verifier will want to know whether the provincial or the central regime collects the duty on this bond.
temporal_note: In force from 2006, no amendment event recorded; in force at 2021-10.

relevant_excerpt: There shall be charged on- (a) every instrument relating to a transfer of situated in the immovable property Western Province; (b) every document presented or filed, in proceedings instituted in any Court of law established by law, in the Western Province of Sri Lanka; (c) every transfer of a motor vehicle effected in Western Province. a stamp duty at the prescribed rate.
why_relevant: The Western Province charging provision reaches only transfers of immovable property, court documents and motor vehicle transfers. A mortgage bond is none of these, so the provincial statute does not charge this instrument and the central Act of 2006 governs. The provincial rate is likewise only 'the prescribed rate' and is not in the corpus.
temporal_note: In force from 1990, no amendment event recorded on this section; in force at 2021-10.

relevant_excerpt: A bond or mortgage for the payment or repayment of money to be lent, advanced, or paid shall be charged, where the total amount secured or to be ultimately recoverable is in any way limited, with the same stamp duty as on a bond or mortgage for the amount so limited.
why_relevant: Background only. It shows the classical base of assessment for a mortgage, the amount secured rather than the value of the land, which is why the Rs.14,000,000 purchase price of the Rajagiriya land is not the base. Its operative force in 2021 is displaced by s.13 of the 2006 Act so far as it is inconsistent, and the Schedule of rates it depends on is not in the corpus.
temporal_note: In force from 1982. Its imposition provisions are displaced for mortgages by Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.13 from 2006, so it is not treated as an operative rule at 2021-10.

relevant_excerpt: Where at the time of the execution of a mortgage bond in favour of a lending institution for the payment of a loan, the principal of which exceeds one hundred and fifty thousand rupees the mortgagor executes a separate instrument, attested by the notary attesting the bond and by the witnesses to the bond containing- (a) a special declaration on the part of the mortgagor that he renounces the benefit of section 46 and that the effect of such renunciation has been explained to him by the notary
why_relevant: This is the provision the Bank's requested declaration is executed under. It is the only route by which a mortgagor's property other than the mortgaged land can be made liable under a decree on the mortgage: a separate instrument, executed at the time of the bond, containing a special declaration renouncing the benefit of section 46. It also sets the two gateway conditions - a lending institution as mortgagee and a loan principal exceeding Rs.150,000.
temporal_note: Inserted by Act No. 3 of 1990 and in force from 1990; no later amendment event is recorded on this section in the corpus. It is therefore in force at the matter reference date of October 2021. Subsection (6) excludes mortgages created before the section came into force, which does not affect a mortgage to be created in 2021.

relevant_excerpt: No decree in any hypothecary action upon any mortgage of land which is created after the coming into force of this section, and no decree in any action for the recovery of any moneys due upon any such mortgage, shall order any property, whatsoever, other than the mortgaged property to be sold for the recovery of any money found to be due under the mortgage, and no property whatsoever, other than the mortgaged property, shall be sold or be liable to be sold in execution of any such decree.
why_relevant: This is the benefit that the s.47A declaration renounces, and it explains the Bank's motive. Without a renunciation the Bank's recovery on a decree is confined to the mortgaged Rajagiriya land; if that land realises less than the debt, the shortfall cannot be recovered against the mortgagor's other property.
temporal_note: Substituted by Act No. 3 of 1990; latest recorded change 1990, so the substituted text is the text in force at October 2021.

relevant_excerpt: For the purpose of this section 'lending institution' means- (a) a licensed Commercial Bank within the meaning of the Banking Act, No.30 of 1988; (b) the State Mortgage and Investment Bank established by the State Mortgage and Investment Bank Act, No. 13 of 1975; (c) the National Development Bank established by the National Development Bank of Sri Lanka Act, No. 2 of 1979; (d) the National Savings Bank established by the National Savings Bank Act, No. 30 of 1971;
why_relevant: Section 47A is available only to a 'lending institution' as defined here. Paragraph (d) names the National Savings Bank expressly, so the mortgagee in this scenario falls squarely within the definition and the section is capable of applying to the proposed bond.
temporal_note: Part of s.47A as inserted in 1990; no later amendment event recorded. The footnote reference to section 2 of Act No. 23 of 1997 in paragraph (e) concerns the DFCC Bank only and does not bear on paragraph (d).

relevant_excerpt: then, in addition to the mortgaged property, any other property belonging to the mortgagor shall, subject To the provisions of subsection(2), be liable to be ordered to be sold and to be sold under the decree in an action upon the mortgage, and the provisions of section 218 of the Civil Procedure Code (Chapter 101) shall, mutatis mutandis, apply to the seizure and sale of such other property.
why_relevant: States the consequence the Bank is buying with the declaration: property of the mortgagor beyond the mortgaged land becomes liable to be ordered sold under the decree, with Civil Procedure Code s.218 applied to the seizure and sale.
temporal_note: Same insertion by Act No. 3 of 1990; in force at October 2021. The corpus text reproduces the printed capitalisation 'subject To' and the unspaced 'subsection(2)'.

relevant_excerpt: no process shall issue for the seizure and sale of any property of the mortgagor, other than the mortgaged property, until the mortgaged property is sold and the proceeds thereof applied in satisfaction of the decree.
why_relevant: Qualifies the extended remedy: the Bank must first sell the mortgaged land and apply the proceeds before touching other property. It confirms that the declaration is a shortfall-recovery device rather than a free choice of assets, which is why the Bank wants it at the outset.
temporal_note: Same insertion by Act No. 3 of 1990; in force at October 2021.

relevant_excerpt: it shall be the duty of the notary to explain to the mortgagor, that the instrument provides for the renunciation of the benefit of section 46 and that the effect of such renunciation is that, in addition to the mortgaged property, other property of the mortgagor is liable to be sold in execution of a decree in an action upon the mortgage.
why_relevant: Explains why the Bank asks for a separate signed instrument attested and endorsed by the notary rather than a clause buried in the bond: the renunciation is only effective if the notary has explained it and endorsed that fact, so the formality is what makes the Bank's extended remedy secure.
temporal_note: Same insertion by Act No. 3 of 1990; in force at October 2021.

relevant_excerpt: The provisions of section 46 shall have effect notwithstanding anything in any other law or in any mortgage bond or other instrument.
why_relevant: Shows that the section 46 restriction cannot be contracted out of by a term in the bond itself, which is why the Bank must use the specific statutory mechanism of a separate s.47A instrument instead of simply drafting a wider recovery clause into the mortgage bond.
temporal_note: In force from 1949 with no recorded later change; in force at October 2021.

relevant_excerpt: the judgment-creditor has the power to seize, and to sell or realize in money by the hands of the Fiscal, except as hereinafter mentioned, all saleable property, movable or immovable, belonging to the judgment-debtor
why_relevant: Background only: the machinery that s.47A(1) applies mutatis mutandis to the seizure and sale of the mortgagor's other property once the benefit of s.46 has been renounced, together with the protected categories in its proviso.
temporal_note: In force from 1889, latest recorded change 1977; in force at October 2021.
verifier_note: Excerpt and background role confirmed, but it stops before the proviso to section 218, which exempts listed property from seizure and sale - including, under paragraph (n), an unmortgaged house that is the judgment-debtor's actual residence - so the extended remedy the declaration unlocks does not reach every asset of the mortgagor.

relevant_excerpt: (b) an endorsement signed by the notary to the effect that he has explained to the mortgagor the effect of such renunciation
why_relevant: Added by the verifier. The separate instrument is effective only if it contains both the mortgagor's declaration in paragraph (a) and the notary's signed endorsement in paragraph (b). The researcher's excerpt for PROV-M059-001 stops at the end of paragraph (a), yet claim CL-M059-Q01-003 and the rule part of the gold answer both assert the endorsement requirement, so it needed its own cited text.
temporal_note: Part of section 47A as inserted by Act No. 3 of 1990; no later amendment event is recorded on the section in the corpus, so it is in force at October 2021.

relevant_excerpt: Save as aforesaid, this Ordinance shall not apply to Kandyans or Muslims, or to Tamils of the Northern Province who are or may become subject to the Tesawalamai.
why_relevant: Fixes the scope of the general law of intestate succession relied on throughout. The devolution proposed here holds only if none of the deceased persons was governed by Kandyan law, Muslim law or the Thesawalamai; the background gives no facts either way, and the answer states that assumption.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus. In force at 2020-10 and at every death in the scenario (2007, 2009, 2012, 2015).

relevant_excerpt: includes land, incorporeal tenements, and things attached to the earth or permanently fastened to anything which is attached to the earth, and any interest in land except that of a mortgagee
why_relevant: Defines "immovable property" for the Ordinance. Lot A with the house at Assessment No.12 is land with a building attached to it, so the inheritance rules in s.21 onwards, not the movable-property conflict rule, govern its devolution.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.
verifier_note: Wording is verbatim, but the corpus body of s.3 has lost the defined-term labels, so the excerpt does not itself say which term it defines; the link to "immovable property" is confirmed only by the corpus definition index (defs 15-1876 "immovable property" and edges 15-1876/s21 both return 15-1876/s3), and the provision is supporting rather than decisive.

relevant_excerpt: The following sections of this Ordinance shall apply to the estates of such persons only as shall die after the proclamation of this Ordinance
why_relevant: Temporal gate on Part III. Every death in the scenario (2007, 2009, 2012, 2015) is long after the proclamation of the Ordinance, so the inheritance sections apply to each estate.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.
verifier_note: The excerpt stops before the second condition in s.20, that the deceased must have been unmarried at death or, if married, married after the proclamation of the Ordinance; the condition is satisfied on these facts but the temporal note should say so rather than resting on the date of death alone.

relevant_excerpt: Inheritance ab interstate to the immovable property in Sri Lanka of a person deceased shall be governed and regulated by the following provisions of this Ordinance wherever such person may have or have had his actual or matrimonial domicile.
why_relevant: Makes the Ordinance the governing law for intestate succession to Lot A, immovable property in Sri Lanka, for each of the three intestacies in the chain.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: When any person shall die intestate as to any of his or her property, leaving a spouse surviving, the surviving spouse shall inherit one-half of the property of such person.
why_relevant: Gives Lochana one-half of Dinesh's estate on 23 November 2009 and Rohan Jayaweera one-half of Neesha's estate on 20 May 2012. Removing it changes both the pedigree and every share.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: Subject to the right of the surviving spouse in the preceding section mentioned, the right of inheritance is divided in the following order as respects (a) descendants, (b) ascendants, (c) collaterals.
why_relevant: Sets the order in which the half not taken by the surviving spouse is distributed, and confirms that the spouse's half is carved out first. It is the link between s.22 and ss.24 to 29.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: Children, grandchildren, and remoter descendants are preferent to all others in the estate of the parents; all the children take equally per capita, but the children or remoter issue of a deceased child take per stirpes or by representation.
why_relevant: Divides the other half of Dinesh's estate equally among his four surviving children (Neesha, Kasun, Kavindu and Piyumi), and excludes his brother Iresh and any ascendant. Neesha, a child of the first marriage, takes on the same footing as the children of the second marriage.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: if only one of the parents be alive, the surviving parent takes half, and the brothers and sisters of the deceased of the full blood, and the issue of any deceased brother or sister of the full blood, by representation, and the brothers and sisters of the half-blood who are related to the intestate by the side of the deceased parent, and the issue of any such deceased brother or sister of the half-blood, by representation, take the other half.
why_relevant: Governs Kasun's estate on 5 July 2015: he died unmarried and issueless, his father Dinesh had predeceased him and his mother Lochana survived, so Lochana takes half of his share and his full brother and sister, Kavindu and Piyumi, take the other half.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.
verifier_note: Wording and role for Kasun's 2015 intestacy are confirmed, but the excerpt omits the closing sentence of s.25 ("In case there is no full or half-brother or sister alive at the death of the deceased, the surviving parent inherits the whole"), which is the exception that has to be checked before the half/half split is applied and which is not triggered here because Kavindu and Piyumi survived.

relevant_excerpt: Father and mother both failing, the property of the intestate goes to his brothers and sisters, whether of the whole or balf-blood, and their children and other issue by representation.
why_relevant: Governs Neesha's estate on 20 May 2012: she left no descendants and both her parents had predeceased her (Dinesh in 2009, Nimali in 2010), so the collateral half of her share passes to her half-blood brothers and sister.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus. The corpus text spells half-blood as "balf-blood", an artefact of the source scan; the excerpt is reproduced as it stands in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: In case all the half-brothers and sisters, their children and remoter issue, are related to the intestate on one side only, they take the whole of the inheritance, unless there be a grandfather or grandmother or higher ascendant yet alive, related to the intestate on the other side
why_relevant: Neesha's only collaterals were half-siblings on her father's side. This section lets them take the whole of the collateral portion rather than the divided share that s.27 and s.28 would produce, subject to the proviso about a surviving ascendant on the mother's side, on which the background is silent.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.
verifier_note: Wording is verbatim and the section is correctly reached, but the excerpt stops before the operative consequence of the proviso ("take one-half only, and the next ascendants per capita the other half"), and the corpus supplies no fact about whether a maternal grandparent or higher maternal ascendant of Neesha Gamage was alive on 20 May 2012, so the whole-taking result is an assumption rather than a verified outcome.

relevant_excerpt: if all those who succeed to the inheritance are equally near in degree to the intestate, they take per capita, and not per stirpes.
why_relevant: Confirms equal per capita division among the four children of Dinesh, among Neesha's three half-siblings, and between Kasun's two full siblings, since in each case the takers are equally near in degree.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.
verifier_note: The excerpt omits the opening words "Except when otherwise expressly provided", which matter because ss.24 and 25 do expressly provide for the mode of division in two of the three steps where s.30 is invoked; s.30 is therefore confirmatory rather than the operative rule for those steps.

relevant_excerpt: shall be in force or avail in law unless - (a) the relevant deed or instrument shall be in writing, signed by every executant
why_relevant: Background only: it explains why the transfer of Lot A to Dinesh had to be, and was, effected by a notarially attested deed (Deed of Gift No.1100 attested by Asanka Silva, Notary Public). It does not decide any share.
temporal_note: In force from 1840; the corpus records amendment events in 1947, 2022 and 2024. The text shown is the consolidated text including changes made after the deed was executed in 2006, so it is used for background only and is not relied on as the operative text at the date of the deed.
verifier_note: The section is real and the excerpt verbatim, but the corpus holds only the consolidated text carrying amendment events of 1947, 2022 and 2024, not the version in force when Deed of Gift No.1100 was executed on 12 January 2006; and s.2(1) enumerates sale, purchase, transfer, assignment and mortgage without naming a gift, so a deed of gift is covered only as a "transfer". Background role only; no share in the answer depends on it.

relevant_excerpt: In all questions relating to the distribution of the property of an intestate, if the present Ordinance is silent, the rules of the Roman-Dutch law as it prevailed in North Holland are to govern and be followed.
why_relevant: The one step in the chain that Part III does not regulate is the effect of Deed of Gift No.1100, an irrevocable gift reserving a life interest to the donor. Section 36 is the provision that tells the reader where that question goes: to Roman-Dutch law, which is outside the corpus. Adding it makes the boundary of the statutory answer explicit instead of leaving it in a prose note, and it is the authority for treating the deed step as governed by law the corpus does not hold.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus. In force at 2020-10 and at every death in the scenario.
verifier_note: Added by the verifier. Excerpt checked verbatim against 15-1876/s36.

relevant_excerpt: Before any deed or instrument (other than a will or codicil) affecting any interest in land or other immovable property is drawn by him, he shall search or cause to be searched the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title in regard to such land and whether any prior deed affecting any interest in such land has been registered
why_relevant: This is the notary's own statutory duty to investigate title. It requires the search to be made before the deed is drawn, and it is the source of the first step in advising the purchasing company.
temporal_note: Rule (17)(a) was not touched by the Notaries (Amendment) Act, No. 31 of 2022 (which repealed and replaced paragraph (b) of rule (17) and added paragraphs (c) to (e)) and was in force in October 2020. The corpus does not label rule numbers inside the section body; the number (17) is taken from its position between rules (16) and (18).
verifier_note: Rule (17)(a) is verbatim and was untouched by the 2022 and 2024 amendments (Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(10) replaced only paragraph (b) and added (c) to (e)), but the excerpt stops before the proviso to rule (17), under which the search is not compulsory if the parties authorise the notary in writing to dispense with it; the duty must be stated subject to that proviso.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument, other than a will or codicil, affecting land or other immovable property, unless the deed or instrument embodies therin or in a Schedule annexed therto an accurate and clear description of the said land or other property affected thereby, showing its boundaries, extent, situation specifying the district, pattu, korale, Divisional Secretary's Division, local authority division and the Grama Niladari Division, and the village within the District in which the land is situated
why_relevant: Fixes what the schedule to the deed must contain. It is the reason the notary must obtain a survey plan and an accurate description of the twenty acres before drawing the deed.
temporal_note: The Notaries (Amendment) Act, No. 31 of 2022 s.16(9)(a) substituted only the closing words of rule (16)(a) about assessment numbers and condominium parcels. The excerpt stops before that substituted tail, so it reflects the text in force in October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless he has an assurance that the required stamp duty is provided.
why_relevant: Grounds the step of satisfying himself that stamp duty on the conveyance has been provided before attestation.
temporal_note: Rule (6) as it stands in the corpus was substituted by the Notaries (Amendment) Act, No. 31 of 2022 s.16(4), after the matter date. A stamp duty rule stood in rule (6) before 2022 but the corpus does not hold its wording, so this provision is carried as supporting only and is not treated as indispensable.
verifier_note: Rule (6) as held in the corpus is the text substituted by Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(4), which took effect after the matter date, and the amending Act does not quote the wording it replaced, so the October 2020 form of the stamp duty rule cannot be checked from the corpus; the matter-date stamp duty duty on the notary is carried instead by the added PROV-M062-902.

relevant_excerpt: He shall without delay duly attest every deed or instrument which shall be executed or acknowledged before him, and shall sign and seal such attestation.
why_relevant: The attestation step itself. The opening words of rule (20) impose the duty to attest without delay and to sign and seal the attestation.
temporal_note: The Notaries (Amendment) Act, No. 31 of 2022 s.16(11) replaced paragraphs (b) and (h) of rule (20) and added paragraph (d) matter; the opening words quoted here were not among the substituted text and were in force in October 2020.
verifier_note: The opening words of rule (20) are verbatim and were not substituted, so the attestation duty stands at the matter date, but the temporal note misdescribes the amendment: Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(11) replaced paragraphs (b) and (e), amended paragraph (g) and added paragraph (h), and Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3(7) later replaced paragraph (g).

relevant_excerpt: Whenever a notary has received instructions to register, and a sufficient sum to meet the necessary expense of registering, any deed drawn or attested by him, and shall in such case fail to use due diligence in effecting such registration, he shall be guilty of an offence
why_relevant: Once the company instructs registration and puts the notary in funds, prompt registration of the deed becomes a duty enforceable against the notary personally.
temporal_note: Last changed in 2005 by the Increase of Fines Act, No. 12 of 2005 (fine levels only). In force in October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: It shall be the duty of every notary to endeavour to ascertain the true and full consideration for the execution of any deed, and to insert and set forth the same in such deed.
why_relevant: The notary must ascertain and state the true price actually agreed for the estate rather than an understated figure.
temporal_note: The Notaries (Amendment) Act, No. 31 of 2022 s.18 amended only the fine in subsection (2). Subsection (1), quoted here, was in force in October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: shall be in force or avail in law unless - (a) the relevant deed or instrument shall be in writing, signed by every executant or by any person duly authorised by such executant and the witnesses in the presence of a licenced notary public present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and the same shall be attested by such notary
why_relevant: The purchase of the estate can only take effect through a notarially executed and attested writing, which is why the company needs a notary at all and why the formalities below matter.
temporal_note: The corpus text is the form produced by the Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Acts No. 30 of 2022 and No. 4 of 2024, both after the matter date. The requirement that a sale of immovable property be in writing, executed before a notary and two witnesses and attested by the notary has stood since 1840; the pre-2022 wording is not in the corpus and the verifier should confirm the October 2020 wording before this excerpt is treated as the operative text.
verifier_note: The whole operative clause of section 2 in the corpus is the text substituted by Act No. 30 of 2022 s.2 and re-cast by Act No. 4 of 2024 s.2; the 2022 Act repealed all the words from 'shall be of force' to the end without quoting them, so the wording in force in October 2020 cannot be reconstructed from the corpus, and the corpus text of paragraph (a) does not itself say 'two witnesses' (see the added PROV-M062-901 and PROV-M062-904).

relevant_excerpt: an obligation which, if entered into by a natural person is required by law to be in writing signed by that person and be notarially attested, may be entered into on behalf of the company in writing signed under the name of the company by - (i) two directors of the company; (ii) if there be only one director, by that director; (iii) if the articles of the company so provide, by any other person or class of persons; or (iv) one or more attorneys appointed by the company, and be notarially executed
why_relevant: Tells the notary who may sign the deed of transfer for the purchasing company: two directors, a sole director, a person permitted by the articles, or an attorney appointed by the company, signing under the company's name.
temporal_note: In force from 2007 with no recorded amendment; the Companies (Amendment) Act, No. 13 of 2019 in the corpus does not touch s.19.

relevant_excerpt: A company shall not enter into any major transaction, unless such transaction is- (a) approved by special resolution; (b) contingent on approval by special resolution; (c) consented to in writing by all the shareholders of the company; or (d) a transaction which the company is expressly authorised to enter into by a provision in its articles, which was included in it at the time the company was incorporated.
why_relevant: If the purchase is a major transaction the notary must see shareholder approval in one of these four forms before the deed is executed.
temporal_note: In force from 2007 with no recorded amendment.

relevant_excerpt: the acquisition of or an agreement to acquire whether contingent or not, assets of a value which is greater than half the value of the assets of the company before the acquisition
why_relevant: Supplies the test that turns this purchase into a major transaction, so the notary must obtain the value of the company's assets before the acquisition and compare it with the price of the estate.
temporal_note: In force from 2007 with no recorded amendment.

relevant_excerpt: Where the articles of a company sets-out the objects of the company, there shall be deemed to be a restriction placed by the articles in carrying on any business or activity that is not within those objects, unless the articles expressly provide otherwise.
why_relevant: Explains why the notary reads the articles: objects stated in them operate as a restriction, and the articles are also where any express authority for a major transaction under s.185(1)(d) would be found.
temporal_note: In force from 2007 with no recorded amendment.

relevant_excerpt: the maximum extent of agricultural land which may be owned by any person, in this Law referred to as the " ceiling ", shall (a) if such land consists exclusively of paddy land, be twenty-five acres; or (b) if such land does not consist exclusively of paddy land, be fifty acres
why_relevant: Sets the fifty acre ceiling on non-paddy agricultural land that the notary must apply to the tea estate.
temporal_note: Last amended by the Land Reform (Amendment) Act, No. 39 of 1981 s.2, long before the matter date.

relevant_excerpt: For the purposes of this Law, where any agricultural land is owned by a private company or co-operative society, the shareholders of such company, or society, as the case may be, shall be deemed to own such land for the purposes of section 3, in proportion to the shares held by each shareholder of such company
why_relevant: Because the purchaser is a private company, the ceiling bites on the shareholders. The notary must look through the company and test each shareholder's holding, not the company's.
temporal_note: In force from 1972 with no recorded amendment.

relevant_excerpt: means land used or capable of being used for agriculture within the meaning given in this Law and shall include private lands, lands alienated under the Land Development Ordinance or the State Lands Ordinance or any other enactment
why_relevant: Brings a private tea property within "agricultural land", since "agriculture" in the same section includes the growing of industrial crops. Without this the ceiling would not apply at all.
temporal_note: Last amended by the Land Reform (Amendment) Act, No. 39 of 1981 s.15. The exclusion in paragraph (a) of the definition is confined to land owned or possessed by a public company on 29 May 1971 and does not reach this purchaser.

relevant_excerpt: means a private company within the meaning of the Companies Ordinance
why_relevant: Confirms that a company such as the purchaser, styled "(Private) Limited", is the kind of company caught by s.8.
temporal_note: The definition points to the Companies Ordinance, which was repealed and replaced by the Companies Act, No. 17 of 1982 and in turn by the Companies Act, No. 7 of 2007. The corpus preserves the original reference and a footnote to the 1982 replacement; the reader has to carry the reference forward to the 2007 Act in force in October 2020.
verifier_note: The excerpt is verbatim, but the definition points to the repealed Companies Ordinance and the corpus holds no transitional provision equating a company incorporated under the Companies Act, No. 7 of 2007 with a 'private company within the meaning of the Companies Ordinance'; the carry-forward is an inference and is properly supporting only.

relevant_excerpt: Where after the date of commencement of this Law any person becomes the owner of agricultural land in excess of the ceiling, any such land owned by such person in excess of the ceiling shall as from that date- (a) be deemed to vest in the Commission; and (b) be deemed to be held by that person under a statutory lease from the Commission.
why_relevant: Supplies the consequence the notary is guarding against: any excess over the ceiling created by this purchase vests automatically in the Land Reform Commission, so part of what the company pays for would be lost.
temporal_note: Amended by the Land Reform (Amendment) Act, No. 39 of 1981 s.3 and the Land Reform (Special Provisions) Act, No. 14 of 1986 s.2, both well before the matter date.

formal_title: Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act
relevant_excerpt: The transfer of ownership of a tea or rubber estate on or after the appointed day shall, subject to the provisions of subsections (2) and (3), be null and void unless- (a) a certificate of consent of the Board to such transfer has been previously obtained by the transferor
why_relevant: The property is planted in tea, so the notary must ask whether a certificate of consent of the Fragmentation Board is a precondition of a valid transfer.
temporal_note: The corpus holds the Act as enacted. No amendment to s.3 is recorded before the matter date.
verifier_note: Section 3(1) is verbatim and no amendment to it is recorded, but the corpus edition is the Act as enacted and the renaming worked by Act No. 20 of 2005 s.3 is recorded as not applied, so at the matter date the Act and the Board are the Tea, Rubber and Coconut Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act and Board; the answer uses the 1958 names.

formal_title: Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act
relevant_excerpt: means a tea estate of not less than one hundred acres in extent which, under the Tea Control Act*, is or is deemed to be an estate registered under that Act
why_relevant: The extent limb of this definition decides the fragmentation question. A twenty acre tea property is below the hundred acre floor and so is not a "tea estate" for the purposes of s.3.
temporal_note: The corpus records amendments to s.25 by Act No. 20 of 2005, including two entries marked substitute_not_applied. The verifier should confirm that the hundred acre extent in the "tea estate" definition was not altered by that Act before the matter date.
verifier_note: The 'one hundred acres' figure cannot be relied on at the matter date: the corpus records that Act No. 20 of 2005 s.10(c) substitutes 'twenty hectares' for 'forty hectares' in this definition and that the substitution could not be applied because the as-enacted baseline reads 'one hundred acres', the intervening metricating instrument being neither in the chain nor held; the extent threshold in force in October 2020 therefore cannot be established from the corpus, although twenty acres (about 8.1 hectares) falls below the threshold on any of the readings.

relevant_excerpt: Notwithstanding any provision to the contrary in any other written law, the transfer of title of any land situated in Sri Lanka, shall be prohibited if such transfer is- (a) to a foreigner; or (b) to a company incorporated in Sri Lanka under the Companies Act where any foreign shareholding in such company, either direct or indirect, is fifty per cent or above; or (c) to a foreign company, unless exempted as provided in section 3.
why_relevant: Because the transferee is a company, the notary must establish the level of direct and indirect foreign shareholding before the deed is drawn; at fifty per cent or above the transfer of title is prohibited.
temporal_note: Deemed to have come into operation on 1 January 2013 (s.1(2)) and amended by Act No. 3 of 2017 and Act No. 21 of 2018, all before the matter date.

relevant_excerpt: For the purpose of maintaining the legal validity of a transfer of land to a company incorporated in Sri Lanka under the Companies Act, with less than fifty per cent of foreign shareholding, the foreign shareholding of such company shall remain less than fifty per cent, for a minimum period of consecutive twenty (20) years from the date of such transfer.
why_relevant: A continuing condition the notary should warn the company about: the transfer stays valid only while foreign shareholding is kept below half for twenty years from the transfer.
temporal_note: Introduced into s.2 before the matter date; in force in October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: it shall be the duty of the Registrar of Lands to confirm himself whether the foreign shareholding of such company is less than fifty per cent, by requiring the secretary of such company to submit documentary proof
why_relevant: Registration will be held up unless the company secretary's documentary proof of shareholding is ready, so the notary should collect it as part of the registration step.
temporal_note: In force before the matter date.

relevant_excerpt: means a person who is not a citizen of Sri Lanka
why_relevant: Fixes the test the notary applies to the shareholders when measuring foreign shareholding under s.2(1)(b).
temporal_note: In force from 2014; no amendment recorded.

relevant_excerpt: Any alienation of land effected in contravention of the provisions of this Act, shall be void and shall have no effect in law.
why_relevant: Shows the cost of getting the shareholding question wrong, and so why the check has to be made before rather than after execution.
temporal_note: In force from 2014; no amendment recorded.

relevant_excerpt: unless it is duly registered under this Chapter, or, if the land has come within the operation of the Land Registration Ordinance, 1877f, in the books mentioned in section 26 of that Ordinance, be void as against all parties claiming an adverse interest thereto on valuable consideration by virtue of any subsequent instrument which is duly registered under this Chapter
why_relevant: Registration decides priority between competing deeds. It is why the notary searches the folio before drawing the deed and why he must register the company's deed promptly after attestation.
temporal_note: In force from 1927; no amendment to s.7 recorded in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument to which at least two witnesses have not subscribed their signatures in letters.
why_relevant: This is the corpus source for the two witnesses the answer requires. The excerpt of Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2 relied on by the researcher says only 'the witnesses'; rule (8) supplies the number.
temporal_note: Rule (8) is untouched by the Notaries (Amendment) Acts No. 47 of 2011, No. 31 of 2022 and No. 6 of 2024, none of which lists rule (8) among the rules it amends, so it stood in this form in October 2020.
verifier_note: Added by the verifier: the answer's two-witness requirement had no supporting provision in force at the matter date.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless the person executing the same and the witnesses shall have signed the same in his presence and in the presence of one another, and unless he shall have signed the same in the presence of the executant and of the attesting witnesses.
why_relevant: Supplies the manner of execution the answer describes - executants and witnesses signing before the notary and in one another's presence - from a rule that was in force at the matter date, which the post-2022 text of Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2 cannot.
temporal_note: Rule (12) is not among the rules amended by the Notaries (Amendment) Acts No. 47 of 2011, No. 31 of 2022 or No. 6 of 2024, so it stood in this form in October 2020.
verifier_note: Added by the verifier as the matter-date source for the execution formality otherwise resting on the post-2022 text of PROV-M062-007.

relevant_excerpt: Every notary public who attests an instrument of conveyance shall before doing so take all reasonable steps to satisfy himself that the value on which the stamp duty is paid represents the value of the property conveyed.
why_relevant: A statutory duty on this notary in this transaction that the research map missed: before attesting the conveyance he must take all reasonable steps to satisfy himself that the value on which stamp duty is paid is the value of the property. It does not depend on the rate, which is not in the corpus.
temporal_note: The Stamp Duty Act, No. 43 of 1982 is in the corpus as a consolidated principal enactment with no recorded amendment to s.22, and s.13 of the Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act, No. 12 of 2006 (PROV-M062-903) leaves its provisions operative for instruments relating to the transfer of immovable property.
verifier_note: Added by the verifier. The map recorded stamp duty as a corpus gap and cited only Notaries Ordinance rule (6), whose matter-date wording is unresolved; this section is in the corpus and imposes a duty on the notary directly.

relevant_excerpt: the provisions of the Stamp Duty Act, No. 43 of 1982, relating to the Imposition of Stamp Duty (other than any instrument relating to the transfer of immovable property, the transfer of motor vehicles or documents filed in Court), Exemptions and any other provision in the aforesaid Act, shall, in so far as the same are inconsistent with the provisions of this Act, have no operation
why_relevant: Carves instruments relating to the transfer of immovable property out of the displacement of the 1982 Act, which is why the notary's duty in PROV-M062-902 still applies to a deed of transfer at the matter date.
temporal_note: In force from 2006 with no recorded amendment to s.13.
verifier_note: Added by the verifier to carry the temporal chain for PROV-M062-902.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not divulge the secrets confided to him or of which he becomes possessed in the execution of his office, unless with the express permission of his employer or when required to do so by law.
why_relevant: This is the statutory duty of secrecy of a notary. It settles the question directly: a notary may not disclose what he learned in the execution of his office, and the only two gateways to disclosure are the express permission of his employer (here, the testator who instructed and executed the will before him) or a legal requirement to disclose. Whether the notary attested a particular will, and what that will contains, is a secret of exactly this kind.
temporal_note: Rule (1) has stood since the Ordinance came into force in 1907 and is in force at 2020-10. The section as a whole shows amendment events for 2011, 2022 and 2024, but Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 and Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 47 of 2011 were read and neither substitutes, amends or repeals rule (1); the 2024 amendment (6-2024 s.3) is in any event after the matter date and so cannot bear on the October 2020 text.

relevant_excerpt: Every notary who acts in violation of or disregards or neglects to observe- (a) rules (1), (31) or (32) set out in section 31, shall be guilty of an offence, and shall, on conviction after summary trial before a Magistrate, be liable to a fine not exceeding five thousand rupees, in addition to any civil liability he may incur thereby
why_relevant: Shows that breach of the duty of secrecy in rule (1) is not merely a matter of etiquette but a criminal offence, and that criminal liability is in addition to any civil liability. It supports the strength of the advice but is not needed to reach the answer.
temporal_note: The corpus text of s.34 is the section substituted by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.17, which post-dates the matter reference date of 2020-10. A penal provision for breach of the s.31 rules existed before 2022, but its text and the fine then applicable are not in the corpus, so this provision is recorded as supporting only and is not relied on for the conclusion.
verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim, but the corpus text of s.34 is the whole section repealed and substituted by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.17, so no penalty for breach of rule (1) can be stated from the corpus as at 2020-10; correctly held to supporting only and not relied on for the conclusion.

relevant_excerpt: has grossly misconducted himself in the discharge of the duties of his office; or (c) has so conducted himself by repeated breaches of any of the rules made by or under this Ordinance that he ought not to be any longer entrusted with the performance of the said duties
why_relevant: Gives the disciplinary consequence of breaching the notarial rules: gross misconduct in the discharge of the office, or repeated breaches of the rules, can lead to an inquiry and to cancellation or suspension of the warrant. Supporting context for why the duty must be observed; not a step in the reasoning.
temporal_note: Section 21 dates from 1907. The only later changes recorded are Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.11, which alters wording in subsection (1)(e) and raises the fine in subsection (4); neither touches subsection (1)(b) or (1)(c), which are the parts relied on here.
verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim and subsections (1)(b) and (1)(c) are untouched at the matter date, but the temporal note is incomplete: the corpus also records an unmapped amendment event 'unknown by 12-2005 s.5 (2005)' on s.21, which is not mentioned.

relevant_excerpt: (25) Where any deed or instrument is executed or acknowledged before more than one notary- (a) the notary who first attests such deed or instrument shall comply with all the requirements of rule (20), and every other notary attesting such deed or instrument shall comply with the requirements of paragraphs (a) to (e) of the aforesaid rule and the provisions of paragraph (g) in respect of erasures, alterations and interpolations made in the signatures attested by him or in his serial number;
why_relevant: This is the provision that expressly permits one deed to be executed or acknowledged before more than one notary and allocates the attestation duties between the notary who attests first and every other attesting notary. It is the direct answer to how two parties who will not meet can execute the same lease, and it fixes the heavier duty on Ruwan Perera as first notary.
temporal_note: Rule (25) has not been touched by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 47 of 2011, No. 13 of 2013, No. 31 of 2022 or No. 6 of 2024, none of which lists rule (25) among the rules amended. The text was therefore in force at October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: In the case of any deed or instrument which is to be executed by two or more parties, both or all of whom, as the case may be, do not sign the deed or instrument at the same time and place- (i) the deed or instrument shall, for the purposes of the application of rules (6), (7), (23) and (25) set out in section 31, be deemed to be executed or acknowledged at the time when it is first signed by a party, or by two or more parties at the same time and place;
why_relevant: Section 32(2) is the statutory recognition that the parties to one deed may sign at different times and in different places, and it fixes the deemed date of execution for the purposes of rule (25). Without it the split signing in Galle and Colombo would have no statutory footing.
temporal_note: Section 32 carries in_force_from_year 1907 and no amendment events in the corpus, so the text was in force at October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument in any area other than that in which he is authorized to practice, nor in any language other than that in which he is authorized to practice nor authenticate or attest any deed or instrument drawn in any language other than that in which he is authorized to practice.
why_relevant: Rule (22) is why the problem exists at all: Anil Fernando cannot attest in Galle and Ruwan Perera cannot attest in Colombo, so a single notary cannot take both signatures unless one party travels. It makes execution before two notaries the necessary route.
temporal_note: Rule (22) is not among the rules amended by the 2011, 2013, 2022 or 2024 amending Acts and was in force at October 2020. Section 4A (inserted 1976) should be read with it: a warrant to practise in a judicial division is deemed to authorise practice in the judicial zone in which the notary resides.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest a deed or instrument drawn in Sri Lanka by any other person, unless there shall be endorsed thereon a certificate signed by a notary certifying that such deed or instrument has been drawn by himself.
why_relevant: Ruwan Perera is to draft the lease. Anil Fernando, who will attest the company's signature, is therefore attesting a deed drawn by another person and may do so only if a certificate signed by the notary who drew it is endorsed on the deed.
temporal_note: Rule (2) is not among the rules amended by the 2011, 2013, 2022 or 2024 amending Acts and was in force at October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless the person executing the same and the witnesses shall have signed the same in his presence and in the presence of one another, and unless he shall have signed the same in the presence of the executant and of the attesting witnesses.
why_relevant: Rule (12) forbids attestation of a signature not made in the notary's presence. It rules out any arrangement by which one notary attests both parties on the strength of a signature obtained elsewhere, and so requires each party to sign before the notary who attests that party.
temporal_note: Rule (12) is not among the rules amended by the 2011, 2013, 2022 or 2024 amending Acts and was in force at October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument to which at least two witnesses have not subscribed their signatures in letters.
why_relevant: Each attestation must be supported by at least two subscribing witnesses, so witnesses must be available at each of the two signings rather than only at the first.
temporal_note: Rule (8) is not among the rules amended by the 2011, 2013, 2022 or 2024 amending Acts and was in force at October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: an obligation which, if entered into by a natural person is required by law to be in writing signed by that person and be notarially attested, may be entered into on behalf of the company in writing signed under the name of the company by - (i) two directors of the company; (ii) if there be only one director, by that director; (iii) if the articles of the company so provide, by any other person or class of persons; or (iv) one or more attorneys appointed by the company, and be notarially executed;
why_relevant: Cyril & Cyril (Private) Limited is a body corporate and cannot sign personally. Section 19(1)(a) states how the company signs a notarially attested obligation such as this lease, and it is the provision that lets the company's directors (whom Anil Fernando knows) execute in Colombo.
temporal_note: Section 19 carries in_force_from_year 2007 and no amendment events in the corpus; the Companies (Amendment) Act No. 13 of 2019 in the corpus does not touch it. In force at October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: no promise, bargain, contract, or agreement for effecting any such object, or for establishing any security, interest, or incumbrance affecting land or other immovable property (other than a lease at will, or for any period not exceeding one month)
why_relevant: This is why a notary is needed at all: a lease of immovable property other than a lease at will or for a period not exceeding one month creates an interest in land and is of no force in law unless it is in writing and notarially attested.
temporal_note: The corpus text of section 2 is the consolidated text carrying amendment events 60-1947 s.2, 30-2022 s.2 and 4-2024 s.2, so the quoted wording is post-matter-date. The requirement of notarial execution for leases exceeding one month long predates October 2020, but that October 2020 wording is not quotable from this corpus, so the provision is used as supporting context only and is not treated as indispensable.
verifier_note: Temporal note needs correction: Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 30 of 2022 s.2 repealed only the words from "shall be of force" to the end of section 2, and No. 4 of 2024 s.2 renumbered the section and rewrote paragraphs (a) and (b), so the words actually quoted here (the classes of transaction caught, including the carve-out for a lease at will or for a period not exceeding one month) stood unchanged at October 2020 and applicable_to_matter_date should read true; what is not quotable at the matter date is the notarial-execution limb in the tail of the section, and the subsection label "(1)" is itself the 2024 renumbering.

relevant_excerpt: (b) every notary attesting the deed or instrument shall number such deed or instrument in accordance with the provisions of rule (23); (c) the notary who first attests such deed or instrument shall preserve as his protocol the draft or copy referred to in rule (24), and shall comply with the requirements of that rule, and every other notary attesting such deed or instrument shall supply himself with a certified copy of the deed or instrument, which shall be deemed to be his protocol for the purposes of that rule; and
why_relevant: Completes the mechanics of a two-notary execution: each notary gives the deed a number in his own series, the first notary keeps the protocol, and the second notary keeps a certified copy as his protocol.
temporal_note: Rule (25) is not among the rules amended by the 2011, 2013, 2022 or 2024 amending Acts and was in force at October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: Where any deed or instrument other than a will or codicil shall be executed or acknowledged by two or more parties before more than one notary, the duplicate of such deed or instrument shall be delivered or transmitted by the notary who first attests such deed or instrument to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which he resides; and it shall not be necessary for the other notary or notaries employed in the execution of such deed or instrument to deliver or transmit any duplicate thereof to such registrar.
why_relevant: Allocates the duty of transmitting the duplicate to the Registrar of Lands to the first attesting notary and relieves the second notary of it, which matters once the parties choose which notary attests first.
temporal_note: Rule (28) is not among the rules amended by the 2011, 2013, 2022 or 2024 amending Acts and was in force at October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: If a deed or instrument other than a will or codicil affects a land situated in a district other than that in which the notary before whom it is signed, and by whom it is attested,
why_relevant: Background on registration logistics: because the warehouse is in Galle and Ruwan Perera practises in Galle, making him the first attesting notary keeps the duplicate and the land in the same district and avoids the extra certified copy this rule would otherwise require.
temporal_note: Rule (29) was substituted by Notaries (Amendment) Law No. 20 of 1976 s.10(1) and thereafter only as to the reference to Form F (No. 6 of 2024 s.3(9)). The quoted words are unaffected by the 2024 change and were in force at October 2020.
verifier_note: Confirmed: Notaries (Amendment) Law No. 20 of 1976 s.10(1) substituted rule (29) in the terms quoted and No. 6 of 2024 s.3(9) changed only "in the Form F" to "in the Form F 1"; the excerpt stops well before that phrase.

relevant_excerpt: (20) He shall without delay duly attest every deed or instrument which shall be executed or acknowledged before him, and shall sign and seal such attestation. In such attestation he shall state- (a) that the said deed or instrument was signed by the party and the witnesses thereto in his presence and in the presence of one another;
why_relevant: The core duty in issue in question 2: the first notary must attest without delay, sign and seal the attestation, and state that the party and the witnesses signed in his presence and in the presence of one another.
temporal_note: The opening words of rule (20) and paragraph (a) were not amended by the 2011, 2013, 2022 or 2024 amending Acts (No. 31 of 2022 s.16(11) touched only paragraphs (b), (e), (g) and added (h); No. 6 of 2024 s.3(7) touched only paragraph (g)). In force at October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: (b) whether the executants of the said deed or instrument are known to him or whether he has identified them by the inspection of the national identity card, bio-page of the passport or the driving licence or whether the witnesses thereto are known to him and in the latter case he shall specify which of the executants or the person acknowledging are known to the said witness;
why_relevant: Identification of the executants is one of the matters a first notary must state, and it is the item that engages the fact that Anil Fernando knows the directors while Ruwan Perera knows Russel Perera. The quoted text is the current wording.
temporal_note: This paragraph is the text substituted by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(11)(a) and so was not in force in October 2020. The amending Act repealed and replaced the paragraph without reciting the repealed words, so the October 2020 wording is not recoverable from this corpus. Recorded as supporting only; the subject matter (whether the executants or the witnesses are known to the notary) existed before 2022 but cannot be quoted.
verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim but is the paragraph substituted by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(11)(a), which recites none of the repealed wording, so this entry verifies the current text only and cannot support any statement of what rule (20)(b) required in October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: (c) the day, month, and year on which and the place where the said deed or instrument was executed or acknowledged, and the full names of the attesting witnesses and their residences; (d) whether the same was read over by the person executing the same, or read and explained by him, the said notary, to the said person in the presence of the attesting witnesses;
why_relevant: Two further compulsory contents of the first notary's attestation: the date and place of execution with the names and residences of the attesting witnesses, and whether the deed was read over or read and explained.
temporal_note: Paragraphs (c) and (d) of rule (20) were not amended by the 2011, 2013, 2022 or 2024 amending Acts and were in force at October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: (e) whether any money was paid or not in his presence as consideration or part of the consideration of the deed or instrument, and if paid, the actual amount in local currency of such payment and if the payment is made by cheque, pay order, bank draft or a banker's cheque the details of such instrument shall be set out in the attestation, in proof of such payment.
why_relevant: Whether consideration was paid in the notary's presence is one of the matters the first notary must state. The quoted text is the current wording.
temporal_note: This paragraph is the text substituted by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(11)(b) and so was not in force in October 2020. The repealed words were not recited in the amending Act, so the October 2020 wording is not recoverable from this corpus. Recorded as supporting only.
verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim but is the paragraph substituted by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(11)(b), which recites none of the repealed wording, so this entry verifies the current text only and cannot support any statement of what rule (20)(e) required in October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: (f) the number and value of the adhesive stamps affixed to or the value of the impressed stamps on such deed or instrument and the duplicate thereof;
why_relevant: The first notary must state in the attestation the number and value of the adhesive stamps, or the value of the impressed stamps, on the deed and on the duplicate.
temporal_note: Paragraph (f) of rule (20) was not amended by the 2011, 2013, 2022 or 2024 amending Acts and was in force at October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: (g) specifically the erasures, alterations, and interpolations which have been made in such deed or instrument, and whether they were made before the same was read over as aforesaid, and the erasures, alterations, and interpolations, if any, made in the signatures thereto, in its serial number, and in the writing on the stamp affixed thereto
why_relevant: The first notary must set out specifically every erasure, alteration and interpolation in the deed, in the signatures, in the serial number and in the writing on the stamp, and say whether they were made before the deed was read over.
temporal_note: The substance of paragraph (g) is unamended. No. 31 of 2022 s.16(11)(c) substituted only the closing words affixed thereto. with affixed thereto; and, and No. 6 of 2024 s.3(7) re-enacted the paragraph in the same terms. The excerpt deliberately stops before the trailing conjunction, so the quoted words stood at October 2020.
verifier_note: Confirmed against both amending Acts: No. 31 of 2022 s.16(11)(c) substituted only "affixed thereto." with "affixed thereto; and", and No. 6 of 2024 s.3(7) re-enacted paragraph (g) in identical terms, so the quoted words stood at October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: (h) in the case of a will- (i) set out in the attestation of the will that the testator was in good and sound mind to execute the will;
why_relevant: Recorded only to show that the eighth item now in rule (20) is confined to wills and is a later insertion, so it is neither applicable to a lease nor part of the October 2020 rule.
temporal_note: Inserted by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(11)(d); not in force at October 2020 and in any event confined to wills.

relevant_excerpt: Every such attestation shall be substantially in the form E in the Second Schedule, and shall be legibly signed by him in the language in which the deed or instrument is written, and also with his usual signature if the language or form of that signature be different from that in which such deed or instrument is written.
why_relevant: Fixes the form of the attestation the first notary must use and requires it to be legibly signed in the language of the deed. The following sentence of the same rule requires any erasure, alteration or interpolation in the attestation itself to be authenticated with the initial letters of the notary's name.
temporal_note: Rule (21) is not among the rules amended by the 2011, 2013, 2022 or 2024 amending Acts and was in force at October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: He shall correctly insert in letters in every deed or instrument executed before him the day, month, and year on which and the place where the same is executed, and shall sign the same.
why_relevant: Runs with rule (20)(c): the date and place of execution must appear in letters in the deed as well as in the attestation, and section 32(2)(ii) makes the deed deemed executed whenever a party signs, so each signing is dated.
temporal_note: Rule (18) is not among the rules amended by the 2011, 2013, 2022 or 2024 amending Acts and was in force at October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: if an executant to any deed or instrument is a corporate body, cause to be affixed the seal of the corporate body and obtain the signatures of the board of directors or any person authorized by the board by resolution to sign such deed or instrument
why_relevant: Bears on how the notary in Colombo takes the company's execution and on the material he must keep, and on describing in the attestation an executant whose name differs from his identification document. The quoted text is the current wording.
temporal_note: Rule (14) was substituted by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(7) and so was not in force in October 2020; the repealed wording is not recited in the amending Act and is not recoverable from this corpus. Recorded as supporting only. Companies Act s.19(1)(a) supplies the in-force authority for how the company signs.
verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim but is the rule substituted by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(7); the duty to cause the corporate seal to be affixed and to obtain the signatures of the board is therefore post-date text and must not be used to state how the company executed in October 2020. No claim in fact relies on it and its role is correctly supporting only.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless one of the executants to the deed or instrument or the two attesting witnesses be known to notary or by the identity of the executants to a deed or instrument is established by such notary by inspection of the national identity card, bio-page of the passport or the driving licence of such executants
why_relevant: Explains why it matters that Anil Fernando knows the directors but not Russel Perera: a notary may not attest unless the executant before him is known to him or to the attesting witnesses, or is identified from a prescribed document.
temporal_note: This is the wording substituted by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(6) and further amended by No. 6 of 2024 s.3(3), so it was not in force in October 2020. The pre-2022 wording survives verbatim in the recital in 31-2022/s16: the notary could not attest unless the person executing the deed was known to him or to at least two of the attesting witnesses. Recorded as supporting only.
verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim but is the post-2022/2024 wording. Unlike rule (20)(b) and (e), the repealed wording of rule (9) is recoverable: Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(6) recites it verbatim, and it is added here as PROV-M065-903 so that the identification point in question 1 rests on matter-date text.

relevant_excerpt: (i) where any deed or instrument which is to be executed or acknowledged by two or more parties is signed during any month by one or more, as the case may be, of such parties, the notary shall, notwithstanding that the deed or instrument has not been signed by all such-parties, include such deed or instrument in the list required to be delivered or transmitted under paragraph (a)
why_relevant: Rule (27) is the rule written for exactly this situation: a deed that two or more parties are to execute but that only one of them has signed. It obliges the notary who took the first signature to list the part-executed deed in his monthly return anyway, to produce the duplicate for inspection if the Registrar of Lands calls for it, and, if the deed is still not signed by all the parties three months after it was first signed, to deliver the duplicate to the registrar, with a right to have it back within two years to complete the deed. It therefore puts a practical limit on the gap between Ruwan Perera taking Russel Perera's signature in Galle and Anil Fernando taking the company's signature in Colombo, which the researcher's map did not record.
temporal_note: Rule (27) was in force at October 2020 and was repealed only later, by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(12). The consolidated corpus text of section 31 still carries the rule verbatim, so the October 2020 wording is quotable; that the consolidation retained repealed text is itself a corpus defect and is recorded as a corpus gap.
verifier_note: Added by the verifier. Excerpt checked verbatim against 1-1907/s31.

relevant_excerpt: (ii) the deed or instrument shall, for the purposes of the application of rules (18) and (20) set out in section 31, be deemed to be executed or acknowledged whenever it is signed by a party, or by two or more parties at the same time and place;
why_relevant: Question 2 asks what the first notary must put in his attestation, and rule (20)(c) makes him state the day and the place of execution. Where the parties sign at different times and places, this is the provision that tells him which day and place to state: for rules (18) and (20) the deed is deemed executed whenever it is signed. It is what allows Ruwan Perera to attest in Galle on the day Russel Perera signs, before the company has signed at all, and it is the counterpart of section 32(2)(i) (PROV-M065-002), which fixes a single date for rules (6), (7), (23) and (25). The researcher's map quoted only paragraph (i) and did not attach section 32 to question 2 at all.
temporal_note: Section 32 carries in_force_from_year 1907 and no amendment events in the corpus, so the text was in force at October 2020.
verifier_note: Added by the verifier. Excerpt checked verbatim against 1-1907/s32.

subsection: s.16(6), reciting the pre-2022 wording of Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (9)
relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless the person executing the same be known to him or to at least two of the attesting witnesses thereto;
why_relevant: This is the October 2020 wording of rule (9), which the scenario turns on: Anil Fernando knows the directors of the company but does not know Russel Perera, and Ruwan Perera is Russel Perera's own notary. On this wording a notary could not attest unless the executant before him was known to him or to at least two of the attesting witnesses, so splitting the execution and letting each party sign before the notary who knows him is not merely convenient, it is how each notary satisfies rule (9). PROV-M065-022 quotes only the post-2022 replacement.
temporal_note: The section_id is the 2022 amending provision, which was not itself in force at October 2020. What is quoted is the wording that Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(6) recites as the words being replaced, that is, the text of Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (9) as it stood immediately before 2022 and therefore at October 2020. It is the only route by which the matter-date wording of rule (9) can be quoted from this corpus.
verifier_note: Added by the verifier. Excerpt checked verbatim against 31-2022/s16.

relevant_excerpt: Every appointment to the office of notary shall be by warrant granted by the Minister, and shall specify the area within which, and the language or languages in which, the person appointed is authorized to practice.
why_relevant: Rule (22) forbids a notary to attest in any area "other than that in which he is authorized to practice", and this is the provision that gives that phrase its content: the area and the language are fixed by the warrant of appointment. It is the definitional anchor for the whole of question 1, and the map carried no provision supplying it. It is to be read with section 4A, which deems a warrant for a judicial division to authorise practice in the judicial zone in which the notary resides, so that Anil Fernando's Colombo warrant does not reach Galle.
temporal_note: Section 2 carries in_force_from_year 1907 and no amendment events in the corpus, so the text was in force at October 2020.
verifier_note: Added by the verifier. Excerpt checked verbatim against 1-1907/s2.

relevant_excerpt: No sale, purchase, transfer, assignment, or mortgage of land or other immovable property, and no promise, bargain, contract, or agreement for effecting any such object, or for establishing any security, interest, or incumbrance affecting land or other immovable property (other than a lease at will, or for any period not exceeding one month)
why_relevant: Brings the proposed sale of the shop premises within the notarial-execution rule: a transfer of immovable property has no force in law unless it is in writing and notarially executed, which is why the transaction must be carried out by a Deed of Transfer drawn and attested by a notary at all.
temporal_note: These opening words are the 1840 text as amended in 1947 and were unchanged in October 2020. The words that follow them in the corpus body were substituted by Act No. 30 of 2022 and again by Act No. 4 of 2024; see PROV-M066-002.

relevant_excerpt: the relevant deed or instrument shall be in writing, signed by every executant or by any person duly authorised by such executant and the witnesses in the presence of a licenced notary public present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and the same shall be attested by such notary
why_relevant: States the execution formality that the deed must satisfy. Recorded so the verifier can see the exact corpus text, but the matter is dated October 2020 and this wording is later law.
temporal_note: This paragraph was inserted by Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 30 of 2022 s.2 and substituted by Act No. 4 of 2024 s.2, both after the matter date. In October 2020 s.2 required the writing to be signed by the party making it in the presence of a licensed notary public and two or more witnesses present at the same time, and to be duly attested by the notary and witnesses. Not treated as indispensable.

relevant_excerpt: Every deed or other instrument, except any will, testament, or codicil required by this Ordinance to be executed or acknowledged before or to be attested by a notary, shall be executed, acknowledged, or attested in triplicate.
why_relevant: The Deed of Transfer must be executed in triplicate (original, duplicate and protocol), which is why the draft has to be prepared in that form.
temporal_note: Section 16 was amended by Act No. 30 of 2022 s.5, after the matter date; the requirement of execution in triplicate itself is long-standing and was in force in October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest a deed or instrument drawn in Sri Lanka by any other person, unless there shall be endorsed thereon a certificate signed by a notary certifying that such deed or instrument has been drawn by himself.
why_relevant: The notary retained by the purchaser is expected to draw the deed himself; if it is drawn by another person the drawer's certificate must be endorsed on it before the attesting notary may attest it.
temporal_note: Rule (2) was not touched by the 2011, 2022 or 2024 amending Acts and stood in this form in October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument, other than a will or codicil, affecting land or other immovable property, unless the deed or instrument embodies therin or in a Schedule annexed therto an accurate and clear description of the said land or other property affected thereby, showing its boundaries, extent, situation specifying the district, pattu, korale, Divisional Secretary's Division, local authority division and the Grama Niladari Division, and the village within the District in which the land is situated
why_relevant: Fixes what the deed must say about the shop premises at Assessment No. 2, Galle Road, Kollupitiya: boundaries, extent, situation and, for property inside a municipality, the assessment number and street name. It is also the provision that makes the omitted Schedule the ordinary place for that description.
temporal_note: Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(9)(a) added the condominium wording at the end of paragraph (a); the words quoted here precede that insertion and were in force in October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: Before any deed or instrument (other than a will or codicil) affecting any interest in land or other immovable property is drawn by him, he shall search or cause to be searched the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title in regard to such land and whether any prior deed affecting any interest in such land has been registered
why_relevant: The notary must search the land registry before drawing the deed. On these facts the search establishes that the vendor's title rests on Deed of Transfer No. 27 of 27 May 1994, and supplies the prior registration reference that has to be written on the deed.
