temporal_note: Paragraph (a) of rule (17) was not altered by the 2022 or 2024 amending Acts (those changed paragraph (b) and added paragraphs (c) to (e)); it stood in this form in October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: He shall correctly insert in letters in every deed or instrument executed before him the day, month, and year on which and the place where the same is executed, and shall sign the same.
why_relevant: Requires the date and place of execution to be written in letters in the deed itself, which is a mandatory element of the draft even though the attestation is not asked for.
temporal_note: Rule (18) is the original 1907 text and was untouched by the 2011, 2022 and 2024 amending Acts.

relevant_excerpt: It shall be the duty of every notary to endeavour to ascertain the true and full consideration for the execution of any deed, and to insert and set forth the same in such deed.
why_relevant: The full consideration of Rs. 30,000,000 must be ascertained and set out in the body of the deed; understating it is an offence under s.38(2).
temporal_note: In force since 1907; the fine in subsection (2) reflects the increase made by Act No. 12 of 2005, which predates the matter.

relevant_excerpt: Every person drawing, making, executing or of attesting any instrument chargeable with stamp duty shall set out therein, the full names and addresses of the parties ofs such instrument, the consideration, the date and manner of payment and all other facts and circumstances affecting the chargeability of such instrument with stamp duty and the amount of the stamp duty with which it is chargeable.
why_relevant: Independently requires the deed to state the full names and addresses of Aruna Silva and Amara Perera, the consideration, the date and manner of payment and the amount of stamp duty chargeable. It links the drafting question to the stamp duty question.
temporal_note: Part of the Statute as enacted in 1990; no amendment recorded in the corpus. Corpus text carries OCR noise ('or of attesting', 'ofs such instrument').

relevant_excerpt: There shall be charged on- (a) every instrument relating to a transfer of situated in the immovable property Western Province;
why_relevant: The charging provision. The shop at Galle Road, Kollupitiya is immovable property in the Western Province, so the Deed of Transfer is the instrument on which provincial stamp duty is charged.
temporal_note: In force since the Statute was brought into operation under s.1; no amendment recorded in the corpus. The corpus text has transposed words ('a transfer of situated in the immovable property Western Province').

relevant_excerpt: a stamp duty at the prescribed rate. Different rates may be prescribed in respect of different classes or categories of instruments.
why_relevant: This is the point at which the calculation asked for in Q02 leaves the corpus: the rate is not stated in the Statute, only 'prescribed'. Without the prescribing regulation no figure can be produced.
temporal_note: Unamended in the corpus. The rate actually in force in October 2020 is contained in subsidiary legislation that is not part of this corpus.

relevant_excerpt: The Minister may make regulations in respect of all or any of the following matters: (a) any matter which is required or authorized by this Statute to be prescribed;
why_relevant: Identifies where the missing rate lives: it is prescribed by regulation published in the Gazette under s.77, not by the Statute itself.
temporal_note: Unamended in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: Where any property is conveyed by an instrument, the stamp duty with which such instrument is chargeable shall be calculated on the value of the property conveyed.
why_relevant: Fixes the base of the calculation: duty runs on the value of the shop premises conveyed, not simply on the sum named as consideration.
temporal_note: Unamended in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: "value" with reference - (a) to any property (other than immovable property which is gifted) and to any date, means the price which in the opinion of the Assessor, that property would have fetched in the open market on that date
why_relevant: Defines the base in s.48. Because the transaction is a sale and not a gift, paragraph (a) applies and the duty base is the open-market price in the opinion of the Assessor, which the stated consideration of Rs. 30,000,000 is taken to represent unless the Assessor differs.
temporal_note: Unamended in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: Except where there is an agreement to the contrary stamp duty shall be payable; (a) in the case of an instrument of transfer by the grantee;
why_relevant: Answers the 'by whom' half of the stamp duty question: absent contrary agreement the duty falls on the grantee, that is the purchaser Amara Perera.
temporal_note: Unamended in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: The stamp duty with which any instrument is chargeable shall be paid before or at the time of execution of the instrument except as otherwise permitted in this Statute and such payment shall be indicated on such instrument by means of adhesive stamps or impressed stamps or a Certificate of payment referred to in subsection (2) hereof.
why_relevant: Sets when and how the duty is to be paid, and subsection (2) allows payment to a prescribed bank against a certificate affixed to the instrument. Relevant to advising the purchaser what he must do about the duty.
temporal_note: Unamended in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: the provisions of the Stamp Duty Act, No. 43 of 1982, relating to the Imposition of Stamp Duty (other than any instrument relating to the transfer of immovable property, the transfer of motor vehicles or documents filed in Court), Exemptions and any other provision in the aforesaid Act, shall, in so far as the same are inconsistent with the provisions of this Act, have no operation
why_relevant: Confirms that instruments relating to the transfer of immovable property are carved out of the national stamp duty regime, which is why the charge on this deed is looked for in the Western Province Statute rather than in the 2006 Act.
temporal_note: In force from 2006; unamended in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: For the purposes of section 3, "specified instrument" means- (a) an affidavit; (b) a policy of insurance; (c) a warrant to act as Notary Public;
why_relevant: Background only. The closed list of specified instruments chargeable under the 2006 Act contains no conveyance or transfer of immovable property, which corroborates that the deed in this matter is not charged under that Act.
temporal_note: In force from 2006; the excerpt reproduces the opening of the list only.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless he has an assurance that the required stamp duty is provided.
why_relevant: Ties the notary's duty to the stamp duty answer: he may not attest the Deed of Transfer until he is satisfied that the duty has been provided for.
temporal_note: Rule (6) was re-enacted in identical terms by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(4); the same words were in force in October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: For the purposes of this Chapter, a minor shall be deemed to have attained majority or full age on his attaining the age of eighteen years, or on marriage, or on obtaining letters of venia aetatis.
why_relevant: Fixes the age of majority used by the Code, so that a person under eighteen is a minor who cannot validly convey immovable property by his own act. It is expressly limited to Chapter XXXVII (actions by and against minors), so it supports rather than supplies a general definition of minority.
temporal_note: In force since 1889; the eighteen-year figure comes from Act No. 12 of 1996, well before the matter date of October 2020. The text as quoted was in force in October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: Every person who shall claim a right to have charge of property in trust for a minor, under a will or deed, or by reason of nearness of kin, or otherwise, may apply to the Family Court for a certificate of curatorship; and no person shall be entitled to institute or defend any action connected with the estate of a minor, of which he claims the charge, until he shall have obtained such certificate
why_relevant: Entry point of the statutory route by which a father who wants to deal with his child's property gets recognised standing: he claims a right to have charge of the minor's property by nearness of kin and applies for a certificate of curatorship.
temporal_note: In force since 1889; last recorded change 1988 (Act No. 79 of 1988, s.41). The corpus text names the Family Court; the corpus records no amendment substituting the District Court, so the identity of the proper court cannot be settled from the corpus. The text as quoted was in force in October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: Any relative or friend of a minor, in respect of whose property such certificate has not been granted, may apply by petition in the way of summary procedure to the Family Court, to appoint a fit person to take charge of the property and person or of either property or person of such minor.
why_relevant: Gives the form of the application the father must make, a petition by way of summary procedure, and confirms that a relative such as the father is a competent applicant where no certificate has yet been granted.
temporal_note: In force since 1889, no recorded amendment. Same Family Court naming point as s.582. The text as quoted was in force in October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: If there is no person so entitled, or if such person is unwilling to undertake the trust and there is any near relative of the minor who is willing and fit to be entrusted with the charge of his property, the court may grant a certificate to such relative. (3) The court may also, if it think fit (unless a guardian has been appointed by the father), appoint such person as aforesaid or such relative, or any other relative or friend of the minor, to be guardian of the person of the minor.
why_relevant: Governs to whom the court may grant the certificate. Subsection (2) lets the court certify a near relative such as the father where no one is entitled under a will or deed; subsection (3) is the only place in the corpus that recognises a guardian appointed by the father.
temporal_note: In force since 1889, no recorded amendment. The text as quoted was in force in October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: If no title to a certificate is established to the satisfaction of the court by a person claiming under a will or deed, and if there is no near relative willing and to be entrusted with the charge of the property of the minor, and the court shall think it necessary for the interest of the minor that provision should be made by the court for the charge of the property and person of such minor, the court may grant a certificate to any fit person whom the court may appoint for the purpose.
why_relevant: The fallback where the father is not found fit or willing, and the section that s.587 refers back to as the last section when the court's power to realise the corpus is engaged.
temporal_note: In force since 1889, no recorded amendment. The text as quoted was in force in October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: The court may also fix such allowance as it may think proper for the maintenance and education of the minor; and such allowance and the allowance of the guardian (if any) shall be paid to the guardian by the other person as aforesaid. (4) In any case in which the court is satisfied that it will be for the interest of the minor, it may direct the raising of such allowance out of the corpus of the estate, by mortgage or sale or such other mode of realization as it thinks fit.
why_relevant: The only provision found in the corpus that expressly authorises the sale of a minor's property: the court, satisfied that it is in the minor's interest, may direct the maintenance and education allowance to be raised out of the corpus by sale. It is drafted as an incident of a curatorship granted under s.586 and of an allowance fixed under s.587(3), not as a free-standing power to sell whenever a good price is offered.
temporal_note: In force since 1889, no recorded amendment. The text as quoted was in force in October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: Every curator other than one deriving title under a will or deed, to whom a certificate shall have been granted under this Chapter, shall, within a time to be fixed by the court, file in court an inventory of the property belonging to the minor, and shall also twice every year, namely, within one month from the first day of January and the first day of July, respectively, in each year, file an account of the property in his charge, exhibiting the amounts received and disbursed on account of the estate and the balance in hand.
why_relevant: Part of the procedure the father would be subject to once certified: an inventory of the minor's property and half-yearly accounts, which is how the proceeds of any sale are accounted for.
temporal_note: In force since 1889, no recorded amendment. The text as quoted was in force in October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: The District Court shall have the like power to make the person appointed manager of the estate of a person of unsound mind, or mentally deficient person, or the person appointed curator of a minor's estate, give security for the due administration of the estate as it has in the case of administrators of deceased persons' estates.
why_relevant: A further procedural step: the District Court may require the certified curator to give security for the due administration of the minor's estate. It is also the one place in the corpus that names the District Court, rather than the Family Court, as the court dealing with a minor's curator.
temporal_note: In force since 1889; last recorded change 1980 (Law No. 53 of 1980, s.18). The text as quoted was in force in October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: But no such manager shall have power to sell or mortgage the estate or any part thereof, or to grant a lease of any immovable property for any period exceeding five years, without an order of the District Court previously obtained.
why_relevant: Background and contrast only. For a person of unsound mind the Code says in terms that the manager cannot sell without a prior District Court order. No equivalent express restriction on a curator or natural guardian of a minor appears in the corpus, which is why the corresponding rule for minors has to come from outside the statute.
temporal_note: In force since 1889, no recorded amendment. The text as quoted was in force in October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: shall be in force or avail in law unless - (a) the relevant deed or instrument shall be in writing, signed by every executant or by any person duly authorised by such executant and the witnesses in the presence of a licenced notary public present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and the same shall be attested by such notary
why_relevant: The form the sale must take: whoever is authorised to convey the minor's land must do so by a written deed signed before and attested by a notary public, otherwise the sale has no effect in law.
temporal_note: The requirement of a notarially attested writing for a sale of land has stood since 1840 and was in force in October 2020. The wording quoted, however, is the consolidated text after the Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Acts No. 30 of 2022 and No. 4 of 2024, both later than the matter date, and the corpus does not hold the pre-2022 text. Subsection (2), including the rule about a guardian acting for a minor transferee, was inserted by the 2022 amendment and was not in force in October 2020, so it is not relied on.

relevant_excerpt: An instrument executed or made on or after the 1st day of January, 1864, whether before or after the commencement of this Ordinance shall, unless it is duly registered under this Chapter, or, if the land has come within the operation of the Land Registration Ordinance, 1877f, in the books mentioned in section 26 of that Ordinance, be void as against all parties claiming an adverse interest thereto on valuable consideration by virtue of any subsequent instrument which is duly registered under this Chapter
why_relevant: The last step of the conveyancing procedure: the deed of transfer should be registered in the land registry, failing which it is void against a later registered instrument taken for value.
temporal_note: In force since 1927; no amendment recorded in the corpus edition, which is consolidated to 1990. The text as quoted was in force in October 2020.

relevant_excerpt: The following sections of this Ordinance shall apply to the estates of such persons only as shall die after the proclamation of this Ordinance
why_relevant: Fixes the temporal scope of Part III. Sunil Peiris died in 2016, long after the proclamation, so the intestacy rules in sections 21 to 36 apply to his estate.
temporal_note: Section stands as originally enacted; the corpus records no amendment event, so the text was in force at the date of death (6 December 2016) and at the matter reference date 2020-04.

relevant_excerpt: Inheritance ab interstate to the immovable property in Sri Lanka of a person deceased shall be governed and regulated by the following provisions of this Ordinance wherever such person may have or have had his actual or matrimonial domicile.
why_relevant: Lot B and the undivided one-third share of Lot R are immovable property in Sri Lanka, so devolution on Sunil Peiris's intestacy is governed by this Ordinance rather than by any other system of personal law.
temporal_note: Section stands as originally enacted; the corpus records no amendment event, so the text was in force at the date of death (6 December 2016) and at the matter reference date 2020-04.

relevant_excerpt: When any person shall die intestate as to any of his or her property, leaving a spouse surviving, the surviving spouse shall inherit one-half of the property of such person.
why_relevant: Gives the widow Kusum Peiris one-half of Sunil Peiris's estate, which is the first and largest step in the devolution of Lot B after his death.
temporal_note: Section stands as originally enacted; the corpus records no amendment event, so the text was in force at the date of death (6 December 2016) and at the matter reference date 2020-04.

relevant_excerpt: Subject to the right of the surviving spouse in the preceding section mentioned, the right of inheritance is divided in the following order as respects (a) descendants, (b) ascendants, (c) collaterals.
why_relevant: Sets the order in which the remaining half devolves and confirms that the widow's half is taken off the top before descendants, ascendants and collaterals are considered.
temporal_note: Section stands as originally enacted; the corpus records no amendment event, so the text was in force at the date of death (6 December 2016) and at the matter reference date 2020-04.

relevant_excerpt: Children, grandchildren, and remoter descendants are preferent to all others in the estate of the parents; all the children take equally per capita
why_relevant: Establishes that descendants would exclude everyone else. Sunil Peiris died without children, so the descendant class fails and the next class must be reached.
temporal_note: Section stands as originally enacted; the corpus records no amendment event, so the text was in force at the date of death (6 December 2016) and at the matter reference date 2020-04.

relevant_excerpt: The children and remoter descendants failing, the inheritance of the deceased goes to his father and mother in case they are both alive; but if only one of the parents be alive, the surviving parent takes half, and the brothers and sisters of the deceased of the full blood, and the issue of any deceased brother or sister of the full blood, by representation, and the brothers and sisters of the half-blood who are related to the intestate by the side of the deceased parent, and the issue of any such deceased brother or sister of the half-blood, by representation, take the other half.
why_relevant: The operative rule. Sunil's father Charles Peiris predeceased him and his mother Pushpa Peiris survived, so Pushpa takes half of the remaining half and the full siblings together with the half-siblings related through the deceased father take the other half. It is also the provision that excludes Keerthi Perera, who is related only through the surviving parent.
temporal_note: Section stands as originally enacted; the corpus records no amendment event, so the text was in force at the date of death (6 December 2016) and at the matter reference date 2020-04.

relevant_excerpt: but if there are only half-brothers and sisters or such issue of one side, the full brothers and sisters and the issue of deceased full brothers and sisters by representation, take then in the first place one-half of the property, and divide the other half with the half-brothers and sisters and their issue by representation.
why_relevant: Governs how the collateral portion is split where the qualifying half-siblings are all on one side. Here only the paternal half-siblings Upul and Wimal qualify, so the full sisters Kanthi and Manel take one-half of the collateral portion first and share the balance with Upul and Wimal.
temporal_note: Section stands as originally enacted; the corpus records no amendment event, so the text was in force at the date of death (6 December 2016) and at the matter reference date 2020-04.
verifier_note: Excerpt and role confirmed against 15-1876/s27; the final limb was applied on the footing that section 25 admits only the paternal half-blood where the mother survives, so within the collateral half there are half-siblings of one side only. An alternative reading that divides the collateral half equally among all four siblings is arguable and would change the fractions; raised for the lawyer, not treated as a defect.

relevant_excerpt: if all those who succeed to the inheritance are equally near in degree to the intestate, they take per capita, and not per stirpes
why_relevant: Supplies the per capita basis on which the four surviving siblings divide the portion they share under section 27, all of them being in the same degree and all taking in their own right.
temporal_note: Section stands as originally enacted; the corpus records no amendment event, so the text was in force at the date of death (6 December 2016) and at the matter reference date 2020-04.

relevant_excerpt: the relevant deed or instrument shall be in writing, signed by every executant or by any person duly authorised by such executant and the witnesses in the presence of a licenced notary public present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and the same shall be attested by such notary
why_relevant: Explains why Deed of Transfer No. 234 of 23 March 2015 attested by a notary public is the form each link in the chain of title must take, and why every earlier and later link must likewise be a notarially attested instrument.
temporal_note: The corpus holds the consolidated text, which incorporates the Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Acts No. 30 of 2022 and No. 4 of 2024 (thumb impression and transferee execution requirements). Those substitutions post-date both the 2015 deed and the matter reference date 2020-04, so this provision is treated as supporting only and not as indispensable. The requirement of writing, witnesses and notarial attestation quoted here is the long-standing core of the section.
verifier_note: Wording verified but temporally corrected: the quoted paragraph (a) is the text substituted by the Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 4 of 2024 s.2(2)(a). At the date of Deed No. 234 (2015) and at 2020-04 section 2 required the writing to be signed by the party in the presence of a licensed notary and two or more witnesses and attested by them; the substance relied on, that a transfer of immovable property must be by a notarially attested deed, held then, the quoted words did not.

relevant_excerpt: Every deed or other instrument, except any will, testament, or codicil required by this Ordinance to be executed or acknowledged before or to be attested by a notary, shall be executed, acknowledged, or attested in triplicate.
why_relevant: Background on why three copies of a notarial deed exist (original, duplicate and protocol), which is what makes a certified copy obtainable from either the Land Registry or the attesting notary.
temporal_note: Amended in 2022, after the matter reference date; used as background only.
verifier_note: Temporal correction: triplicate is the word substituted by the Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 30 of 2022 s.5. At 2020-04 section 16 read in duplicate. The background point (original, duplicate and protocol) survives, but the Q03 rule statement that deeds are executed in triplicate under s.16 is anachronistic for this matter.

relevant_excerpt: be void as against all parties claiming an adverse interest thereto on valuable consideration by virtue of any subsequent instrument which is duly registered under this Chapter
why_relevant: Registration priority. It is why the devolution has to be traced through the Land Registry folios and why a search at the Colombo Land Registry is the step that tests whether the paper chain is also the registered chain.
temporal_note: Section stands as originally enacted; the corpus records no amendment event, so the text was in force at the date of death (6 December 2016) and at the matter reference date 2020-04.

relevant_excerpt: If the land consists of an undivided share in a land, the proportion which the share bears to the entire land shall be staled, and a description of the entire land shall be given as required by subsection (1).
why_relevant: Relevant to the description of Lot B as a divided allotment and of the one-third share of the road reservation Lot R as an undivided share, both of which must be described in the deed and traced separately.
temporal_note: Last amended in 1982, before the matter reference date.

relevant_excerpt: all duplicates and copies and all books and indexes kept under this Ordinance may be searched and examined by any person claiming to be interested therein or by his attorney-at-law or agent duly authorized thereto in writing, and certified copies of or extracts from any such duplicate, copy, or book may be obtained if required.
why_relevant: The statutory basis on which the purchaser's attorney-at-law may search the Colombo Land Registry and obtain certified copies of and extracts from the folios and registered duplicates relating to the land.
temporal_note: Section stands as originally enacted; the corpus records no amendment event, so the text was in force at the date of death (6 December 2016) and at the matter reference date 2020-04.

relevant_excerpt: A copy or extract purporting to be certified under the hand of a Registrar to be a true copy of or extract from any duplicate or copy preserved under this Ordinance or of or from any book kept pursuant to this Ordinance shall be admissible in evidence without proof of the signature or appointment of the Registrar, and shall be prima facie evidence of the contents of such duplicate, copy, or book
why_relevant: Gives the certified folio extract and certified copies of registered duplicates their evidentiary value, which is what makes them worth obtaining as proof of the chain of title rather than mere information.
temporal_note: Section stands as originally enacted; the corpus records no amendment event, so the text was in force at the date of death (6 December 2016) and at the matter reference date 2020-04.

subsection: rule requiring a search of the land registry
relevant_excerpt: Before any deed or instrument (other than a will or codicil) affecting any interest in land or other immovable property is drawn by him, he shall search or cause to be searched the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title in regard to such land and whether any prior deed affecting any interest in such land has been registered
why_relevant: Puts the title search on a statutory footing as a duty of the notary who will draw the conveyance to the purchaser, and so identifies the search and its supporting documents as a necessary step before the sale is completed.
temporal_note: The corpus holds the consolidated section 31, which the Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 and the Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 6 of 2024 substituted in several places after the matter reference date; in particular the sub-paragraph requiring the notary to obtain a certified extract of the folio was substituted by No. 31 of 2022 (s.16). The quoted chapeau creating the search duty is not part of the substituted text, but because the section as held is a post-2022 consolidation this provision is used as supporting only, not as indispensable.
verifier_note: Rule (17)(a), the search duty quoted here, was not touched by the Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or No. 6 of 2024 s.3, both of which amend only paragraph (b) of rule (17); the quoted duty was therefore in force at 2020-04. The certified-folio-extract sub-paragraph is post-date and is not relied on.

relevant_excerpt: furnish to such person copies of the judgment, decree or proceedings in an action or any part thereof
why_relevant: The route by which certified copies of the final decree in the partition action and of the proceedings in the testamentary case are obtained from the District Court record.
temporal_note: Section 205 was substituted by Act No. 20 of 2023, after the matter reference date 2020-04, so it is used as supporting only and not as indispensable. The verifier should confirm the pre-2023 wording of the entitlement to certified copies.
verifier_note: Section 205 was wholly substituted by Act No. 20 of 2023, after the matter reference date, and the corpus holds only the substituted text, so the pre-2023 entitlement to certified copies cannot be established from the corpus. Correctly kept as supporting rather than indispensable; the excerpt should not be quoted as the 2020 wording.

relevant_excerpt: The decree or such certified copy thereof shall constitute the sole primary evidence of the decision or order passed by the court.
why_relevant: Explains why a certified copy of the final decree in the partition action is the document that has to be produced to prove what the court decided about the original land.
temporal_note: Section stands as originally enacted; the corpus records no amendment event, so the text was in force at the date of death (6 December 2016) and at the matter reference date 2020-04.

relevant_excerpt: The certificates of heir ship issued under subsection (1) (b) (ii) above shall be sufficient proof of the true heirs of the deceased referred to therein, and may be produced for the purpose of claiming any share in respect of any right, title or interest, accruing upon intestacy.
why_relevant: Identifies the District Court order or certificate of heirship in the testamentary case as the document that proves who the heirs of Sunil Peiris are and what share each takes, which is exactly the link the purchaser must document.
temporal_note: Last amended in 1993, before the matter reference date; Testamentary Case No. 345/16/T concluded on 7 May 2018, also before that date.

relevant_excerpt: A duplicate of any probate or letters of administration sealed with the seal of the court granting the same, or a copy thereof certified as correct by or under the authority of such court shall have the same effect as the original
why_relevant: Confirms that a sealed duplicate or certified copy of the letters of administration issued in the testamentary case may be relied on in place of the original.
temporal_note: Last amended in 1977, before the matter reference date.
verifier_note: Section 554X sits in the FOREIGN PROBATES chapter (ss.554U-554BB) and, with the interpretation in s.554BB, applies to probate or letters of administration granted by a foreign court and resealed in Sri Lanka. It does not govern the grant made by the District Court in Testamentary Case No. 345/16/T, so it does not support the proposition for which it was cited.

relevant_excerpt: No plan or map or copy or tracing of a plan or map shall be receivable in evidence in any court in Sri Lanka unless such plan or map has been prepared
why_relevant: Sets the condition a survey plan must satisfy to be usable as proof, and so supports requiring a plan certified by a registered licensed surveyor when Lot B and Lot R are identified on the ground against Plan No. 1125 and Partition Plan No. 567.
temporal_note: Section stands as originally enacted; the corpus records no amendment event, so the text was in force at the date of death (6 December 2016) and at the matter reference date 2020-04.

relevant_excerpt: unless grant of probate has been issued in the case of a person dying testate, or letters of administration or certificates of heirship have been issued in the case of a person dying intestate
why_relevant: Added by the verifier in place of the rejected section 554X. It is the provision that makes the testamentary-case documents legally necessary rather than merely useful: no transfer may be effected of property in the estate of a person who died within the five years before the transfer unless letters of administration or certificates of heirship have issued. Sunil Peiris died on 6 December 2016, so a conveyance at the matter reference date 2020-04 falls inside that window and the purchaser must see the grant made in District Court Testamentary Case No. 345/16/T.
temporal_note: Last substituted by Act No. 11 of 2010, before the death, before the termination of the testamentary case on 7 May 2018 and before the matter reference date 2020-04.
verifier_note: Excerpt checked verbatim against 2-1889/s545.

relevant_excerpt: if the present Ordinance is silent, the rules of the Roman-Dutch law as it prevailed in North Holland are to govern and be followed
why_relevant: Added by the verifier because M068-Q02's authority_requirement_reason turns on it but no provision entry carried it. It is the provision that makes Roman-Dutch law residual only, and so the provision on which the statute_only classification of Q02 depends: the Ordinance is not silent on any step of this distribution, so the enquiry never leaves the statute.
temporal_note: Section stands as originally enacted; the corpus records no amendment event, so it was in force at the date of death and at 2020-04.
verifier_note: Excerpt checked verbatim against 15-1876/s36.

relevant_excerpt: Any person (in this section called a " transferee") acquiring or proposing to acquire for valuable consideration from any other person (in this section called the " transferor") any interest or benefit in any land may before the execution of the instrument by the transferor with his written consent, or after the execution of the instrument by the transferor without such consent, present for registration a notice (in this Ordinance called a " priority notice ") of his intention to register the instrument.
temporal_note: In force from 1927; no amendment to section 30 appears in the corpus. The Registration of Documents (Amendment) Acts in the corpus that post-date the matter (No. 32 of 2022, No. 18 of 2024) touch sections 8, 25, 29, 32, 33, 41, 50 and the Schedules, not section 30.
why_relevant: This is the provision that creates the notice the Bank asked for: a priority notice of the transferee's intention to register the instrument. It fixes who the parties to the notice are (transferee and transferor), that the acquisition must be for valuable consideration, and whether the transferor's written consent must appear on the face of the notice (needed if it is lodged before execution of the deed, not needed after).

relevant_excerpt: The Registrar shall, on receiving a priority notice, register it in the same manner as other instruments, but shall retain the notice.
temporal_note: In force from 1927; unamended in the corpus as at April 2020.
why_relevant: This is the bridge between the priority notice and the ordinary presentation rules. Because the Registrar registers the notice 'in the same manner as other instruments', the drafting requirements that apply to instruments presented for registration (section 13(1) description of land, section 13(7) folio reference at the head) govern the notice as well, and because the Registrar retains the notice a duplicate must be tendered for endorsement.

relevant_excerpt: Every instrument (except a will) presented for registration shall contain embodied therein, or in a schedule annexed thereto, an accurate and clear description of the land affected thereby, its boundaries, extent, and situation specifying the district and the village, pattu, korale, or other division of the district in which the land is situated; and in case the land is situated in any town, the name, if any, of the street in which it is situated.
temporal_note: In force from 1927. The corpus records a 1982 change to section 13 (Registration of Documents No. 50 of 1982 s.2) and Registration of Documents (Amendment) Act No. 21 of 2013 s.5 amends only the fee words in subsection (6). Subsection (1) as reproduced in the consolidated text was in force in April 2020.
why_relevant: Supplies the content of the schedule to the drafted notice: the land must be described by boundaries, extent and situation, with the district and the division, and (the premises being in a town) the name of the street. It is why the draft cannot simply say 'Assessment No. 23, 1st Lane, Ratmalana' but must add boundaries, extent and district.

relevant_excerpt: There shall be typewritten or written in ink at the head of every instrument (except a will) presented for registration a reference to the volume and folio in which some earlier instrument relating to the same land is registered
temporal_note: In force from 1927; the corpus shows no change to subsection (7) before April 2020.
why_relevant: Explains the Bank's instruction to submit the notice 'together with the folio': the volume and folio in which an earlier instrument affecting the same land is registered must appear at the head of the document presented for registration.

relevant_excerpt: The forms contained in the Second Schedule shall be used with such variations as circumstances may require, but such Schedule may be altered or added to by regulation.
temporal_note: In force from 1927. Registration of Documents (Amendment) Act No. 32 of 2022 s.4 amends section 50 and s.5 replaces a Second Schedule form, but both post-date April 2020 and are not applied here.
why_relevant: A drafting answer must reproduce the statutory form. Section 50 makes the Second Schedule form mandatory (subject to variation as circumstances require), and that Schedule is not in the corpus, so the prescribed wording of the priority notice cannot be verified from the frozen corpus. This is the provision that blocks the question.

relevant_excerpt: A priority notice shall remain in force for six weeks from the date of registration of the notice
temporal_note: In force from 1927; unamended in the corpus as at April 2020.
why_relevant: Fixes the currency of the notice and therefore the date the draft must carry and the deadline within which the transfer deed and mortgage bond must be executed and registered; it also supports a renewal clause where the six weeks are likely to run out.

relevant_excerpt: any person claiming any interest or benefit thereunder; (c) any person having any interest in or charge on any property affected thereby; or (d) the agent of any such person or a attorney-at-law or notary acting on behalf of any such person.
temporal_note: In force from 1927; unamended in the corpus as at April 2020.
why_relevant: Identifies who may sign and present the notice at the Land Registry, so the draft may be subscribed by the transferee himself or by the notary or attorney-at-law acting for him.

relevant_excerpt: An endorsement by the Registrar in the prescribed form on a duplicate of an application for registration of a lis pendens, or on a duplicate of a priority notice or seizure priority notice or an application for renewal of such a notice, or on a duplicate of a caveat shall be admissible in evidence without proof of the signature or appointment of the Registrar
temporal_note: In force from 1927; unamended in the corpus as at April 2020.
why_relevant: Shows that the notice is tendered in duplicate: the Registrar retains the original under section 30(4) and endorses the duplicate, and that endorsed duplicate is the proof of registration the Bank will want before releasing the loan.

relevant_excerpt: If, at any time while a priority notice remains in force, any instrument is registered whereby the transferee or a person deriving title under him acquires for valuable consideration from the transferor or a person deriving title under him any interest or benefit in the land described in the priority notice, such instrument shall, for the purposes of this Ordinance, be deemed to have been registered at the time of registration of the priority notice.
temporal_note: In force from 1927; unamended in the corpus as at April 2020.
why_relevant: Background to the drafting task: it is this back-dating effect that makes the notice worth lodging and that explains why the instrument the notice describes must be identified accurately in the draft.

formal_title: Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act, No. 12 of 2006
relevant_excerpt: there shall be charged a duty (hereinafter to be called "stamp duty") at such rate as the Minister may determine by Order published in the Gazette on every "specified instrument"- (a) executed, drawn or presented in Sri Lanka
why_relevant: The charging provision. It is the source of the liability to stamp duty on the mortgage bond and it is also the reason the quantum cannot be computed from the corpus: the rate is not in the Act but in a Ministerial Order published in the Gazette, which is not in the corpus.
temporal_note: In force from 2006; no amendment events recorded for this section. In force at 2020-04.

formal_title: Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act, No. 12 of 2006
relevant_excerpt: (g) a bond or mortgage for any definite and certain sum of money and affecting any property;
why_relevant: Defines "specified instrument" for the purposes of section 3 and brings the mortgage bond within the charge. The bond secures a definite and certain sum (Rs. 3,000,000) and affects the Ratmalana property, so it falls within paragraph (g).
temporal_note: In force from 2006; no amendment events recorded for this section. In force at 2020-04.

formal_title: Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act, No. 12 of 2006
relevant_excerpt: (e) in all other cases, by the person drawing, making or executing such instrument.
why_relevant: The question asks for the duty payable by him. A mortgage is not within paragraphs (a) to (ddd), so the residual paragraph (e) applies and the duty falls on the person executing the bond, that is the mortgagor Gamini Perera, subject to the opening words of the section allowing an agreement to the contrary.
temporal_note: In force from 2006; amended by Act No. 10 of 2008 s.2, which inserted paragraphs (dd) and (ddd). The corpus text is the consolidated post-2008 text, in force at 2020-04.

formal_title: Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act, No. 12 of 2006
relevant_excerpt: Stamp duty payable on any specified instrument relating to a mortgage or lease of any immovable property may be paid, prior to, or at the time of, the execution of the specified instrument, to a prescribed bank.
why_relevant: Supporting: it governs how and when the computed duty on a mortgage of immovable property is to be paid, which matters because this bond is to be executed simultaneously with the transfer. It does not affect the amount.
temporal_note: In force from 2006; substituted by Act No. 10 of 2008 s.3. The corpus text is the consolidated post-2008 text, in force at 2020-04.

formal_title: Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act, No. 12 of 2006
relevant_excerpt: the provisions of the Stamp Duty Act, No. 43 of 1982, relating to the Imposition of Stamp Duty (other than any instrument relating to the transfer of immovable property, the transfer of motor vehicles or documents filed in Court), Exemptions and any other provision in the aforesaid Act, shall, in so far as the same are inconsistent with the provisions of this Act, have no operation and the provisions of this Act shall prevail.
why_relevant: Fixes which of the two stamp duty statutes in the corpus governs a mortgage bond. A mortgage is not a transfer of immovable property, a motor vehicle transfer or a court document, so the imposition of duty on this bond is governed by Act No. 12 of 2006 wherever the 1982 Act is inconsistent with it.
temporal_note: In force from 2006; no amendment events recorded. In force at 2020-04.

relevant_excerpt: A bond or mortgage for the payment or repayment of money to be lent, advanced, or paid shall be charged, where the total amount secured or to be ultimately recoverable is in any way limited, with the same stamp duty as on a bond or mortgage for the amount so limited.
why_relevant: Supporting only: it states the computation base for a bond securing money to be lent, namely the limited sum secured. It supports treating Rs. 3,000,000 as the base if it still operates, but its continued operation after section 13 of Act No. 12 of 2006 is not resolvable from the corpus, so nothing indispensable rests on it.
temporal_note: In force from 1982; no amendment events recorded. Its operation at 2020-04 is qualified by section 13 of Act No. 12 of 2006, which disapplies provisions of the 1982 Act relating to the imposition of stamp duty in so far as they are inconsistent with the 2006 Act. Treated as supporting, not indispensable, for that reason.

relevant_excerpt: (12) He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless the person executing the same and the witnesses shall have signed the same in his presence and in the presence of one another, and unless he shall have signed the same in the presence of the executant and of the attesting witnesses.
why_relevant: The core rule. A notary may attest only signatures placed before him: the executant and the witnesses must sign in his presence and in the presence of one another, and he must sign in their presence. Nimal Perera therefore cannot attest the bedridden father's signature placed in Kandy before another notary.
temporal_note: Section 31 is held in the corpus as a consolidated text carrying later amendments, but this rule was not touched by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or No. 6 of 2024 s.3; the wording relied on was in force in April 2020.

relevant_excerpt: (22) He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument in any area other than that in which he is authorized to practice, nor in any language other than that in which he is authorized to practice nor authenticate or attest any deed or instrument drawn in any language other than that in which he is authorized to practice.
why_relevant: Territorial limit on attestation. A notary authorised for Colombo cannot attest in Kandy, so Nimal Perera cannot cure the problem by travelling to the father.
temporal_note: Section 31 is held in the corpus as a consolidated text carrying later amendments, but this rule was not touched by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or No. 6 of 2024 s.3; the wording relied on was in force in April 2020.

relevant_excerpt: (25) Where any deed or instrument is executed or acknowledged before more than one notary- (a) the notary who first attests such deed or instrument shall comply with all the requirements of rule (20), and every other notary attesting such deed or instrument shall comply with the requirements of paragraphs (a) to (e) of the aforesaid rule and the provisions of paragraph (g) in respect of erasures, alterations and interpolations made in the signatures attested by him or in his serial number;
why_relevant: The Ordinance expressly contemplates one deed executed before more than one notary, and allocates the attestation duties between the notary who first attests and every other attesting notary. This is the mechanism that makes the proposed two-notary execution lawful.
temporal_note: Section 31 is held in the corpus as a consolidated text carrying later amendments, but this rule was not touched by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or No. 6 of 2024 s.3; the wording relied on was in force in April 2020.

relevant_excerpt: (b) every notary attesting the deed or instrument shall number such deed or instrument in accordance with the provisions of rule (23);
why_relevant: Each attesting notary must give the deed a number in his own consecutive series, so the deed will bear two numbers, one from the Colombo notary and one from the Kandy notary.
temporal_note: Section 31 is held in the corpus as a consolidated text carrying later amendments, but this rule was not touched by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or No. 6 of 2024 s.3; the wording relied on was in force in April 2020.

relevant_excerpt: (c) the notary who first attests such deed or instrument shall preserve as his protocol the draft or copy referred to in rule (24), and shall comply with the requirements of that rule, and every other notary attesting such deed or instrument shall supply himself with a certified copy of the deed or instrument, which shall be deemed to be his protocol for the purposes of that rule; and (d) every notary attesting such deed shall, in addition, as far as possible, comply with the other provisions of section 31.
why_relevant: Allocates the protocol: the notary who first attests keeps the protocol under rule (24); the other notary must supply himself with a certified copy which is deemed his protocol. Both must otherwise comply with section 31 as far as possible.
temporal_note: Section 31 is held in the corpus as a consolidated text carrying later amendments, but this rule was not touched by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or No. 6 of 2024 s.3; the wording relied on was in force in April 2020.

relevant_excerpt: (2) In the case of any deed or instrument which is to be executed by two or more parties, both or all of whom, as the case may be, do not sign the deed or instrument at the same time and place- (i) the deed or instrument shall, for the purposes of the application of rules (6), (7), (23) and (25) set out in section 31, be deemed to be executed or acknowledged at the time when it is first signed by a party, or by two or more parties at the same time and place;
why_relevant: The special-case provision for exactly this fact pattern: parties who do not sign at the same time and place. It fixes the time of execution for rules (6), (7), (23) and (25) at the first signing.
temporal_note: Section unamended since enactment (no amendment events in the corpus); in force at April 2020.

relevant_excerpt: (ii) the deed or instrument shall, for the purposes of the application of rules (18) and (20) set out in section 31, be deemed to be executed or acknowledged whenever it is signed by a party, or by two or more parties at the same time and place; and (iii) the provisions of rule (19) set out in section 31, shall apply after the deed or instrument is first signed by a party, or by two or more parties at the same time and place.
why_relevant: For the date and place rule (18) and the attestation rule (20) the deed is deemed executed on each occasion of signing, so each notary dates and attests his own execution; rule (19), which bars alteration after signature, bites from the first signing.
temporal_note: Section unamended since enactment (no amendment events in the corpus); in force at April 2020.

relevant_excerpt: (28) Where any deed or instrument other than a will or codicil shall be executed or acknowledged by two or more parties before more than one notary, the duplicate of such deed or instrument shall be delivered or transmitted by the notary who first attests such deed or instrument to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which he resides; and it shall not be necessary for the other notary or notaries employed in the execution of such deed or instrument to deliver or transmit any duplicate thereof to such registrar.
why_relevant: Where two or more parties execute before more than one notary, only the notary who first attests transmits the duplicate to his district Registrar of Lands; the other notary need not.
temporal_note: Section 31 is held in the corpus as a consolidated text carrying later amendments, but this rule was not touched by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or No. 6 of 2024 s.3; the wording relied on was in force in April 2020.

relevant_excerpt: (i) where any deed or instrument which is to be executed or acknowledged by two or more parties is signed during any month by one or more, as the case may be, of such parties, the notary shall, notwithstanding that the deed or instrument has not been signed by all such-parties, include such deed or instrument in the list required to be delivered or transmitted under paragraph (a)
why_relevant: A part-executed deed must still be included in the monthly list, and the duplicate produced for inspection if the Registrar of Lands calls for it. Relevant because the deed will be incomplete between the two executions.
temporal_note: Section 31 is held in the corpus as a consolidated text carrying later amendments, but this rule was not touched by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or No. 6 of 2024 s.3; the wording relied on was in force in April 2020.
verifier_note: Wording is verbatim, but the corpus consolidated text of section 31 has lost the "(26)" and paragraph "(a)/(c)" markers (the passage runs straight on after rule (25)(d)), so the subsection label "rule (26)(c)(i)" is reconstructed from the cross-references in 6-2024 s.3(8) and section 34(2) rather than read off the corpus; the excerpt also stops before the words "and shall, if called upon so to do ... produce the duplicate ... for inspection", which claim CL-M071-Q01-009 relies on and which are present in the corpus body.

relevant_excerpt: (ii) where any such deed or instrument is not signed by all the parties thereto before the expiry of a period of three months from the date on which it is first signed by one of such parties, the notary shall, if called upon so to do by written notice served on him personally or by registered post and signed by the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the notary resides, deliver or transmit to the registrar the duplicate of such deed or instrument;
why_relevant: Sets the outer limit for completing a split execution: if all parties have not signed within three months of the first signature, the notary may be called on to deliver the duplicate to the registrar.
temporal_note: Section 31 is held in the corpus as a consolidated text carrying later amendments, but this rule was not touched by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or No. 6 of 2024 s.3; the wording relied on was in force in April 2020.
verifier_note: Wording is verbatim and unaffected by 31-2022 s.16 or 6-2024 s.3, but the subsection label "rule (26)(c)(ii)" is reconstructed: the corpus consolidated text does not print the "(26)" or "(c)" markers.

relevant_excerpt: (18) He shall correctly insert in letters in every deed or instrument executed before him the day, month, and year on which and the place where the same is executed, and shall sign the same.
why_relevant: Each notary must insert in letters the day, month and year and the place of execution, so the Colombo and Kandy executions must be separately and correctly dated and located on the deed.
temporal_note: Section 31 is held in the corpus as a consolidated text carrying later amendments, but this rule was not touched by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or No. 6 of 2024 s.3; the wording relied on was in force in April 2020.

relevant_excerpt: (20) He shall without delay duly attest every deed or instrument which shall be executed or acknowledged before him, and shall sign and seal such attestation. In such attestation he shall state- (a) that the said deed or instrument was signed by the party and the witnesses thereto in his presence and in the presence of one another;
why_relevant: Each notary must attest without delay, sign and seal, and state that the party and the witnesses signed in his presence and in the presence of one another. Each notary can only certify the execution he actually witnessed.
temporal_note: Section 31 is held in the corpus as a consolidated text carrying later amendments, but this rule was not touched by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or No. 6 of 2024 s.3; the wording relied on was in force in April 2020.

relevant_excerpt: (c) the day, month, and year on which and the place where the said deed or instrument was executed or acknowledged, and the full names of the attesting witnesses and their residences;
why_relevant: The attestation must record the date and place of the execution and the attesting witnesses, which is what keeps the two separate executions distinguishable on the face of the deed.
temporal_note: Section 31 is held in the corpus as a consolidated text carrying later amendments, but this rule was not touched by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or No. 6 of 2024 s.3; the wording relied on was in force in April 2020.

relevant_excerpt: (8) He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument to which at least two witnesses have not subscribed their signatures in letters.
why_relevant: At least two witnesses must subscribe. Each of the two executions, in Kandy and in Colombo, needs its own two attesting witnesses signing in the presence of the notary attesting it.
temporal_note: Section 31 is held in the corpus as a consolidated text carrying later amendments, but this rule was not touched by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or No. 6 of 2024 s.3; the wording relied on was in force in April 2020.

relevant_excerpt: (23) He shall number with consecutive integral numbers the documents executed or acknowledged before him, including wills and codicils, according to the order in which they are executed or acknowledged before him.
why_relevant: The numbering rule that rule (25)(b) applies to each attesting notary separately.
temporal_note: Section 31 is held in the corpus as a consolidated text carrying later amendments, but this rule was not touched by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or No. 6 of 2024 s.3; the wording relied on was in force in April 2020.

relevant_excerpt: (24) He shall carefully preserve as his protocol a draft or copy of every deed or instrument executed or acknowledged before him, to which shall be attached his signature and those of the party and witnesses to the original deed or instrument, and he shall keep a register thereof with a convenient index for the purpose of easy reference;
why_relevant: The protocol and register obligation that rule (25)(c) splits between the first attesting notary and the other notary.
temporal_note: Section 31 is held in the corpus as a consolidated text carrying later amendments, but this rule was not touched by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or No. 6 of 2024 s.3; the wording relied on was in force in April 2020.

relevant_excerpt: (29) If a deed or instrument other than a will or codicil affects a land situated in a district other than that in which the notary before whom it is signed, and by whom it is attested, 'shall reside, such notary, or in case such deed or instrument is attested by two or more notaries, then the notary upon whom is cast the duty of transmitting to the Registrar of Lands the duplicate of such deed or instrument, shall on or before the fifteenth day of the month next following that in which the same was executed (besides transmitting the duplicate in manner aforesaid) deliver or transmit to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which such land shall be situated a copy thereof certified by him as correct
why_relevant: If the land partitioned lies in a district other than that in which the transmitting notary resides, a certified copy must also go to the Registrar of Lands of the district where the land is situated. Background here because the location of the land is not stated in the facts.
temporal_note: Section 31 is held in the corpus as a consolidated text carrying later amendments, but this rule was not touched by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or No. 6 of 2024 s.3; the wording relied on was in force in April 2020.
verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim and the quoted words were unchanged at April 2020, but the temporal note is wrong to say rule (29) was not touched by 6-2024 s.3: s.3(9) substituted "in the Form F 1" for "in the Form F" in that rule, in the part of it that falls after the end of this excerpt.

relevant_excerpt: No instrument shall be deemed to be invalid by reason only of the failure of any notary to observe any provision of any rule set out in section 31 in respect of any matter of form:
why_relevant: Non-compliance with a rule in section 31 that is a matter of form does not by itself invalidate the instrument. Background: it does not save a breach of rule (12), which goes to the fact of execution and not to form.
temporal_note: Section unamended since enactment (no amendment events in the corpus); in force at April 2020.

relevant_excerpt: (c) any other rule set out in section 31, shall be guilty of an offence, and shall, on conviction after summary trial before a Magistrate, be liable to a fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, in addition to any civil liability he may incur thereby.
why_relevant: Breach of a section 31 rule other than those separately listed is an offence punishable on summary trial, in addition to civil liability. Shows the consequence for Nimal Perera if he attested a signature not made before him.
temporal_note: Section 34 was replaced by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.17, so the fine levels in the corpus text post-date April 2020. The shape of the offence, that breach of a section 31 rule is punishable on summary trial in addition to civil liability, predates the matter, but the quoted penalty figure does not. Treated as supporting only and marked not applicable to the matter date.
verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim and the researcher is right to mark it inapplicable at the matter date, but the corpus holds only the text substituted by 31-2022 s.17, so nothing in the corpus establishes the April 2020 shape of the offence or its penalty; treat it as supporting background only.

relevant_excerpt: Every notary shall be bound to have his office within the area specified in his warrant; and any notary infringing this provision shall be liable to have his warrant withdrawn by the Minister.
why_relevant: Background to rule (22): a notary is tied to the area specified in his warrant.
temporal_note: Section unamended since enactment (no amendment events in the corpus); in force at April 2020.

relevant_excerpt: Every warrant issued to a notary under the provisions of section 3* or section 4* authorizing him to practice as a notary in any judicial division in which he resides, shall be deemed to authorize him to practice as a notary in the judicial zone in which he resides.
why_relevant: Background: a warrant for a judicial division is deemed to authorise practice in the judicial zone in which the notary resides, which fixes the outer reach of the area referred to in rule (22).
temporal_note: Section unamended since enactment (no amendment events in the corpus); in force at April 2020.
verifier_note: Text and 2020 applicability are right, but the temporal note is wrong to say there are no amendment events: section 4A was inserted by Notaries (Amendment) Law No. 20 of 1976 s.4 and has been in force since 1976.

relevant_excerpt: (19) He shall not make any erasure, alteration, or interpolation in any deed or instrument after the same has been signed by the executing party or parties.
why_relevant: Added by the verifier. Section 32(2)(iii) only names rule (19); the map's claims that nothing may be altered after the first signature depend on what rule (19) actually says, so the rule itself has to be on the map.
temporal_note: Rule (19) was not amended by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or No. 6 of 2024 s.3 (neither Act lists rule (19)); the wording was in force in April 2020.
verifier_note: Added by the verifier; excerpt checked verbatim against 1-1907/s31.

relevant_excerpt: Every appointment to the office of notary shall be by warrant granted by the Minister, and shall specify the area within which, and the language or languages in which, the person appointed is authorized to practice.
why_relevant: Source of the territorial limit on a notary's competence: the warrant, not the Ordinance at large, fixes the area within which Gayan Alwis may act. His warrant covers the Galle High Court jurisdiction only.
temporal_note: In force from 1907; the corpus records no amendment event on this section, so the text quoted is the text in force in April 2020.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument in any area other than that in which he is authorized to practice, nor in any language other than that in which he is authorized to practice
why_relevant: The operative prohibition. It bars Gayan Alwis from attesting a deed anywhere outside the area in his warrant, so he cannot travel to the vendor in Ratnapura and attest there. It is what forces the answer to the second half of the question.
temporal_note: Section 31 as a whole carries amendment events in 1976, 2011, 2022 and 2024, but none of the recorded events is directed at rule (22); the 1976 amendment law substituted 'zone' for 'division' throughout the Ordinance. The prohibition was in force in April 2020.

relevant_excerpt: the relevant deed or instrument shall be in writing, signed by every executant or by any person duly authorised by such executant and the witnesses in the presence of a licenced notary public present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and the same shall be attested by such notary
why_relevant: Sets the validity condition for any transfer of immovable property and, critically, allows the deed to be signed by a person duly authorised by the executant instead of the executant in person. That is the statutory opening for the power-of-attorney method.
temporal_note: The section was in force in April 2020, but the corpus holds the consolidated text incorporating amendments by Act No. 30 of 2022 and Act No. 4 of 2024 (thumb impressions, transferee signature). The element relied on here, that the deed may be signed by the executant or by a person duly authorised by him before a notary and witnesses and attested by that notary, is the long-standing content of the section; the exact wording quoted post-dates the matter date.
verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim but is the text as substituted by Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 4 of 2024 s.2(2)(a); the corpus copy of Act No. 30 of 2022 s.2 shows that between 2022 and 2024 paragraph (a) read 'signed by every executant and attested by a notary public before two witnesses present at the same time', with no authorised-signatory limb, so the researcher's note that this wording is the long-standing content of the section is wrong as stated; the April-2020 wording is not in the corpus and the only corpus support for an authorised signatory at that date is the parallel recital in the unamended 17-1852/s2.

relevant_excerpt: means any written power or authority other than that given to an attorney at law for the purpose of appearing as an attorney at law on behalf of such person, given by one person to another, to represent him, to perform any work, do any act, or carry on any trade or business, and - (a) if it is executed in Sri Lanka, executed before two witnesses and attested by a notary public
why_relevant: Defines the instrument by which the Ratnapura vendor can authorise someone else to sign the deed of transfer, and fixes its own formalities: two witnesses and notarial attestation. The vendor can satisfy these in Ratnapura, before a notary authorised for that area, without travelling.
temporal_note: The definition was in force in April 2020, but the corpus text is the definition as repealed and substituted by Act No. 28 of 2022 and further substituted by Act No. 3 of 2024. The two elements relied on here, a written authority given by one person to another to act for him and execution before two witnesses with notarial attestation when executed in Sri Lanka, were in the section before those amendments; the verifier should confirm the April-2020 wording against a pre-2022 edition.
verifier_note: The whole definition of 'power of attorney' was repealed and substituted by Powers of Attorney (Amendment) Act No. 28 of 2022 s.2(1) and substituted again by Act No. 3 of 2024 s.2, and the corpus holds no pre-2022 text, so it cannot be shown from the corpus that the limb relied on, execution before two witnesses and attestation by a notary public, formed part of the definition in April 2020.

relevant_excerpt: If he attest any deed or instrument executed before him by means of an attorney, he shall preserve a true copy of the power of attorney with his protocol, and shall forward a like copy with the duplicate to the Registrar of Lands.
why_relevant: Statutory recognition that a notary may attest a deed 'executed before him by means of an attorney', and the duty that attaches when he does. This is the rule that confirms Gayan Alwis himself can attest in the power-of-attorney method.
temporal_note: Rule (30) was in force in April 2020. Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(13) substituted the tail of the rule from the words 'he shall preserve a true copy of the registered power of attorney with his protocol', and Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3(10) amended it further, so the April-2020 rule referred to the registered power of attorney. The proposition relied on, that a notary may attest a deed executed before him by means of an attorney and must keep a copy of the power with his protocol, is unaffected.
verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim but the corpus consolidation of rule (30) is stale rather than post-2022 as the researcher's note says: 31-2022 s.16(13) substituted the tail of the rule from the words 'he shall preserve a true copy of the registered power of attorney with his protocol' and 6-2024 s.3(10) substituted it again, and neither change is reflected in the corpus text; the April-2020 rule required a copy of the registered power of attorney, while the opening limb relied on, 'If he attest any deed or instrument executed before him by means of an attorney', is untouched by either amendment and was in force at the matter date.

relevant_excerpt: deliver or transmit to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which such land shall be situated a copy thereof certified by him as correct, together with a list in duplicate in the Form F 1 in the Second Schedule
why_relevant: Shows that the Ordinance contemplates a notary attesting a deed that affects land in a district other than his own, and imposes the extra filing duty in that case. It answers the objection that a Galle notary cannot deal with Ratnapura land at all: the limit in rule (22) is on where he attests, not on where the land lies.
temporal_note: The rule in its present shape dates from Notaries (Amendment) Law No. 20 of 1976 s.10(1); Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3(9) only substituted the form reference 'Form F 1' for 'Form F'. The duty relied on was in force in April 2020, with the form then cited as Form F.
verifier_note: Wording and supporting role are right, but the excerpt quotes 'Form F 1', which 6-2024 s.3(9) substituted for 'Form F', so the excerpt is not the text in force in April 2020 even though the filing duty relied on is.

formal_title: Deeds and Documents (Execution before Public Officers) Ordinance
relevant_excerpt: be valid and effectual, so far as relates to the execution thereof, if the same be signed by the party making the same or by some person lawfully authorized by him, and by two or more witnesses present at the same time, in the presence of some District Judge or Commissioner of a Court of Requests* for the district in which the party making such writing, deed, or instrument, or the person signing the same as such attorney, resides
why_relevant: A further statutory route to a valid deed that does not need a notary at all: execution before the District Judge, or a specially authorised Justice of the Peace, for the district where the executant resides. It is available to the Ratnapura vendor locally, and it is a route in which Gayan Alwis plainly cannot be the attesting officer.
temporal_note: In force from 1852; the corpus records no amendment event. The reference to a Commissioner of a Court of Requests is marked in the corpus as a superseded office.

relevant_excerpt: Every power of attorney executed in Sri Lanka or any other country shall be registered with the Registrar General.
why_relevant: Registration duty that attaches to the power of attorney once granted. It is a step the advice should mention, but the validity of the deed of transfer under Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2 does not turn on it, so it is supporting rather than indispensable.
temporal_note: Section 3 was in force in April 2020 but the corpus text is the section as repealed and substituted by Act No. 28 of 2022 s.3, which also introduced the one-month and three-month filing windows. The verifier should check the April-2020 registration requirement against a pre-2022 edition before this is relied on.
verifier_note: Section 3 was repealed and substituted in its entirety by Powers of Attorney (Amendment) Act No. 28 of 2022 s.3 and the corpus holds no pre-2022 text, so the April-2020 registration duty cannot be established from the corpus; the pre-2022 wording of Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (30) quoted in 31-2022 s.16(13) refers to a registered power of attorney, which shows registration was contemplated at the matter date but does not fix the terms of the duty.

relevant_excerpt: Every warrant issued to a notary under the provisions of section 3* or section 4* authorizing him to practice as a notary in any judicial division in which he resides, shall be deemed to authorize him to practice as a notary in the judicial zone in which he resides.
why_relevant: Fixes the unit of a notary's territorial competence as the judicial zone of residence, which is how the warrant area in section 2 is read today and why a Galle warrant does not reach Ratnapura.
temporal_note: Inserted by Notaries (Amendment) Law No. 20 of 1976 s.4; in force from 1976, well before the matter date.

relevant_excerpt: any other rule set out in section 31, shall be guilty of an offence, and shall, on conviction after summary trial before a Magistrate, be liable to a fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, in addition to any civil liability he may incur thereby
why_relevant: Gives the sanction for breach of rule (22), which is why attesting outside his area is not a course Gayan Alwis may take as a matter of convenience.
temporal_note: Section 34 was substituted by Act No. 31 of 2022 s.17, so the fifty thousand rupee ceiling quoted post-dates April 2020. A penalty for breach of the section 31 rules existed at the matter date, at a lower figure that the corpus does not hold; the amount is not relied on in the answer.
verifier_note: Section 34 was substituted wholesale by 31-2022 s.17, so the entire quoted paragraph (1)(c), not only the fifty thousand rupee ceiling, post-dates April 2020, and the corpus does not hold the penalty provision in force at the matter date (the Increase of Fines Act No. 12 of 2005 amends the Notaries Ordinance through schedules the corpus does not carry); the proposition actually relied on, that breach of a section 31 rule is an offence triable summarily before a Magistrate, is not in doubt.

relevant_excerpt: A power of attorney granted to be used for the purpose of a transaction which falls within the scope of section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance (Chapter 70) shall be executed subject to the provisions specified in subsection (2) or (3), as the case may be.
why_relevant: Recorded as background only. It is the modern, much stricter code for a power of attorney used in a land transaction. It did not exist at the matter date and must not be used to grade an April 2020 answer, but a reader of the current statute book would expect to see it.
temporal_note: Inserted by Powers of Attorney (Amendment) Act No. 28 of 2022 s.4; in force from 2022, after the matter reference date of April 2020. Not relied on in the gold answer.
verifier_note: Correctly recorded as background with applicable_to_matter_date false; 4-1902/s3A carries an insert event by 28-2022 and must not bear on an April-2020 answer.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless the person executing the same and the witnesses shall have signed the same in his presence and in the presence of one another, and unless he shall have signed the same in the presence of the executant and of the attesting witnesses.
why_relevant: Added by the verifier. This is the rule that makes the vendor's inability to travel a legal problem rather than an inconvenience: the notary may not attest unless the person executing the deed signed it in his presence and in the presence of the witnesses. It is why the answer must choose between sending an attorney to Galle and moving the attestation to Ratnapura, and unlike Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2 it is temporally stable.
temporal_note: Rule (12) is not among the rules amended by 20-1976 s.10 (rule (29) only), 47-2011 ss.2 and 3 (rules (16) and (26)), 31-2022 s.16 (rules (3) to (7), (9), (14) to (17), (20), (27) and (30)) or 6-2024 s.3 (rules (5), (7A), (9), (10), (15A), (17), (20), (26), (29) and (30)), so the text quoted is the text in force in April 2020.
verifier_note: Added by the verifier as an indispensable and temporally stable anchor for the presence requirement that PROV-M072-003 would otherwise have to carry on post-2022 wording.

relevant_excerpt: to whom or to whose wife or husband any beneficial devise, legacy, estate, interest, gift, disposition, or appointment of or affecting any immovable or movable property (other than and except charges and directions for the payment of any debt or debts) shall be thereby given or made, such devise, legacy, estate, interest, gift, disposition, or appointment shall, so far only as concerns such person attesting the execution of such will, testament, or codicil, or the wife or husband of such person, or any person claiming under such person or wife or husband, be utterly null and void
why_relevant: The operative provision. It avoids the beneficial gift taken by an attesting witness or that witness's spouse, preserves the witness's competence to prove the will, and carves out charges and directions for the payment of debts. Every limb of the advice turns on it.
temporal_note: In force from 1840; the corpus records no amendment event for this section, so the text read is the text in force at 2020-04.
