why_relevant: Background on the drafting notary's own duty. The instructing lawyer must satisfy himself that the value on which duty is paid is the statutory value, which is why the paragraph (c) computation matters at the drafting stage and not only when the Assessor looks at the deed.
temporal_note: In force from 1990 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded; treated as in force in October 2019.

number_and_year: Statute No. 6 of 1990 (Provincial Council, Western Province)
relevant_excerpt: Except where there is an agreement to the contrary stamp duty shall be payable; (a) in the case of an instrument of transfer by the grantee
why_relevant: Identifies who bears the duty on the Deed of Gift: the grantee, that is the donee son, unless the deed provides otherwise. Needed to answer 'the stamp duty payable' as a liability and not merely as an amount.
temporal_note: In force from 1990 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded; treated as in force in October 2019.
verifier_note: Wording is verbatim, but s.51 is not the whole rule on incidence: s.52(1) makes every person executing an unstamped instrument relating to Western Province immovable property liable to the Commissioner, and s.52(3) applies notwithstanding s.51, with a right of recovery under s.52(2) against the person liable under s.51. The map records the primary incidence on the grantee without that override.

relevant_excerpt: the provisions of the Stamp Duty Act, No. 43 of 1982, relating to the Imposition of Stamp Duty (other than any instrument relating to the transfer of immovable property, the transfer of motor vehicles or documents filed in Court), Exemptions and any other provision in the aforesaid Act, shall, in so far as the same are inconsistent with the provisions of this Act, have no operation and the provisions of this Act shall prevail.
why_relevant: Background. The national stamp duty statute expressly carves instruments relating to the transfer of immovable property out of the regime it displaces, which is consistent with a Deed of Gift of Kohuwala land being dealt with by the Western Provincial Council's Assessor under Statute No. 6 of 1990 rather than by the Commissioner-General under the 2006 Act.
temporal_note: In force from 2006 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded; in force at October 2019.

relevant_excerpt: Any person (in this Ordinance called a "caveator") may present for registration a caveat in the prescribed form requiring to be served with notice of the presentation for registration of any instrument affecting the land described in the caveat.
why_relevant: Identifies the document that may be presented (a caveat in the prescribed form), who may present it (any person, who thereby becomes the caveator) and the entitlement it creates (service of notice of the presentation for registration of any instrument affecting the land described in the caveat). This is the direct answer to what document may be presented.
temporal_note: In force from 1927 and unamended in the corpus text at October 2019; the corpus records no amendment event on s.32 before Act No. 32 of 2022, which is after the matter date.

relevant_excerpt: The Registrar shall on receiving a caveat register it in the same manner as other instruments, but shall retain the caveat.
why_relevant: Answers to whom the document goes: the caveat is presented for registration to the Registrar, who must register it in the same manner as other instruments and retain the caveat itself rather than return it. It also establishes that registration by the Registrar, not any court order, is what brings the caveat into operation.
temporal_note: In force from 1927 and unamended at October 2019.

relevant_excerpt: The notice to be given to the caveator shall be in the prescribed form and shall be sent by registered letter to the address mentioned in the caveat.
why_relevant: Fixes the first limb of the effect of the document: how the caveator is warned. The notice is in the prescribed form and is posted by registered letter to the address stated in the caveat, which is why the caveat must state an address for service.
temporal_note: In force from 1927; the wording was replaced only by Act No. 32 of 2022 s.2(4), which is after the matter date.
verifier_note: Wording confirmed verbatim, but s.32(4) is passive and by itself neither names the Registrar as the officer bound to give the notice nor states the event that triggers it; both come from s.32(1) and the opening words of s.32(5), so this provision cannot carry the notice duty on its own.

relevant_excerpt: in an action commenced by the caveator in a competent court within thirty days from posting of the notice required by subsection (4) it is proved to the satisfaction of the court that the instrument presented for registration is or was at the time of registration void or voidable by the caveator or fraudulent as against him or in derogation of his lawful rights the court may order the instrument to be rectified or cancelled as may be necessary to preserve the rights of the caveator
why_relevant: The second and decisive limb of the effect. It supplies the thirty-day time limit running from the posting of the notice, the grounds the caveator must prove (void, voidable, fraudulent as against him, or in derogation of his lawful rights) and the relief the court may give (rectification or cancellation of the instrument and correction of the register). It matches the wording of the background almost exactly.
temporal_note: In force from 1927 with the thirty-day period intact at October 2019; the period was extended to sixty days only by Act No. 32 of 2022 s.2(5), after the matter date.
verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim but begins mid-subsection and omits both the opening condition of s.32(5) ("If, while a caveat is in force, an instrument affecting the land described in the caveat is presented for registration, and") and the closing limb ("and may order the necessary correction to be made in the register"), each of which the gold answer relies on.

relevant_excerpt: A caveat shall be in force for such period as may be specified therein, not being longer than the period covered by the fee paid on the caveat.
why_relevant: Limits how long the protection lasts and ties duration to the fee paid, which matters because s.32(5) operates only while a caveat is in force.
temporal_note: In force from 1927 at the matter date; replaced by a flat two-year maximum only by Act No. 32 of 2022 s.2(3).
verifier_note: Confirmed verbatim and promoted from supporting to indispensable, because s.32(5) operates only "while a caveat is in force" and the duration rule in s.32(3) is therefore a necessary condition of the remedy the answer states.

relevant_excerpt: Nothing in this section shall affect any other power which may be possessed by any court of ordering any instrument to be rectified or cancelled.
why_relevant: Keeps the answer accurate about the limits of the caveat: the thirty-day route is additional to, and does not displace, any other power of a court to rectify or cancel an instrument.
temporal_note: In force from 1927 and untouched at October 2019.

relevant_excerpt: The business of the land register office and branch offices shall be conducted by a Registrar-General of Lands (in this Ordinance called the "Registrar-General"), a Deputy Registrar-General of Lands and such number of Assistant Registrars-General (in this Ordinance called "Assistant Registrars-General") and Registrars of Lands (in this Ordinance called "Registrars")
why_relevant: Identifies the office to which the caveat goes. Registrar in s.32 means a Registrar of Lands appointed under this subsection, working in the land register office or a branch office, so the caveat is presented at a land registry and not to a court.
temporal_note: In force from 1927; the corpus records no amendment event on s.2, so it stands as printed at October 2019.

relevant_excerpt: Every instrument presented for registration shall be registered in the book allotted to the division in which the land affected by the instrument is situated
why_relevant: Explains which Registrar. Since s.32(2) directs the Registrar to register a caveat in the same manner as other instruments, the caveat belongs in the book of the division in which the land is situated, so it is presented at the land registry serving the division that covers the Colombo 5 property.
temporal_note: In force from 1927 with an amendment recorded in 1974 (Act No. 14 of 1974 s.2); the corpus text is the amended text and predates October 2019.

relevant_excerpt: all instruments, including wills, decrees and orders of any court or authority, and awards, which purport or operate to create, confer, declare, limit, assign, transfer, charge, incumber, release, or extinguish any right, title, or interest, whether vested or contingent, past, present, or future, to, in or over land
why_relevant: Fixes the trigger for the notice. The caveator is entitled to notice only of an instrument affecting the land, and this section says which instruments are deemed to affect land, so it determines whether a purported transfer of the Colombo 5 property would set the caveat working.
temporal_note: In force from 1927; no amendment event recorded in the corpus, so applicable at October 2019.
verifier_note: Excerpt of s.8(b) is verbatim but omits the eleven-limb proviso to s.8 that excludes certain instruments from the deeming provision; none of the exclusions covers a deed of transfer, so the answer is unaffected, but the exception should be recorded.

relevant_excerpt: Registration of a priority notice, seizure notice, seizure priority notice, caveat, or lis pendens may be cancelled at the request in writing of the person by whom or on whose behalf it was presented for registration. (2) A District Court may, on the application of any person interested in any property affected by registration of a priority notice, seizure notice, seizure priority notice, caveat, or lis pendens, if it is satisfied that the registration was or has become unnecessary, order that the registration be cancelled.
why_relevant: Completes the description of the effect by showing that it is neither permanent nor unilateral: the caveator may have the registration cancelled on written request, and any person interested in the property may ask a District Court to cancel it as unnecessary.
temporal_note: In force from 1927 at the matter date; the references to a caveat were removed from s.33(1) only by Act No. 32 of 2022 s.3, after the matter date.

relevant_excerpt: Any person injured by reason of the registration or renewal of a priority notice, seizure priority notice, caveat, or Us pendens without reasonable cause, or by unreasonable failure to request cancellation of registration of a priority notice, seizure priority notice, caveat, or lis pendens may recover compensation from the person who applied for such registration or renewal.
why_relevant: The counterweight to the remedy: registering a caveat without reasonable cause, or unreasonably refusing to have it cancelled, exposes the caveator to a claim for compensation. It is part of a complete statement of the effect of presenting the document.
temporal_note: In force from 1927 with no amendment event recorded in the corpus. The corpus text carries a scanning error, 'Us pendens' for 'lis pendens', which is reproduced verbatim in the excerpt.

relevant_excerpt: An endorsement by the Registrar in the prescribed form on a duplicate of an application for registration of a lis pendens, or on a duplicate of a priority notice or seizure priority notice or an application for renewal of such a notice, or on a duplicate of a caveat shall be admissible in evidence without proof of the signature or appointment of the Registrar, and shall be prima facie evidence of registration
why_relevant: Gives the caveator his proof. The Registrar's endorsement on the duplicate caveat is admissible without further proof and is prima facie evidence that the caveat was registered, which is what the caveator will produce in the s.32(5) action.
temporal_note: In force from 1927 with no amendment event recorded in the corpus, so applicable at October 2019.

relevant_excerpt: The forms contained in the Second Schedule shall be used with such variations as circumstances may require, but such Schedule may be altered or added to by regulation.
why_relevant: Locates the prescribed form that s.32(1) and s.32(4) require: the forms in the Second Schedule, as altered by regulation made under s.49.
temporal_note: In force from 1927 with no amendment event recorded in the corpus.
verifier_note: Verbatim, but s.50 only says the Second Schedule forms are to be used; the Schedule is not in the corpus, so it cannot be confirmed which form is the October 2019 caveat form, and the map does not record s.49, which is what makes "prescribed" mean prescribed by regulation.

relevant_excerpt: (6) For each land described in the Caveat, for each Land Registry in which each caveat in respect of each such land is registered and for each period of two years, a fee of 2500.00
why_relevant: Supplies the fee that governs duration under s.32(3): the fee is charged per land described in the caveat, per land registry in which it is registered, and per two-year period, so the practical unit of protection at the matter date was two years per fee paid.
temporal_note: Enacted in 2013 and therefore in force at October 2019. It amends the First Schedule of the principal enactment, which is itself not in the corpus, so only the amending text can be quoted.
verifier_note: Commencement confirmed from 21-2013 s.1, which deems the Act to have come into operation on 1 January 2013, so the substituted fee item was in force at the matter date.

relevant_excerpt: (3) A caveat shall be in force for a maximum period of two years.
why_relevant: Recorded only to mark the temporal boundary. This Act rewrote s.32 by restricting caveators to persons who have or claim a right, title or interest, requiring an affidavit and an attorney-at-law certificate, capping the caveat at two years and extending the time to sue from thirty days to sixty. None of that governs an October 2019 answer, and an answer keyed to the current text would be wrong for this matter.
temporal_note: Enacted in 2022, about three years after the matter reference date of October 2019. It must not be applied to this answer; it is listed as background so the verifier can see that the post-2019 change was checked and excluded.
verifier_note: Correctly excluded as post-dating the matter, but the subsection field claims "(3) and (5)" while the excerpt quotes only the new subsection (3); the thirty-to-sixty-day change made by 32-2022 s.2(5) is not in the quoted text.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not divulge the secrets confided to him or of which he becomes possessed in the execution of his office, unless with the express permission of his employer or when required to do so by law.
why_relevant: This is the notary's statutory duty of secrecy and the direct answer to the question. Knowledge that a particular person has executed a will before the notary, and the contents of that will, is information the notary became possessed of in the execution of his office. The rule is a prohibition subject to two exhaustive exceptions - express permission of his employer, and a legal requirement to disclose - so the whole analysis turns on whether either exception is made out.
temporal_note: Section 31 is in force from 1907. Rule (1) has not been amended: the substitutions of section 31 effected by the Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 and the Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 6 of 2024 begin at rule (3), and no amendment Act in the corpus mentions rule (1) or the word 'divulge'. The text quoted therefore stood unchanged at October 2019.

relevant_excerpt: he shall keep a register thereof with a convenient index for the purpose of easy reference; and every such register shall be substantially in the form F in the Second Schedule, but in the case of wills and codicils only the number and date of the instrument shall be inserted in the register.
why_relevant: Supports the reading of rule (1) as covering wills. The Ordinance singles wills and codicils out from the notary's ordinary record-keeping: even in the notary's own protocol register, only the number and date of a will may be entered, not the parties or the substance. That statutory treatment shows the confidentiality of a will is protected by the Ordinance itself and is not merely a matter of professional courtesy.
temporal_note: In force from 1907; no amendment Act in the corpus substitutes rule (24) (the 1976, 2011, 2022 and 2024 amendment Acts do not touch it). Applicable at October 2019.
verifier_note: Wording and temporal note confirmed (rule (24) is untouched by 20-1976 s.10, 47-2011 ss.2-3, 31-2022 s.16 and 6-2024 s.3), but the why_relevant overstates it: rule (24) governs what the notary enters in his own protocol register and states no duty of non-disclosure, so it supports the answer only by analogy; role moved from supporting to background.

relevant_excerpt: rules (1), (31) or (32) set out in section 31, shall be guilty of an offence, and shall, on conviction after summary trial before a Magistrate, be liable to a fine not exceeding five thousand rupees, in addition to any civil liability he may incur thereby
why_relevant: Shows that the duty of secrecy in rule (1) is enforced by penal sanction and not merely by professional convention: a notary who divulges is liable to be convicted and fined, in addition to any civil liability. It supports the strength of the advice given, but the answer to the question would be the same without it.
temporal_note: The corpus text of section 34 is the version substituted by the Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022, which post-dates the October 2019 matter date. The pre-2022 penalty text is not in the corpus, so the fine figure quoted here must not be treated as the figure applicable in October 2019. Recorded as supporting only; it is not indispensable and nothing in the answer turns on the amount.
verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim in the corpus, but the corpus body of s.34 is wholly the text substituted by 31-2022 s.17 (confirmed by reading that section), so neither the fine figure nor the paragraph structure can be attributed to October 2019; the corpus cannot establish what penalty attached to a breach of rule (1) at the matter date, and the provision is retained as supporting only.

relevant_excerpt: Provided, however, that in the case of wills and codicils only the number and date of the document shall be inserted in such list
why_relevant: Background reinforcement of the same policy: even in the monthly list of attested instruments that a notary must deliver to the Registrar of Lands, a will is entered by number and date only. The Ordinance therefore withholds the substance of a will even from a public registration officer, which tells against any suggestion that the notary may volunteer it to private inquirers.
temporal_note: Rule (26) in its present form derives from the Notaries (Amendment) Law No. 20 of 1976; no amendment Act in the corpus alters this proviso after 1976. Applicable at October 2019.
verifier_note: The proviso is verbatim and is untouched by every amendment Act in the corpus, so it applied in October 2019; but the temporal note is wrong on the history - 20-1976 s.10 amended rules (29) and (36), not rule (26); rule (26)(a) was renumbered as (26)(a)(i) by 47-2011 s.3 and the words 'Form F' in that subparagraph were replaced by 'Form F 1' by 6-2024 s.3(8), so the surrounding corpus text of (26)(a)(i) is post-2019 even though the proviso is not.

relevant_excerpt: in rule (9) thereof, by the substitution for the words, "He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless the person executing the same be known to him or to at least two of the attesting witnesses thereto;"
why_relevant: This amending subsection recites verbatim the opening words of rule (9) of section 31 of the Notaries Ordinance as they stood immediately before the 2022 substitution, and therefore as they stood at the matter reference date. Those words are the operative rule for this question: a notary may attest only where the executant is known to him, or is known to at least two of the attesting witnesses.
temporal_note: Act No. 31 of 2022 was itself not in force in October 2019. What is recorded and relied on here is the wording it quotes as the wording it replaced, which is the rule (9) text in force at the matter reference date. The replacing wording (identity by inspection of a national identity card, passport bio-page or driving licence) came into force only in 2022 and must not be applied to this matter. This is the one entry in the map where the section_id points at an instrument later than the matter date; it is recorded this way because the corpus holds no pre-2022 edition of section 31.
verifier_note: Wording confirmed verbatim in 31-2022/s16(6), and the recited words are indeed the rule (9) opening words replaced in 2022, so the substantive law relied on is right for October 2019; the entry is only partially verified because the section_id and act_id point to a 2022 amending Act that was not itself in force at the matter reference date, and a lawyer should confirm the 2019 text from a pre-2022 edition.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless one of the executants to the deed or instrument or the two attesting witnesses be known to notary or by the identity of the executants to a deed or instrument is established by such notary by inspection of the national identity card, bio-page of the passport or the driving licence of such executants;
why_relevant: Recorded to show what rule (9) says now and to mark the difference from the text applied to this matter. The identity-document route in these words was introduced after the matter reference date and is not available to the notary in October 2019.
temporal_note: Substituted into section 31 by Act No. 31 of 2022, s.16(6), which is after the matter reference date of October 2019. Not applied; recorded only so the verifier can see the divergence between the corpus text and the text in force at the matter date.

relevant_excerpt: he shall satisfy himself, before accepting them as witnesses, that they are persons of good repute and that they are well acquainted with the executant and know his proper name, occupation, and residence, and the witnesses shall sign a declaration at the foot of the deed or instrument that they are well acquainted with the executant and know his proper name, occupation, and residence.
why_relevant: Where the notary does not know the executant and proceeds on the witnesses, this limb obliges him to satisfy himself that the attesting witnesses are of good repute and are well acquainted with the executant and know his proper name, occupation and residence, and to have the witnesses sign a declaration to that effect. It is stated of the witnesses in the plural, so one acquainted witness is not enough.
temporal_note: This limb was in force at the matter reference date. The only change made to it since is by Act No. 6 of 2024, s.3(3), which substituted the words "he shall" for the introductory words "and in the latter case, he shall". That change is verbal and does not alter the substance relied on. In October 2019 the limb read with the introductory words "and in the latter case,", which tied it to the situation where the notary relies on the witnesses rather than on his own knowledge, which is this matter.
verifier_note: Excerpt confirmed verbatim against the consolidated (post-2024) text, and the substance was in force in October 2019, but the quoted words are not the 2019 wording exactly: until Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3(3) the limb opened "and in the latter case, he shall satisfy himself", which the map's temporal_note states correctly.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument to which he is a party.
why_relevant: This is the only personal disqualification the rules impose on the notary himself. It bars him where he is a party to the deed. It does not reach a case where a relative of his signs as an attesting witness, and no other rule in section 31 disqualifies a witness by reason of kinship to the notary. The rule is therefore what supports the conclusion that the fraternal relationship is not, of itself, a bar to attestation.
temporal_note: In force since 1907 and untouched by Acts No. 20 of 1976, No. 47 of 2011, No. 13 of 2013, No. 31 of 2022 or No. 6 of 2024 on the amendment record held in the corpus. In force at the matter reference date.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument to which at least two witnesses have not subscribed their signatures in letters.
why_relevant: Fixes the minimum of two attesting witnesses, which is what makes the plural in the acquaintance and declaration limb bite: there must be at least two attesting witnesses, and the acquaintance requirement is stated of them collectively.
temporal_note: Untouched by any amending Act recorded against section 31 in the corpus. In force at the matter reference date.

relevant_excerpt: in rule (9) thereof, by the substitution for the words "and in the latter case, he shall", of the words, "he shall"; (4) by the repeal of rule (10) thereof;
why_relevant: Evidence of how rule (9) read before 2024: the acquaintance and declaration limb was introduced by the words "and in the latter case,", tying it to the case where the notary relies on the witnesses rather than his own knowledge. It also shows that a separate rule (10) existed at the matter reference date and was repealed only in 2024.
temporal_note: A 2024 amending section, later than the matter reference date. Recorded only as the corpus evidence for the wording of rule (9) before 2024 and for the existence of a then rule (10). Not applied as law to this matter.

relevant_excerpt: every instrument relating to a transfer of situated in the immovable property Western Province; (b) every document presented or filed, in proceedings instituted in any Court of law established by law, in the Western Province of Sri Lanka; (c) every transfer of a motor vehicle effected in Western Province. a stamp duty at the prescribed rate.
why_relevant: This is the charging provision for the transaction in the matter: stamp duty on an instrument transferring immovable property situated in the Western Province is a provincial charge levied by this Statute. Rajagiriya is in the Colombo District, Western Province, so a deed of transfer of that property is chargeable under paragraph (a). The provision also shows why the amount cannot be computed from the Statute alone: it charges duty only at the prescribed rate.
temporal_note: Corpus in_force_from_year 1990, amendment_events empty; no amending Western Province statute is in the corpus, so the text is treated as in force at 2019-10 on the corpus record. The word order of the extracted text is garbled ('a transfer of situated in the immovable property Western Province') but the sense of the paragraph is not in doubt.

relevant_excerpt: (1) Where any property is conveyed by an instrument, the stamp duty with which such instrument is chargeable shall be calculated on the value of the property conveyed.
why_relevant: Fixes the base on which the duty is computed. It directs the calculation to the value of the property conveyed, which is why the Rs. 3 million market value in the scenario, and not some lower stated consideration, is the figure the rate is applied to.
temporal_note: Corpus in_force_from_year 1990, amendment_events empty; treated as in force at 2019-10.

relevant_excerpt: "value" with reference - (a) to any property (other than immovable property which is gifted) and to any date, means the price which in the opinion of the Assessor, that property would have fetched in the open market on that date
why_relevant: Defines the term on which s.48(1) turns. For a transfer that is not a gift, 'value' is the open market price at the relevant date, which is what the scenario supplies as the market value of Rs. 3 million. Without this definition the s.48(1) base is undetermined.
temporal_note: Corpus in_force_from_year 1990, amendment_events empty; treated as in force at 2019-10. Most defined-term headwords in this section were lost in extraction; the 'value' definition retains its headword.

relevant_excerpt: Except where there is an agreement to the contrary stamp duty shall be payable; (a) in the case of an instrument of transfer by the grantee;
why_relevant: Identifies the person liable. The question asks for the duty payable on the deed of transfer; on an instrument of transfer the grantee bears it unless the parties agree otherwise. It affects who pays rather than how much, so it supports the calculation without driving it.
temporal_note: Corpus in_force_from_year 1990, amendment_events empty; treated as in force at 2019-10.

relevant_excerpt: (1) The Minister may make regulations in respect of all or any of the following matters: (a) any matter which is required or authorized by this Statute to be prescribed;
why_relevant: Locates the missing authority precisely. The rate that s.37 calls prescribed is set by regulation under this section and published in the Gazette. That regulation, not the Statute, carries the percentages needed to turn Rs. 3 million into a rupee figure, and it is not in the corpus.
temporal_note: Corpus in_force_from_year 1990, amendment_events empty; treated as in force at 2019-10.

relevant_excerpt: For the purposes of section 3, "specified instrument" means- (a) an affidavit; (b) a policy of insurance; (c) a warrant to act as Notary Public;
why_relevant: Background: it rules out the national charging regime as the source of the answer. The closed list of specified instruments chargeable under s.3 of the 2006 Act does not include a deed transferring immovable property, so the duty on this deed is not levied under that Act.
temporal_note: Corpus in_force_from_year 2006, amendment_events empty; in force well before 2019-10.

relevant_excerpt: the provisions of the Stamp Duty Act, No. 43 of 1982, relating to the Imposition of Stamp Duty (other than any instrument relating to the transfer of immovable property, the transfer of motor vehicles or documents filed in Court)
why_relevant: Background: the express carve-out confirms that instruments relating to the transfer of immovable property were deliberately left outside the 2006 Act's displacement of the earlier national regime, which is consistent with duty on such transfers being a provincial charge under the Western Province Financial Statute.
temporal_note: Corpus in_force_from_year 2006, amendment_events empty; in force well before 2019-10.

relevant_excerpt: The following instruments and documents shall be exempted from the payment of stamp duty:- (1) bail bond in criminal proceedings; conveyance or transfer of any immovable L vehicle by the Government property or motor or by a person for or on behalf of the 5 Government;
why_relevant: The exemption list has to be checked before duty is charged. None of the listed exemptions covers a private sale between two private persons, so the charge under s.37(a) is not displaced. Included because the answer turns in part on the exemption section not applying.
temporal_note: Corpus in_force_from_year 1990, amendment_events empty; treated as in force at 2019-10. The extracted text of paragraph (2) is garbled but plainly concerns Government transfers.

relevant_excerpt: of lands or immovable property, by a title adverse to or independent of that of the claimant or plaintiff in such action (that is to say, a possession unaccompanied by payment of rent or produce, or performance of service or duty, or by any other act by the possessor, from which an acknowledgment of a right existing in another person would fairly and naturally be inferred) for ten years previous to the bringing of such action, shall entitle the defendant to a decree in his favour with costs.
why_relevant: This is the source of whatever right Sunimal Peiris has. The facts given track the language of the section almost word for word: undisturbed and uninterrupted possession, by a title adverse to or independent of that of any other, by him and by those under whom he claims. The section fixes the qualifying period at ten years and the scenario gives over thirty. The second limb of the section, which covers a plaintiff or intervenient who sues to be quieted in possession or to establish his claim in any other manner, is what makes prescription available to him affirmatively and not only as a shield.
temporal_note: In force from 1871 with no recorded change to section 3. The corpus records no amendment event on this section, so the same text governed the whole of the thirty-year period of possession and was in force in October 2019.

relevant_excerpt: shall be taken to include all shares and interests in such property, and all rights, easements, and servitudes thereunto belonging or appertaining.
why_relevant: The interpretation section for the expression immovable property used in section 3. It matters here because Lot X is a divided allotment of thirty perches carved out of a larger land called Ambagahawatta, so the answer depends on prescription being capable of running to a share or a defined part and to the rights belonging to it. The corpus body of this section has lost the defined expression itself, which is recorded separately in the section's defined_terms field.
temporal_note: In force from 1871, no recorded amendment event, so in force in October 2019.

relevant_excerpt: affect the alienable or inalienable rights of the State; or (b) apply to any proceedings in any action for divorce, or to any case in which special provision has been or may hereafter be made
why_relevant: The one qualification the notary must clear before drawing any deed. Prescription does not run against the State, so if the land is State land or the possession is under a permit or grant, no amount of possession will found the declaration. The scenario says the land is called Ambagahawatta and gives an assessment number and a private survey plan, but does not say whether the land or any part of it is State land, so the point has to be checked rather than assumed.
temporal_note: The present text was substituted by section 2 of the Prescription (Amendment) Act No. 26 of 2014, which is five years before the matter date, so the substituted text is the text in force in October 2019. The predecessor text also excluded the rights of the Crown, so the exclusion covered the whole period of possession, but the precise wording relied on here dates only from 2014.

relevant_excerpt: all instruments, including wills, decrees and orders of any court or authority, and awards, which purport or operate to create, confer, declare, limit, assign, transfer, charge, incumber, release, or extinguish any right, title, or interest, whether vested or contingent, past, present, or future, to, in or over land
why_relevant: This is the only place in the corpus that recognises a purely declaratory instrument affecting land. The verb declare stands alongside transfer and assign, so an instrument that does no more than declare an existing right, title or interest in land is nevertheless deemed to affect land for the purposes of the Ordinance and is therefore registrable. Without this provision the proposed deed of declaration would have nowhere to go in the register, and the whole point of the exercise, which is to manifest the title on the folio, would fail.
temporal_note: In force from 1927, no recorded amendment event on section 8, and paragraph (b) applies to instruments executed after the commencement of the Ordinance, which covers a deed drawn in or after 2019.

relevant_excerpt: be void as against all parties claiming an adverse interest thereto on valuable consideration by virtue of any subsequent instrument which is duly registered under this Chapter
why_relevant: This supplies the reason for choosing a registrable deed at all rather than, say, an affidavit kept in the client's file. Once the declaration is registered it takes its place in the priority scheme and later purchasers for value are on notice of it; if it is left unregistered it is void against a later registered instrument taken for value. That is what better manifestation of title means in practice.
temporal_note: In force from 1927, no recorded amendment event, so in force in October 2019.

relevant_excerpt: Registration of an instrument under this Chapter shall not cure any defect in the instrument or confer upon it any effect or validity which it would not otherwise have except the priority conferred on it by this section.
why_relevant: The limit on what the proposed deed can achieve, and the reason the advice must be qualified. Registering a declaration does not turn a bad claim into a good one. The deed and its registration record and publicise the prescriptive title; they do not create it, and they do not bind a paper owner who has never been heard. This is why the honest answer names the deed and then tells the client what it does not do.
temporal_note: In force from 1927, no recorded amendment event, so in force in October 2019.

relevant_excerpt: Every instrument (except a will) presented for registration shall contain embodied therein, or in a schedule annexed thereto, an accurate and clear description of the land affected thereby, its boundaries, extent, and situation specifying the district and the village, pattu, korale, or other division of the district in which the land is situated
why_relevant: Drafting instruction for the schedule of the proposed deed. The scenario already supplies every particular the subsection asks for: Lot X on Survey Plan No. 657 dated 3 April 2013 by Saliya Silva, Licensed Surveyor, thirty perches in extent, the land called Ambagahawatta at Thalawathugoda, Palle Pattu of Salpiti Korale, District of Colombo, and the street name through the assessment number for Hokandara Road. Subsection (5) obliges the Registrar to refuse registration of an instrument that does not state these particulars, so the schedule has to reproduce them.
temporal_note: Latest recorded change is by section 2 of the Registration of Documents (Amendment) Act No. 50 of 1982, well before the matter date, so the corpus text is the text in force in October 2019.

relevant_excerpt: An instrument, whether registered before or after the commencement of this Ordinance, shall not be deemed to be duly registered under this Chapter unless it is registered in accordance with the foregoing provisions of this section.
why_relevant: Registration only counts if it is in the right folio. Subsection (1) requires the instrument to go into the folio of the division in which the land lies and in which the first registered instrument affecting the same land is registered, or a folio opened in continuation with cross references, and where no instrument affecting the land has been registered before, into a new folio allotted by the Registrar. The second limb is the likely case here, because a possessor without paper title may have nothing earlier on the folio. The point matters because a declaration registered in the wrong folio buys the client no priority under section 7.
temporal_note: Latest recorded change is 1974, well before the matter date, so the corpus text is the text in force in October 2019.

relevant_excerpt: It shall be the duty of every notary to submit for registration to the Registrar, every deed or instrument attested by him before the expiry of thirty days from the date of attestation thereof
why_relevant: The client consults a notary, and this rule turns the registration step from a matter for the client into the notary's own statutory duty. Having drawn and attested the declaration, the notary must lodge it for registration within thirty days, or sixty days where the land lies outside the area in which he practises.
temporal_note: This rule was inserted by section 3(2) of the Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 47 of 2011, eight years before the matter date, so it was in force in October 2019. The corpus edition of section 31 as a whole is a consolidation carrying later amendments made by Act No. 31 of 2022 and Act No. 6 of 2024, so the surrounding rules in the same section cannot be relied on for a 2019 matter without checking each one. The rule is treated as supporting only.

relevant_excerpt: No sale, purchase, transfer, assignment, or mortgage of land or other immovable property, and no promise, bargain, contract, or agreement for effecting any such object, or for establishing any security, interest, or incumbrance affecting land or other immovable property
why_relevant: Included to mark out what the proposed deed is not. The transactions listed here are dispositive: sale, purchase, transfer, assignment, mortgage, and agreements to effect them. A declaration of a title already acquired by possession is none of these, and there is no grantor from whom the client can take a conveyance, so no transfer deed can be drawn. The section is background because it explains the exclusion rather than supplying a condition the client must satisfy.
temporal_note: The corpus text of section 2 is a consolidation incorporating the Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 30 of 2022 and Act No. 4 of 2024, both after the matter date, which is where the subsection numbering, the thumb impression requirement and the transferee provisions in subsection (2) come from. The opening words quoted here list the same transactions as the text in force in October 2019, but a verifier should confirm the 2019 wording against a pre-2022 edition. The provision is background only and is not relied on for any operative condition.

relevant_excerpt: Inheritance ab interstate to the immovable property in Sri Lanka of a person deceased shall be governed and regulated by the following provisions of this Ordinance wherever such person may have or have had his actual or matrimonial domicile.
why_relevant: The matter concerns immovable property in Colombo devolving on two intestacies. This is the gateway provision that makes Part III of the Ordinance the governing law for that devolution.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; the corpus records no amendment event, so the text applies to the deaths in 2014 and to the reference date 2019-04.

relevant_excerpt: When any person shall die intestate as to any of his or her property, leaving a spouse surviving, the surviving spouse shall inherit one-half of the property of such person.
why_relevant: Fixes the half share of Kamal De Silva on Kanthi Perera's intestacy and the half share of Anura Fernando on Amali Perera's intestacy. Both deceased left a surviving spouse.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus. Applies to both deaths in 2014.

relevant_excerpt: Subject to the right of the surviving spouse in the preceding section mentioned, the right of inheritance is divided in the following order as respects (a) descendants, (b) ascendants, (c) collaterals.
why_relevant: Sets the order in which the remaining half devolves. It links s.22 to the class provisions: s.24 for Kanthi Perera's children, and ss.25 to 29 for Amali Perera's collaterals.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: Children, grandchildren, and remoter descendants are preferent to all others in the estate of the parents; all the children take equally per capita, but the children or remoter issue of a deceased child take per stirpes or by representation.
why_relevant: Gives Kanthi Perera's three surviving children, Amali, Anusha and Anuk, the half not taken by the surviving spouse, in equal per capita shares. It also confirms that a child of an earlier marriage takes equally with the children of the later marriage.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: The children and remoter descendants failing, the inheritance of the deceased goes to his father and mother in case they are both alive; but if only one of the parents be alive, the surviving parent takes half
why_relevant: Amali Perera died issueless, so descendants fail. This section would have given a surviving parent a share, but both her parents were dead before her, which is what carries the devolution on to s.26.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.
verifier_note: Wording is verbatim but the excerpt stops mid-sentence at 'the surviving parent takes half' and drops the rest of s.25, under which a surviving parent takes half and the brothers and sisters (including half-blood siblings related through the deceased parent) take the other half; s.25 is displaced here only on the researcher's unstated reading that Amali Perera's father died before her.

relevant_excerpt: Father and mother both failing, the property of the intestate goes to his brothers and sisters, whether of the whole or balf-blood, and their children and other issue by representation.
why_relevant: Both of Amali Perera's parents predeceased her, so the half of her estate not taken by her surviving husband goes to her brothers and sisters. Anusha and Anuk are her half-blood siblings on the mother's side and are expressly included.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus. The corpus body carries the typographical error balf-blood for half-blood; the excerpt is reproduced exactly as it stands in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: In case all the half-brothers and sisters, their children and remoter issue, are related to the intestate on one side only, they take the whole of the inheritance, unless there be a grandfather or grandmother or higher ascendant yet alive, related to the intestate on the other side
why_relevant: Amali Perera left no full brother or sister; her only siblings were the two half-blood siblings on her mother's side. This section, not the split in s.27, governs and gives them the whole of the collateral half, subject to there being no surviving ascendant on her father's side.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: if all those who succeed to the inheritance are equally near in degree to the intestate, they take per capita, and not per stirpes.
why_relevant: Anusha and Anuk are equally near in degree to Amali Perera, so the collateral half is divided between them per capita and not by representation.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.
verifier_note: Verbatim but the excerpt drops the opening qualifier 'Except when otherwise expressly provided,', which matters because ss.25, 26 and 27 expressly provide for taking by representation.

relevant_excerpt: Save as aforesaid, this Ordinance shall not apply to Kandyans or Muslims, or to Tamils of the Northern Province who are or may become subject to the Tesawalamai.
why_relevant: Sets the boundary of the Ordinance. The devolution answers hold only if the family is governed by the general law rather than by Kandyan law, Muslim law or the Tesawalamai. Nothing in the scenario suggests any of the three, and the property and the parties are in Colombo.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: The following sections of this Ordinance shall apply to the estates of such persons only as shall die after the proclamation of this Ordinance, and shall be then unmarried or (if married) shall have been married after the proclamation of this Ordinance.
why_relevant: Confirms that Part III applies to these estates: both Kanthi Perera and Amali Perera died in 2014 and both were married long after the proclamation of the Ordinance.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: the relevant deed or instrument shall be in writing, signed by every executant or by any person duly authorised by such executant and the witnesses in the presence of a licenced notary public present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and the same shall be attested by such notary
why_relevant: Every inter vivos link in the pedigree, the 2000 transfer, the 2005 gift, the 2013 sale, the 2015 administrator's conveyance and the later gift by the administrator, is a notarially attested deed, because a disposition of immovable property has no force in law otherwise.
temporal_note: The corpus holds the consolidated text carrying the amendments by Act No. 30 of 2022 and Act No. 4 of 2024. The quoted wording therefore post-dates the matter reference date of April 2019 and all the deeds in the scenario. The underlying requirement of a written, notarially attested deed dates from 1840, but the exact wording relied on here cannot be shown from the corpus to have been in force in 2005, 2013 or 2015. Used as background only.
verifier_note: Excerpt and temporal note both check out: the corpus body is the consolidated text with latest_change_year 2024 and amendment events for 60-1947, 30-2022 and 4-2024, so the quoted wording cannot be shown to have been in force for the 2000 to 2015 deeds; correctly confined to background.

relevant_excerpt: if the transferee is a minor, a guardian shall be a competent person to act on behalf of the transferee for the purpose of this section.
why_relevant: Bears directly on the second question: it is the one provision in the corpus that names a guardian as the competent person to act for a minor transferee, which is the point raised by the gift of Lot 1 to Amali Perera when she was sixteen.
temporal_note: Subsection (2) comes from the amendments recorded in the corpus for Act No. 30 of 2022 and Act No. 4 of 2024. It did not exist when Deed of Gift No. 1054 was executed in 2005 and was not in force at the matter reference date of April 2019. It cannot support the answer and is recorded only to show that the corpus holds no contemporaneous equivalent.
verifier_note: Confirmed: s.2(2) exists only in the post-2022 consolidated text, so it cannot govern the 2005 deed of gift; correctly recorded as unusable rather than relied on.

relevant_excerpt: If any of the heirs, legatees or beneficiaries of the deceased is a minor without a natural guardian, or person of unsound mind, without a guardian, steps shall be taken for the appointment of a guardian or manager, upon the making of an application to the District Judge
why_relevant: Relevant to the second question as a statutory instance of a step that must be taken before an estate is dealt with when a beneficiary is a minor. It does not apply on these facts, because the heirs in DC Colombo case No. 567/T were adults, but it is the nearest statutory analogue in the corpus.
temporal_note: In force from 1889; the corpus records changes by Act No. 14 of 1993 and Act No. 11 of 2010, both before the 2015 administration and before the reference date.

relevant_excerpt: If it shall appear that any person claiming a right to have charge of the property of a minor is entitled to such right by virtue of a will or deed, and-is willing to undertake the trust, the court shall grant a certificate of curatorship to such person.
why_relevant: The route by which a court-recognised person takes charge of a minor's property. It is the statutory hook in the corpus for the proposition that someone other than the minor must act in relation to Lot 1 while Amali Perera was under age.
temporal_note: In force from 1889; no amendment event recorded in the corpus. Quoted exactly as it stands in the corpus, including the typographical error and-is.

relevant_excerpt: the power of administration, which is authenticated by the grant of probate, or is conveyed by the grant of letters of administration, extends to every portion of the deceased person's property, movable and immovable, within Sri Lanka
why_relevant: Bears on the Administrator's Conveyance of 3rd December 2015, written after the testamentary proceedings had been terminated on 6th November 2015. The section fixes the reach and the duration of the administrator's power and is the starting point for asking whether a further step in court was needed.
temporal_note: In force from 1889; the corpus records a change by Act No. 14 of 1993, before the 2015 conveyance and before the reference date.
verifier_note: Verbatim but the excerpt drops the opening condition 'If no limitation is expressed in the order making the grant' and the section 554A carve-out; s.541(c) is the section that actually limits an administrator's power to convey, and neither section says whether a conveyance may follow termination of the proceedings.

relevant_excerpt: Such woman shall, subject and without prejudice to any such trusts as aforesaid, have as full power of disposing of and dealing with such property, by any lawful act inter vivos with the written consent of her husband, but not otherwise, or by last will without such consent, as if she were unmarried.
why_relevant: On the face of the corpus text, a married woman's inter vivos disposition of her separate immovable property needs her husband's written consent. Kanthi Perera was married to Kamal De Silva when she executed Deed of Gift No. 1054 in 2005 and when the 2013 sale took place, so this is the most direct candidate answer to the second question about joining another party.
temporal_note: The corpus text records no amendment event and shows the husband's consent wording as still standing. The Married Women's Property Ordinance No. 18 of 1923, generally understood to have removed that requirement, is not in the corpus. Because the corpus cannot settle whether the requirement survived into 2005 and 2013, this provision is marked not applicable and is recorded only to flag the point.
verifier_note: Cannot be checked from the corpus: the corpus carries the unamended s.8 consent wording with no amendment events and holds neither the Married Women's Property Ordinance No. 18 of 1923 nor any repealing instrument, so whether the husband's written consent was required in 2005 and 2013 is unresolvable here; note also that s.11, the District Court dispensation procedure, is the cross-referenced step the map does not record.

relevant_excerpt: In all questions relating to the distribution of the property of an intestate, if the present Ordinance is silent, the rules of the Roman-Dutch law as it prevailed in North Holland are to govern and be followed.
why_relevant: Marks the outer edge of the statutory scheme. Where the Ordinance is silent the answer comes from Roman-Dutch law, which the corpus does not hold. It is the reason the second question cannot be answered from statute alone.
temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: there shall be charged a duty (hereinafter to be called "stamp duty") at such rate as the Minister may determine by Order published in the Gazette on every "specified instrument"- (a) executed, drawn or presented in Sri Lanka
why_relevant: The charging provision for stamp duty on the lease agreement, which is to be executed in Sri Lanka. It also shows that the rate is not fixed in the Act but by Ministerial Order in the Gazette, which is why the amount cannot be computed from the corpus.
temporal_note: In force from 2006; the corpus records no amendment to s.3, so the text applies at 2019-04.

relevant_excerpt: (h) a promissory note; (i) a lease or hire of any property; (j) a receipt or discharge given for any money or other property;
why_relevant: Defines 'specified instrument' for s.3 and lists a lease of any property. It is what brings the two-year lease of the upstair floor at Nawala Road within the charge to stamp duty.
temporal_note: In force from 2006; the corpus records no amendment to s.4, so the text applies at 2019-04.

relevant_excerpt: Otherwise than in cases where there is an agreement to the contrary, stamp duty shall be payable:- (a) in the case of a policy of insurance, by the person effecting the insurance; (b) in the case of a transfer or assignment of any share, by the transferee or assignee of such share; (c) in the case of a lease, by the lessee;
why_relevant: Fixes who bears the duty on a lease, namely the lessee, unless the parties agree otherwise. It identifies Ravi Perera as the person who must pay, subject to any contrary term the parties put in the lease.
temporal_note: In force from 2006; amended by Act No. 10 of 2008, which predates the matter date, so the consolidated text applies at 2019-04.

relevant_excerpt: the stamp duty payable on any specified instrument shall be paid by means of affixing adhesive stamps to the required value, prior to, or at the time of, the execution of the instrument. The value of the stamp duty so paid shall be specified on the face of the instrument so executed
why_relevant: Gives the default manner and timing of payment: adhesive stamps to the required value, before or at execution, with the value stated on the face of the instrument. It is the fallback where the bank route in s.8(2) is not used.
temporal_note: In force from 2006; substituted by Act No. 10 of 2008, which predates the matter date, so the consolidated text applies at 2019-04.

relevant_excerpt: Stamp duty payable on any specified instrument relating to a mortgage or lease of any immovable property may be paid, prior to, or at the time of, the execution of the specified instrument, to a prescribed bank. Where however, the stamp duty cannot be so paid due to reasons beyond the control of the person by whom the stamp duty is payable, the stamp duty shall be paid to the prescribed bank within seven days from the date of such execution. The bank shall thereupon issue a certificate in the prescribed form certifying that the stamp duty has been duly paid
why_relevant: This answers 'to whom do you pay' for a lease of immovable property: payment goes to a prescribed bank, which issues a certificate in the prescribed form to be affixed to the instrument. It also gives the seven-day outer limit where payment before execution is impossible.
temporal_note: In force from 2006; substituted by Act No. 10 of 2008, which predates the matter date, so the consolidated text applies at 2019-04.

relevant_excerpt: All stamp duty payable to a Provincial Council in respect of documents and instruments referred to in List I of the Ninth Schedule to the Constitution, shall be paid to the respective Provincial Council within whose limits the instrument was executed or the property situated as the case may be
why_relevant: Identifies the ultimate recipient where the duty is a Provincial Council duty: the Council within whose limits the instrument was executed or the property is situated. The demised premises are at Nawala Road, Rajagiriya, which points to the Western Provincial Council.
temporal_note: In force from 2006; the corpus records no amendment to s.9, so the text applies at 2019-04.
verifier_note: Wording is verbatim and unamended, but the role is overstated: s.9 reaches only duty payable to a Provincial Council in respect of List I documents, List I is outside the corpus, and the Western Province's own charging section (6-1990/s37) charges transfers, court documents and motor vehicle transfers but not leases, so this section is demoted to background for M088-Q02.

relevant_excerpt: the provisions of the Stamp Duty Act, No. 43 of 1982, relating to the Imposition of Stamp Duty (other than any instrument relating to the transfer of immovable property, the transfer of motor vehicles or documents filed in Court), Exemptions and any other provision in the aforesaid Act, shall, in so far as the same are inconsistent with the provisions of this Act, have no operation and the provisions of this Act shall prevail.
why_relevant: Explains why the imposition provisions of the Stamp Duty Act No. 43 of 1982 cannot be used to compute duty on this lease: so far as they are inconsistent with Act No. 12 of 2006 they have no operation, and a lease is not one of the carved-out categories.
temporal_note: In force from 2006; the corpus records no amendment to s.13, so the text applies at 2019-04.

relevant_excerpt: There shall be charged on- (a) every instrument relating to a transfer of situated in the immovable property Western Province; (b) every document presented or filed, in proceedings instituted in any Court of law established by law, in the Western Province of Sri Lanka; (c) every transfer of a motor vehicle effected in Western Province. a stamp duty at the prescribed rate.
why_relevant: The premises are in the Western Province, so the provincial stamp duty statute was checked. Its charging section covers transfers of immovable property, documents filed in court and motor vehicle transfers, and does not list a lease, which is why the charge on this lease is looked for in Act No. 12 of 2006.
temporal_note: In force from 1990; the corpus records no amendment to s.37, so the text applies at 2019-04. The corpus text of paragraph (a) is visibly garbled ('a transfer of situated in the immovable property Western Province') and should be read against the Gazette.
verifier_note: Excerpt is a verbatim copy of the corpus body, but paragraph (a) is visibly corrupted in the corpus text and must be read against the Gazette before the negative inference, that the Western Province statute does not charge leases, is relied on.

relevant_excerpt: no promise, bargain, contract, or agreement for effecting any such object, or for establishing any security, interest, or incumbrance affecting land or other immovable property (other than a lease at will, or for any period not exceeding one month)
why_relevant: A lease for two years is outside the exception for a lease at will or for a period not exceeding one month, so the instrument must be in writing and notarially executed and attested to be of force in law. This is the frame in which the lessee's covenants and the reddendum are drafted, but it says nothing about their content.
temporal_note: In force from 1840. The corpus text is consolidated to 2024, and its lettered paragraphs (a) and (b), including the thumb impression requirement, come from Act No. 30 of 2022 and Act No. 4 of 2024, both after 2019-04. The words quoted here, the scope of the section and the lease exception, predate those amendments and are unaffected by them. Used as background only.
verifier_note: The quoted words sit before the phrase from which 30-2022 s.2 repealed and substituted the rest of the section, so the excerpt itself is safe for 2019-04, but the execution requirement in force at that date is not in the corpus (only the post-2024 text is) and is corroborated only indirectly by 7-1840/s19 and 17-1852/s2.

relevant_excerpt: shall, be charged with the proper implementation and administration of this Act
why_relevant: Added by the verifier. The Act is administered by the Commissioner-General, which is the statutory anchor for the answer to 'to whom do you pay': duty under Act No. 12 of 2006 is administered centrally and collected through the machinery in s.8, not paid to the lessor or to the notary.
temporal_note: In force from 2006; the corpus records no amendment to s.2, so the text applies at 2019-04.
verifier_note: Added by the verifier; excerpt checked verbatim against 12-2006/s2.

relevant_excerpt: The Minister may make regulations in respect of all matters which are required by this Act to be prescribed
why_relevant: Added by the verifier. Section 8(2) routes payment to a 'prescribed bank' against a certificate 'in the prescribed form'; s.12 is the only source of that prescription, and no such regulation is in the corpus, so the bank cannot be named from corpus text.
temporal_note: In force from 2006; the corpus records no amendment to s.12, so the text applies at 2019-04.
verifier_note: Added by the verifier; excerpt checked verbatim against 12-2006/s12.

relevant_excerpt: all streets within the Municipality (except such streets as may be specially exempted by the President) together with the pavements, stones and other materials thereof
why_relevant: This is the vesting provision the third question assumes has operated. Once Lot R1 is a street within the Municipality, the road reservation is vested in the Municipal Council rather than in any private owner, and access over it ceases to depend on a private grant.
temporal_note: In force from 1947; the corpus records no amendment event on s.37, so the text applies at 2019-04.

relevant_excerpt: includes any road, square, court, alley, lane, or passage, river or canal, whether a thoroughfare or not, over which the public have a right of way
why_relevant: Defines the term on which the vesting in s.37(1)(b) turns. A road reservation that is a street for the purposes of the Ordinance is one over which the public have a right of way, so a member of the public may pass over it without any private servitude.
temporal_note: Section 327 was last touched in 1987 on the corpus record (amendment events 1969, 1977, 1981, 1987); the definition text is therefore the text in force at 2019-04.
verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim and in force at 2019-04, but the s.327 definition is inclusive and makes a public right of way a criterion of being a "street", not a consequence of vesting, so the answer must state the premise that Lot R1 is vested as a street under s.37(1)(b) rather than by some other route.

relevant_excerpt: includes all messages, buildings, lands, and servitudes, and all servitudes shall be deemed to be part of the property to which they appertain, or in connexion with which they are enjoyed
why_relevant: Statutory recognition, for the purposes of this Ordinance, that a servitude is treated as part of the property to which it appertains. It is consistent with the common-law rule that a right of way is appurtenant to a dominant tenement, but it is an interpretation clause of one Ordinance and does not itself govern conveyancing between private parties.
temporal_note: Same section as PROV-M089-002; last recorded change 1987, so in force at 2019-04.
verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim, but it is the "premises" interpretation clause of this Ordinance alone and cannot carry a general rule of servitude law, so its role is demoted to background in both M089-Q01 and M089-Q02.

relevant_excerpt: to maintain and cleanse all public streets and open spaces vested in the Council or committed to its management
why_relevant: Shows that a street vested in the Council is held and maintained by it as a public street, which supports the conclusion that use of Lot R1 after vesting is public use rather than use under a private right.
temporal_note: In force from 1947; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: Whenever any street or any part of any street vested in a Municipal Council ceases to be used as a street, the Council, with the prior approval of the President, may sell, lease, or exchange such street or part thereof
why_relevant: Confirms that a vested street stays available for street use unless and until it ceases to be used as a street and is disposed of with the President's prior approval, so the vesting is not a temporary or precarious arrangement.
temporal_note: In force from 1947; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: to any person obstructing or encroaching upon any street under control of the Council, forthwith to remove or abate the obstruction or encroachment
why_relevant: Gives the Council the power to clear obstructions on a street under its control, which is the practical protection of the access Kapila Fernando would enjoy over Lot R1 after vesting.
temporal_note: In force from 1947; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: subject to the condition that by an appropriate instrument such road is constituted a public road and is vested in the Council
why_relevant: Illustrates one statutory route by which a road serving private owners is constituted a public road and vested in the Council. It is background to how a private road reservation such as Lot R1 may come to be vested; it is not the only route and the question does not say which was used.
temporal_note: In force from 1947; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: No sale, purchase, transfer, assignment, or mortgage of land or other immovable property, and no promise, bargain, contract, or agreement for effecting any such object, or for establishing any security, interest, or incumbrance affecting land or other immovable property
why_relevant: A right of way is an interest affecting immovable property, so any transfer of Lot A2 with the right of way, or any purported transfer of the right of way on its own, must be by notarially executed and attested deed. This governs the form of the transaction; it does not decide whether the right of way is capable of being transferred in the way proposed.
temporal_note: The corpus holds only the current consolidated text of s.2, which incorporates the amendments made by Act No. 30 of 2022 and Act No. 4 of 2024 (thumb impressions, transferee signature). A requirement of writing, signature and notarial attestation existed in April 2019, but the excerpt above is not the April 2019 text, so this provision is treated as not applicable to the matter date and is never relied on as indispensable.
verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim only in the post-2022/2024 consolidated text; the corpus does not hold s.2 as it stood in April 2019, so it cannot give direct support to a rule claim at the matter date and is correctly marked applicable_to_matter_date=false.

relevant_excerpt: the word "street" includes any road, footway, or passage used or intended to be used as a means of access to two or more houses or sites of houses whether the public have a right of way there over or not
why_relevant: Added by the verifier. Section 71(6) has to extend "street", for that section only, to roads used as access to two or more houses "whether the public have a right of way there over or not". That extension would be unnecessary unless the general s.327 definition required a public right of way. It therefore confirms that a road reservation is a street for the purposes of s.37(1)(b) only where the public already have a right of way over it, which is the premise the third answer must assume rather than derive.
temporal_note: Section 71 records one amendment event (No. 4 of 1975, s.3); latest recorded change 1975, so the text applies at 2019-04.
verifier_note: Excerpt checked verbatim against 29-1947/s71.

relevant_excerpt: (20) He shall without delay duly attest every deed or instrument which shall be executed or acknowledged before him, and shall sign and seal such attestation. In such attestation he shall state- (a) that the said deed or instrument was signed by the party and the witnesses thereto in his presence and in the presence of one another;
why_relevant: The primary duty owed in respect of the original: the notary must without delay duly attest the deed executed before him, sign and seal the attestation, and set out in it the prescribed particulars.
temporal_note: Rule (20) has stood since 1907. Paragraph (b) was substituted by the Notaries (Amendment) Act, No. 31 of 2022 (identification by national identity card, passport or driving licence) and paragraph (g) by the Notaries (Amendment) Act, No. 6 of 2024; the excerpt taken here stops at paragraph (a) and so is text that was in force in April 2019. The corpus holds only the consolidated post-2024 edition, so the April 2019 wording of the later paragraphs cannot be quoted from it.

relevant_excerpt: (f) the number and value of the adhesive stamps affixed to or the value of the impressed stamps on such deed or instrument and the duplicate thereof;
why_relevant: Ties the original and the duplicate together in the attestation: the notary must state the number and value of the stamps affixed to the deed and to its duplicate.
temporal_note: Paragraph (f) of rule (20) was not touched by the 2011, 2022 or 2024 amending Acts, so this wording was in force in April 2019.

relevant_excerpt: (i) He shall deliver or transmit to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which he resides the following documents, so that they shall reach the registrar on or before the fifteenth day of every month, namely, the duplicate of every deed or instrument (except wills and codicils) executed or acknowledged before or attested by him during the preceding month, together with a list in duplicate, signed by him, of all such deeds or instruments, which list shall be substantially in the Form F 1 in the Second Schedule:
why_relevant: The central duty in respect of the duplicate: it must be delivered or transmitted to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the notary resides, so as to reach the registrar on or before the fifteenth day of the month following execution, with a signed list in duplicate.
temporal_note: The duty itself long predates the matter date. Paragraph (a) was renumbered as sub-paragraph (i) and sub-paragraph (ii) inserted by the Notaries (Amendment) Act, No. 47 of 2011, so the paragraph structure quoted here was in force in April 2019. One later change: the words 'in the Form F' were replaced by 'in the Form F 1' by the Notaries (Amendment) Act, No. 6 of 2024, s. 3(8); in April 2019 the list was in Form F. That affects the form reference only, not the duty.
verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim in the corpus and the duty is correctly stated, but two corrections stand: the words "in the Form F 1" were substituted for "in the Form F" by the Notaries (Amendment) Act, No. 6 of 2024 s.3(8), so the April 2019 text read "Form F"; and the rule label "(26)" is not printed in the corpus text, which runs straight from rule (25) into "(i) He shall deliver or transmit", the number being recoverable only from Act No. 47 of 2011 s.3, Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3(8) and sections 32(1) and 34(2).

relevant_excerpt: (29) If a deed or instrument other than a will or codicil affects a land situated in a district other than that in which the notary before whom it is signed, and by whom it is attested, 'shall reside, such notary, or in case such deed or instrument is attested by two or more notaries, then the notary upon whom is cast the duty of transmitting to the Registrar of Lands the duplicate of such deed or instrument, shall on or before the fifteenth day of the month next following that in which the same was executed (besides transmitting the duplicate in manner aforesaid) deliver or transmit to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which such land shall be situated a copy thereof certified by him as correct,
why_relevant: The rule that decides this scenario: where the land lies in a district other than the notary's district of residence, he must, in addition to transmitting the duplicate, send a certified copy of the deed with a list in duplicate to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the land is situated, by the fifteenth of the following month.
temporal_note: Rule (29) was in force in April 2019. The only later change is the substitution of 'in the Form F 1' for 'in the Form F' by the Notaries (Amendment) Act, No. 6 of 2024, s. 3(9); in April 2019 the list was in Form F. The duty is unchanged.
verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim and rule (29) is the provision that decides the scenario, but "in the Form F 1" is the substitution made by the Notaries (Amendment) Act, No. 6 of 2024 s.3(9); in April 2019 rule (29) read "in the Form F".

relevant_excerpt: (24) He shall carefully preserve as his protocol a draft or copy of every deed or instrument executed or acknowledged before him, to which shall be attached his signature and those of the party and witnesses to the original deed or instrument, and he shall keep a register thereof with a convenient index for the purpose of easy reference;
why_relevant: Completes the picture of what the notary keeps: the protocol, a draft or copy of the deed signed by the parties and witnesses to the original, and a register of protocols. It distinguishes the protocol from the original and the duplicate.
temporal_note: Rule (24) was not amended by the 2011, 2022 or 2024 Acts and was in force in April 2019.

relevant_excerpt: Whenever a notary has received instructions to register, and a sufficient sum to meet the necessary expense of registering, any deed drawn or attested by him, and shall in such case fail to use due diligence in effecting such registration, he shall be guilty of an offence
why_relevant: Fixes the notary's duty in respect of the original once the parties instruct him to register it and put him in funds: he must use due diligence in effecting registration.
temporal_note: Section 37 was in force in April 2019; the only change recorded in the corpus is the increase of the fine by the Increase of Fines Act, No. 12 of 2005, which predates the matter date.

relevant_excerpt: Whenever the duplicate of any deed shall be transmitted to the registrar by any notary under any rule in section 31 of this Ordinance, or whenever any document shall be delivered up to any registrar under section 41, such notary or other person transmitting or delivering the same shall tender to the registrar two lists thereof, and the said registrar shall, after ascertaining the correctness thereof, sign the said lists, and return one of them to the said notary or other party, and file the remaining list,
why_relevant: The mechanics of transmitting the duplicate: the notary tenders two lists to the registrar, who signs and returns one and files the other, keeping it with the duplicate among the records of his office.
temporal_note: No amendment to section 42 is recorded in the corpus; the text was in force in April 2019.

relevant_excerpt: (1) Every instrument presented for registration shall be registered in the book allotted to the division in which the land affected by the instrument is situated
why_relevant: Explains where the original has to be taken for registration: an instrument is registered in the book allotted to the division in which the land affected is situated, which for this deed is the Nuwara Eliya division and not the notary's own district.
temporal_note: The latest change recorded for section 14 is 1974, well before the matter date.

relevant_excerpt: (1) Every Registrar shall from time to time cause all duplicates and copies transmitted or delivered to him under the preceding section or any other written law, or by any notary under the provisions of the Notaries Ordinance, to be bound in convenient volumes
why_relevant: Background: what becomes of the duplicate once the notary transmits it. The Registrar binds the duplicates delivered by a notary under the Notaries Ordinance into volumes and preserves them in his office.
temporal_note: No amendment to section 5 is recorded in the corpus; the text was in force in April 2019.

relevant_excerpt: (1) An instrument executed or made on or after the 1st day of January, 1864, whether before or after the commencement of this Ordinance shall, unless it is duly registered under this Chapter, or, if the land has come within the operation of the Land Registration Ordinance, 1877f, in the books mentioned in section 26 of that Ordinance, be void as against all parties claiming an adverse interest thereto on valuable consideration by virtue of any subsequent instrument which is duly registered under this Chapter,
