why_relevant: Background: when the duty on the deed must be paid. Not needed to fix the amount, but part of the practical answer.
temporal_note: In force at October 2018.

relevant_excerpt: A Commissioner or a Deputy Commissioner may exercise, perform or discharge any power, duty or function conferred or imposed on, or assigned to, an Assessor by this Statute.
why_relevant: Bridges the gap the researcher flagged. Section 48(1) computes duty on the value of the property conveyed and the section 106 definition of value is the open-market price in the opinion of the Assessor, an office section 106 defines as a Provincial Assessor of Revenue. The facts give the opinion of valuation of the Commissioner of Revenue of the Western Provincial Council. Section 104(4) lets a Commissioner discharge any function assigned to an Assessor, so the Commissioner's Rs. 7,500,000 opinion is an opinion within the section 106 definition. Without it the step from the Commissioner's valuation to the statutory base is unsupported.
temporal_note: In force at October 2018 on the same footing as the rest of the Statute; section 104 shows no amendment event in the corpus.
verifier_note: Added by the verifier. Excerpt checked verbatim against 6-1990/s104.

relevant_excerpt: It is and shall be the duty of every notary strictly to observe and act in conformity with the following rules
why_relevant: Makes each numbered rule in section 31 a mandatory duty of the notary rather than a matter of good practice, so every witness rule relied on below is owed by this notary when he attests the will at the hospital.
temporal_note: Section 31 has been in force since 1907. The corpus edition is consolidated to 2024 and prints the text as altered by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 47 of 2011, Act No. 31 of 2022 and Act No. 6 of 2024. No amendment event is recorded for the chapeau by any of those Acts, so these words also stood at October 2018.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument to which at least two witnesses have not subscribed their signatures in letters.
why_relevant: The first precaution about witnesses: there must be at least two of them and each must subscribe his signature in letters rather than make a mark. It fixes both the minimum number of witnesses and the form of their subscription.
temporal_note: Part of section 31, in force since 1907. Neither Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 nor Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3 touches rule (8), so this text stood unchanged at October 2018.

relevant_excerpt: he shall satisfy himself, before accepting them as witnesses, that they are persons of good repute and that they are well acquainted with the executant and know his proper name, occupation, and residence, and the witnesses shall sign a declaration at the foot of the deed or instrument that they are well acquainted with the executant and know his proper name, occupation, and residence.
why_relevant: The central witness-vetting rule: before he accepts anyone as a witness the notary must satisfy himself that the person is of good repute and well acquainted with the executant and knows his proper name, occupation and residence, and he must obtain the witnesses' signed declaration to that effect at the foot of the instrument.
temporal_note: The words quoted are unaltered, but their opening context differed at the matter date. In October 2018 rule (9) began 'He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless the person executing the same be known to him or to at least two of the attesting witnesses thereto;' (those words were replaced by Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(6), recorded at PROV-M100-017) and the quoted duty was introduced by the words 'and in the latter case,' (deleted by Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3(3), recorded at PROV-M100-018). At the matter date the quoted duty therefore attached in terms to the case where the notary relies on the attesting witnesses' knowledge of the executant rather than on his own.
verifier_note: Wording is verbatim and the temporal reconstruction is right, but the role needs a correction: because Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3(3) shows that in October 2018 the vetting and declaration duty was introduced by the words "and in the latter case", that duty attached in terms to the case where the notary relied on the attesting witnesses' knowledge of the executant, and this Notary knows the testator himself, so on these facts the rule (9) duty is a prudent precaution rather than one the corpus shows to be owed.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless the person executing the same and the witnesses shall have signed the same in his presence and in the presence of one another, and unless he shall have signed the same in the presence of the executant and of the attesting witnesses.
why_relevant: Governs the manner of signing: the testator and both witnesses must sign in the notary's presence and in the presence of one another, and the notary must sign in front of all of them. This is the precaution that requires nobody to leave the bedside until every signature is on the will.
temporal_note: Part of section 31, in force since 1907. No amendment event is recorded for rule (12) in Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3, so the rule stood in this form at October 2018.

relevant_excerpt: that the said deed or instrument was signed by the party and the witnesses thereto in his presence and in the presence of one another
why_relevant: Requires the notary to state in his attestation the very fact that rule (12) obliges him to secure, so the precaution taken at the bedside must also appear on the face of the will.
temporal_note: Part of section 31, in force since 1907. Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(11) and Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3(7) alter paragraphs (b), (e) and (g) of rule (20) and add paragraph (h); paragraph (a) is untouched and stood in this form at October 2018.

relevant_excerpt: the day, month, and year on which and the place where the said deed or instrument was executed or acknowledged, and the full names of the attesting witnesses and their residences
why_relevant: Requires the full names and residences of the attesting witnesses, and the place of execution, to appear in the attestation. Here the place is a hospital ward, so the notary must know and record where each witness lives.
temporal_note: Part of section 31, in force since 1907. Paragraph (c) of rule (20) is not among the paragraphs amended by Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(11) or Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3(7); it stood in this form at October 2018.

formal_title: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance No. 7 of 1840
relevant_excerpt: such devise, legacy, estate, interest, gift, disposition, or appointment shall, so far only as concerns such person attesting the execution of such will, testament, or codicil, or the wife or husband of such person, or any person claiming under such person or wife or husband, be utterly null and void
why_relevant: The disqualification that matters most in choosing witnesses to a will: a beneficiary, or the spouse of a beneficiary, who attests the will loses the gift. The notary's precaution is to ensure that neither witness, nor either witness's spouse, takes anything under the will.
temporal_note: Section 11 has been in force since 1840. No amendment event is recorded for it in the corpus, and neither Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 30 of 2022 nor Act No. 4 of 2024 touches it, so this is also the October 2018 text.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument in any case in which the person executing or acknowledging the same shall be or profess to be unable to read the same, or in which such person shall require him to read over the same, unless and until he shall have read over and explained the same, or caused the same to be explained, in the presence and hearing of such person and, except in the case of wills and codicils, in the presence of the attesting witnesses.
why_relevant: Qualifies what the witnesses must be present for. Where the testator cannot read the will or asks for it to be read, the notary must read and explain it to him, but wills and codicils are expressly excepted from the requirement that this be done in the presence of the attesting witnesses.
temporal_note: Part of section 31, in force since 1907. No amendment event is recorded for rule (11) in Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3; it stood in this form at October 2018. Section 34(1)(b) treats a breach of rule (11) as an offence.
verifier_note: Rule (11) itself is verified verbatim and was unamended at the matter date, but the temporal note's reference to section 34(1)(b) reads the post-2022 penalty section: section 34 was substituted in its entirety by Act No. 31 of 2022 s.17, so the corpus does not show how a breach of rule (11) was punished in October 2018.

relevant_excerpt: whether the same was read over by the person executing the same, or read and explained by him, the said notary, to the said person in the presence of the attesting witnesses
why_relevant: The attestation must record whether the will was read over by the testator himself or read and explained to him in the presence of the attesting witnesses, so the notary must settle which course was followed and then state it.
temporal_note: Part of section 31, in force since 1907. Paragraph (d) of rule (20) is untouched by the 2022 and 2024 amendments and stood in this form at October 2018.

relevant_excerpt: He shall carefully preserve as his protocol a draft or copy of every deed or instrument executed or acknowledged before him, to which shall be attached his signature and those of the party and witnesses to the original deed or instrument
why_relevant: The witnesses' task does not end with the original: the same two witnesses must also sign the protocol copy the notary keeps, so the notary must have the protocol ready at the bedside before they disperse.
temporal_note: Part of section 31, in force since 1907. No amendment event is recorded for rule (24) in Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3; in force in this form at October 2018.

relevant_excerpt: the attesting witnesses having appeared personally before him at the time when such deed was executed or acknowledged
why_relevant: Attesting without the attesting witnesses having appeared personally before the notary at the time of execution is a criminal offence, not merely a breach of a rule. It is the sanction that makes the presence requirement in rule (12) a real precaution.
temporal_note: Section 39 has been in force since 1907. Act No. 31 of 2022 s.19(1) altered other words of paragraph (c) ('signature or mark' became 'signature, and the left or right thumb impression or any other finger impression or toe impression, as the case may be') and s.19(2) raised the penalty; the words quoted here fall outside both substitutions and stood in this form at October 2018.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument to which he is a party.
why_relevant: Keeps the notary himself out of the instrument. He cannot make up the number by acting as one of the two witnesses to a will he attests, and cannot attest a will in which he takes an interest.
temporal_note: Part of section 31, in force since 1907. No amendment event is recorded for rule (13) in Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3; in force in this form at October 2018.

formal_title: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance No. 7 of 1840
relevant_excerpt: If any person who shall attest the execution of any will, testament, or codicil shall at the time of the execution thereof, or at any time afterwards, be incompetent to be admitted a witness to prove the execution thereof, such will, testament, or codicil shall not on that account be invalid.
why_relevant: Limits the consequence of a bad choice of witness: incompetency of an attesting witness does not by itself invalidate the will. It shows that the sanction for a poorly chosen witness lies elsewhere, chiefly in section 11.
temporal_note: In force since 1840; no amendment event recorded in the corpus, so this is also the October 2018 text.

formal_title: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance No. 7 of 1840
relevant_excerpt: before a notary public and two witnesses who shall be present at the same time
why_relevant: Sets the number of witnesses and the requirement that they be present at the same time as the notary when the testator signs. It is the source of the two-witness requirement that the notarial rules then work out in detail.
temporal_note: The corpus text of section 4 is the text as renumbered and substituted by Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 30 of 2022 s.3, which is after the October 2018 matter date, so the wording quoted is not the wording in force at the matter date. The corpus does not carry the pre-2022 text: Act No. 30 of 2022 s.3(2) repeals the words from 'in the manner hereinafter mentioned;' to the end of the section without reproducing them. The requirement of a notary and two witnesses present at the same time is common to the corpus text and to the surviving description of the older text, but for this reason the provision is treated as supporting and not as indispensable.

formal_title: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance No. 7 of 1840
relevant_excerpt: No obliteration, interlineations, or other alteration made in any will, testament, or codicil after the execution thereof shall be valid or have any effect, except so far as the words or effect of the will, testament, or codicil before such alteration shall not be apparent, unless such alteration shall be executed in like manner as herein before is required for the execution of the will
why_relevant: Extends the witness requirement to any alteration made after execution: an alteration has no effect unless executed in the same manner as the will itself, which means before the same class of witnesses.
temporal_note: Section 7 has been in force since 1840. Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 30 of 2022 s.4 substituted words later in the section ('signature of the testator or testatrix') and added a proviso, both after the matter date; the words quoted here fall outside both changes and stood in this form at October 2018.

relevant_excerpt: He shall, before any executant or witness signs or makes a mark and before any executant affixes his left or right thumb impression or any other finger impression or toe impression, ascertain the full names of the executant and witnesses to such deed or instrument
why_relevant: Requires the notary to ascertain the full names of the witnesses before anyone signs, and to describe a witness by both names where the name signed differs from the name in his identification documents.
temporal_note: Rule (14) as printed in the corpus is the rule substituted by Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(7), which is after the matter date, so this wording was not in force in October 2018 and the provision is treated as supporting only. The corpus does not carry the pre-2022 text, because s.16(7) substitutes the rule without reproducing what it replaced.

relevant_excerpt: in rule (9) thereof, by the substitution for the words, "He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless the person executing the same be known to him or to at least two of the attesting witnesses thereto;"
why_relevant: Recovers the opening words of rule (9) as they stood before 2022, and therefore as they stood at the matter date: the notary could proceed either because he himself knew the executant or because at least two of the attesting witnesses knew him. This is the wording against which the facts of this matter, where the notary knows the testator, have to be tested.
temporal_note: Act No. 31 of 2022 is later than the October 2018 matter date and is not applied as operative law here. It is recorded because the words it repeals are the words that were in force at the matter date, and the corpus preserves them only in this amending section.

relevant_excerpt: in rule (9) thereof, by the substitution for the words "and in the latter case, he shall", of the words, "he shall"; (4) by the repeal of rule (10) thereof;
why_relevant: Shows two things about the October 2018 text of section 31. First, the witness-vetting duty in rule (9) was then introduced by the words 'and in the latter case, he shall', so it attached in terms to the case where the notary relies on the attesting witnesses' knowledge of the executant. Second, a rule (10) existed at the matter date and was repealed only in 2024, so the consolidated text used here is missing a rule that was in force when this will would have been executed.
temporal_note: Act No. 6 of 2024 is later than the October 2018 matter date and is not applied as operative law. It is recorded because it identifies wording and a whole rule that were in force at the matter date but are absent from the consolidated corpus text of section 31.

formal_title: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance No. 7 of 1840
relevant_excerpt: such creditor, notwithstanding such charge, shall be admitted a witness to prove the execution of such will, testament, or codicil, or to prove the validity or invalidity thereof.
why_relevant: Background on who may safely be used as a witness: a creditor whose debt is charged on the property by the will is not disqualified from attesting it.
temporal_note: In force since 1840; no amendment event recorded in the corpus, so this is also the October 2018 text.

formal_title: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance No. 7 of 1840
relevant_excerpt: No person shall, on account of his or her being an executor or executrix of a will, testament, or codicil, be incompetent to be admitted a witness to prove the execution of such will, testament, or codicil
why_relevant: Background on who may safely be used as a witness: an executor named in the will is not incompetent to attest it and does not forfeit his commission by doing so.
temporal_note: In force since 1840; no amendment event recorded in the corpus, so this is also the October 2018 text.

relevant_excerpt: No instrument shall be deemed to be invalid by reason only of the failure of any notary to observe any provision of any rule set out in section 31 in respect of any matter of form
why_relevant: Background on consequences: a failure in a matter of form under section 31 does not of itself invalidate the instrument, but the proviso preserves invalidity arising under any other written law, which is where the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance bites.
temporal_note: Section 33 has been in force since 1907 and no amendment event is recorded for it in the corpus; in force in this form at October 2018.

relevant_excerpt: whether the executants of the said deed or instrument are known to him or whether he has identified them by the inspection of the national identity card, bio-page of the passport or the driving licence or whether the witnesses thereto are known to him and in the latter case he shall specify which of the executants or the person acknowledging are known to the said witness
why_relevant: Added by the verifier. Paragraph (b) of rule (20) is the attestation paragraph that turns on the witnesses: the notary must state whether he knows the executants himself or whether the witnesses know them, and in the latter case which executant each witness knows. It is the counterpart in the attestation of the identification limb of rule (9), and the researcher's map records paragraphs (a), (c) and (d) of rule (20) but not (b).
temporal_note: The text quoted is paragraph (b) as substituted by Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(11)(a), which is after the October 2018 matter date, so this wording was not then in force. Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(11)(a) repeals the old paragraph (b) without reproducing it, so the October 2018 wording of the one attestation paragraph that turns on the witnesses' knowledge of the executant is not recoverable from the corpus. Recorded as a supporting provision and as a corpus gap.
verifier_note: Excerpt checked verbatim against 1-1907/s31. Added because the map covered rule (20)(a), (c) and (d) but not the witness-facing paragraph (b); it is recorded as inapplicable at the matter date because only the post-2022 wording survives in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument in any area other than that in which he is authorized to practice, nor in any language other than that in which he is authorized to practice nor authenticate or attest any deed or instrument drawn in any language other than that in which he is authorized to practice.
why_relevant: The notary is licensed in English only, so the deed of transfer must be drawn in English and attested in English. This rule is what makes a Sinhala signature a signature in a language other than the notary's language of practice, and it is the reason the executants must be instructed that the instrument itself will be in English.
temporal_note: Rule (22) is original 1907 text; it is not amended by 47-2011, 13-2013, 31-2022 or 6-2024, so the corpus text is the text in force in October 2018.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument in any case in which the person executing or acknowledging the same shall be or profess to be unable to read the same, or in which such person shall require him to read over the same, unless and until he shall have read over and explained the same, or caused the same to be explained, in the presence and hearing of such person and, except in the case of wills and codicils, in the presence of the attesting witnesses.
why_relevant: One executant cannot sign in any language and cannot read; the other reads only Sinhala while the deed is in English. Both are therefore unable to read the instrument, so the notary must read it over and explain it, or cause it to be explained, in their presence and hearing and in the presence of the attesting witnesses before he attests.
temporal_note: Rule (11) is original 1907 text; not amended by 47-2011, 31-2022 or 6-2024. In force in October 2018.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless the person executing the same and the witnesses shall have signed the same in his presence and in the presence of one another, and unless he shall have signed the same in the presence of the executant and of the attesting witnesses.
why_relevant: Fixes the manner of execution the notary must instruct the parties to follow: both brothers and both witnesses must sign, or in the case of the illiterate brother make his mark, in the notary's presence and in the presence of one another, and the notary must sign in their presence.
temporal_note: Rule (12) is original 1907 text; not amended by 47-2011, 31-2022 or 6-2024. In force in October 2018.

relevant_excerpt: If any deed or instrument executed or acknowledged before him be signed by any of the parties or witnesses thereto with a mark, or with a signature in a language other than that in which the notary is authorized to practice, he shall write over such mark or signature in his own handwriting and at the time of execution the words "This is the mark (or signature, as the case may be) of A. B."
why_relevant: This is the certification rule the question asks about. It covers both executants at once: the brother who cannot sign signs with a mark, and the brother who signs in Sinhala signs in a language other than English, the language of the notary's warrant. In each case the notary must write over the mark or signature, in his own hand and at the time of execution, the words prescribed, inserting the name of the person signing.
temporal_note: Rule (15) is original 1907 text. Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(8) inserted a new rule (15A) after it but did not alter rule (15) itself. In force in October 2018.

relevant_excerpt: and in the case of a mark he shall besides require such person to affix to the deed or instrument the impression of his left thumb and shall write over such impression at the time and in the manner aforesaid the words "This is the left thumb impression of A. B."
why_relevant: Adds the extra step required only for the executant who signs with a mark: the notary must require the left thumb impression and write the prescribed words over it. This is the step that distinguishes the treatment of the brother who cannot sign from the treatment of the brother who signs in Sinhala.
temporal_note: Part of the original rule (15); not amended by 31-2022 or 6-2024. In force in October 2018. The general obligation on every executant of a deed affecting immovable property to affix a thumb impression comes from rule (15A), inserted only in 2022, and is therefore not applied here.

relevant_excerpt: He shall without delay duly attest every deed or instrument which shall be executed or acknowledged before him, and shall sign and seal such attestation. In such attestation he shall state- (a) that the said deed or instrument was signed by the party and the witnesses thereto in his presence and in the presence of one another;
why_relevant: The second half of the question is how the notary certifies. Rule (20) requires an attestation, signed and sealed without delay, which states that the parties and witnesses signed in his presence and in the presence of one another, and (paragraph (d)) whether the deed was read over by the executant or read and explained by the notary in the presence of the attesting witnesses. That last statement is what records compliance with rule (11) on the face of the deed.
temporal_note: The opening words of rule (20) and paragraphs (a), (c), (d) and (f) are original text. Paragraphs (b) and (e) were substituted and (h) added by 31-2022 s.16(11), and (g) was substituted by 6-2024 s.3(7); none of those later paragraphs is relied on here.
verifier_note: Wording and 2018 applicability confirmed against 31-2022 s.16(11) and 6-2024 s.3(7), but the subsection label reads "(20)(a) and (20)(d)" while the excerpt covers only the opening words of rule (20) and paragraph (a); paragraph (d) is carried separately by PROV-M101-007, and the label should be read as rule (20) opening words and paragraph (a).

relevant_excerpt: (d) whether the same was read over by the person executing the same, or read and explained by him, the said notary, to the said person in the presence of the attesting witnesses;
why_relevant: Requires the attestation itself to record that the deed was read over and explained to these executants in the presence of the attesting witnesses, which is the certification counterpart of the rule (11) duty triggered by an executant who cannot read.
temporal_note: Paragraph (d) of rule (20) is original text and was not touched by 31-2022 s.16(11) or 6-2024 s.3(7). In force in October 2018.

relevant_excerpt: Every such attestation shall be substantially in the form E in the Second Schedule, and shall be legibly signed by him in the language in which the deed or instrument is written, and also with his usual signature if the language or form of that signature be different from that in which such deed or instrument is written.
why_relevant: Fixes the form and language of the certification: the attestation must follow Form E substantially and must be legibly signed by the notary in English, the language in which this deed is written, and in addition with his usual signature if that differs.
temporal_note: Rule (21) is original 1907 text; not amended by 47-2011, 31-2022 or 6-2024. In force in October 2018. Form E itself is not in the corpus.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument to which at least two witnesses have not subscribed their signatures in letters.
why_relevant: Explains why the witnesses, unlike the executants, must sign in letters and cannot sign by mark, and so shapes the instruction the notary gives about who may witness this deed.
temporal_note: Rule (8) is original text and was not amended by 31-2022 or 6-2024. In force in October 2018.

relevant_excerpt: He shall correctly insert in letters in every deed or instrument executed before him the day, month, and year on which and the place where the same is executed, and shall sign the same.
why_relevant: Supports the execution instructions: the date and place of execution must be inserted in letters and the notary must sign the deed itself, in addition to signing the attestation.
temporal_note: Rule (18) is original text; not amended by 31-2022 or 6-2024. In force in October 2018.

relevant_excerpt: He shall, before any executant or witness signs or makes a mark and before any executant affixes his left or right thumb impression or any other finger impression or toe impression, ascertain the full names of the executant and witnesses to such deed or instrument
why_relevant: The notary must ascertain the full names of the executants before the mark or signature is made, because rule (15) requires him to write the correct name into the words he places over the mark or the Sinhala signature.
temporal_note: The corpus text of rule (14) is the text substituted by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(7), which postdates October 2018. A duty in similar terms to ascertain the full names before signing appears to have existed earlier, but the corpus does not hold the pre-2022 wording, so this provision is carried as supporting only and nothing indispensable rests on it.
verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim but the corpus text of rule (14) is the wording substituted by 31-2022 s.16(7), so it is not the October 2018 text; the provision may stand as supporting only, and the gold answer's rule paragraph should not state s.31(14) as law applicable at the reference date.

relevant_excerpt: the relevant deed or instrument shall be in writing, signed by every executant or by any person duly authorised by such executant and the witnesses in the presence of a licenced notary public present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and the same shall be attested by such notary
why_relevant: Background: it is this section that makes notarial execution and attestation a condition of a transfer of land having force in law, which is why the manner of signing and of certification matters at all.
temporal_note: The corpus holds only the consolidated text of section 2, which records amendment events for 30-2022 s.2 and 4-2024 s.2. The quoted wording and the thumb-impression requirement in paragraph (b) are post-2018 text, so the section is used as background only and no claim rests on it.
verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim but is the post-30-2022 / 4-2024 text of section 2; confirmed against 30-2022 s.2 that paragraph (1)(b) and subsection (2) date from 2022, so the section is correctly carried as background only and no claim may rest on its wording.

relevant_excerpt: He shall carefully preserve as his protocol a draft or copy of every deed or instrument executed or acknowledged before him, to which shall be attached his signature and those of the party and witnesses to the original deed or instrument
why_relevant: Added by the verifier. The gold answer instructs the executant who cannot sign to make his mark on the deed, the duplicate and the protocol, but no provision in the map supported signing anything beyond the deed itself once rule (15A) was excluded as post-2018. Rule (24) is the provision that requires the protocol to carry the signatures of the party and the witnesses, and it is untouched by 20-1976 s.10, 47-2011, 31-2022 s.16 and 6-2024 s.3.
temporal_note: Rule (24) is original 1907 text. The amendment events on section 31 record no change to rule (24) by 20-1976 s.10, 47-2011 s.2 or s.3, 31-2022 s.16 or 6-2024 s.3, so the corpus text is the text in force in October 2018.
verifier_note: Added by the verifier to give the protocol element of the execution instruction a cited basis; excerpt checked verbatim. It does not support the duplicate element of that instruction, for which the corpus holds no October 2018 provision.

relevant_excerpt: by the insertion, immediately after rule (15) thereof, of the following new rule:- (a) Every- (i) executant; (ii) attorney; or (iii) board of directors or the authorized person of a corporate body; executing a deed or instrument in respect of an immovable property, in addition to the provisions of rule (15) shall affix his thumb impression of any hand above or beside his signature to the original, duplicate and the protocol of such deed or instrument
why_relevant: Added by the verifier. Claim CL-M101-Q01-016 concludes that the brother who signs in Sinhala need not affix a thumb impression as at October 2018. That negative conclusion turns on the date rule (15A) entered the law, which is this amending provision; it was cited only in a temporal note and not as authority for the claim.
temporal_note: This is the amending provision that inserted rule (15A), with effect from 2022, four years after the matter reference date. It is carried as supporting authority for the temporal proposition that no general thumb impression duty applied to a signing executant in October 2018; it is not applied to the matter.
verifier_note: Added by the verifier so that the temporal conclusion rests on a cited provision rather than on a temporal note; excerpt checked verbatim.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not divulge the secrets confided to him or of which he becomes possessed in the execution of his office, unless with the express permission of his employer or when required to do so by law.
why_relevant: This is the notarial secrecy rule and it decides the question. Whether a named person executed a will before the notary, and the date and number of that will, is knowledge the notary came by in the execution of his office. Rule (1) forbids him to divulge it and admits only two exits: the express permission of his employer, or a legal compulsion to disclose. Neither is present where the testator is alive, has given no permission, and no court order or statutory demand has been made.
temporal_note: Section 31 has been amended many times (20-1976 s.10, 47-2011 ss.2-3, 31-2022 s.16, 6-2024 s.3), but none of those amending sections touches rule (1). Rule (1) stands as enacted in 1907 and was in force at 2018-10.

relevant_excerpt: He shall carefully preserve as his protocol a draft or copy of every deed or instrument executed or acknowledged before him, to which shall be attached his signature and those of the party and witnesses to the original deed or instrument, and he shall keep a register thereof with a convenient index for the purpose of easy reference; and every such register shall be substantially in the form F in the Second Schedule, but in the case of wills and codicils only the number and date of the instrument shall be inserted in the register.
why_relevant: Supports the characterisation of the notary's knowledge as official rather than personal: he holds the will as protocol because his office obliges him to. It also shows that the Ordinance itself withholds the particulars of wills, recording only their number and date in the register kept for inspection, which is consistent with reading rule (1) strictly against disclosure of a will. It is not needed to reach the conclusion.
temporal_note: Rule (24) is unamended by 20-1976, 47-2011, 31-2022 or 6-2024 and was in this form at 2018-10.

relevant_excerpt: Provided, however, that in the case of wills and codicils only the number and date of the document shall be inserted in such list
why_relevant: A second illustration of the same legislative policy: even the monthly return a notary must make to the Registrar of Lands excludes the duplicate of a will and discloses only its number and date. It confirms that the confidentiality of a will attested by a notary is not displaced by the Ordinance's own reporting duties. Supporting only.
temporal_note: Rule (26) was amended by 47-2011 s.3 (inserting sub-paragraph (a)(ii)) and by 6-2024 s.3(8) (substituting 'Form F 1' for 'Form F' in (a)(i)). Neither touches the wills proviso quoted here, which was in force at 2018-10. The excerpt deliberately stops short of the Form reference for that reason.

relevant_excerpt: rules (1), (31) or (32) set out in section 31, shall be guilty of an offence, and shall, on conviction after summary trial before a Magistrate, be liable to a fine not exceeding five thousand rupees, in addition to any civil liability he may incur thereby
why_relevant: Shows that rule (1) is penal and not merely hortatory: a notary who divulges is guilty of an offence triable summarily, on top of any civil liability. Supporting; the answer to 'should he divulge' does not depend on the size of the penalty.

A penalty for breach of the section 31 rules existed at 2018-10 (the earlier s.34, with fines as increased by the Increase of Fines Act No. 12 of 2005), but the pre-2022 wording and the exact fine are not in the corpus, so the excerpt must not be treated as the text in force in October 2018 and this provision is not indispensable.

relevant_excerpt: Save as aforesaid, this Ordinance shall not apply to Kandyans or Muslims, or to Tamils of the Northern Province who are or may become subject to the Tesawalamai.
why_relevant: Fixes the personal-law gateway. Nothing in the facts indicates that Nimal or his family were Kandyan, Muslim or Tamils of the Northern Province subject to the Thesawalamai, so the general law of intestate succession in this Ordinance applies to the devolution of lots 6 and 7.
temporal_note: Section is part of the 1876 principal Ordinance; corpus records in_force_from_year 1876 and no amendment events, so the text was in force at each death (2008, 2009, 2010) and at the matter reference date 2018-04.

relevant_excerpt: The following sections of this Ordinance shall apply to the estates of such persons only as shall die after the proclamation of this Ordinance, and shall be then unmarried or (if married) shall have been married after the proclamation of this Ordinance.
why_relevant: Temporal condition on Part III. Every death in the scenario (2008, 2009, 2010) and every marriage in it post-dates the 1876 proclamation, so the inheritance sections apply to each of these estates.
temporal_note: Section is part of the 1876 principal Ordinance; corpus records in_force_from_year 1876 and no amendment events, so the text was in force at each death (2008, 2009, 2010) and at the matter reference date 2018-04.

relevant_excerpt: Inheritance ab interstate to the immovable property in Sri Lanka of a person deceased shall be governed and regulated by the following provisions of this Ordinance wherever such person may have or have had his actual or matrimonial domicile.
why_relevant: The subject matter is divided and defined lots of land in Galle, that is immovable property in Sri Lanka, and each of the three deaths was intestate. This subsection makes the Ordinance the governing law of the devolution, irrespective of domicile.
temporal_note: Section is part of the 1876 principal Ordinance; corpus records in_force_from_year 1876 and no amendment events, so the text was in force at each death (2008, 2009, 2010) and at the matter reference date 2018-04.

relevant_excerpt: When any person shall die intestate as to any of his or her property, leaving a spouse surviving, the surviving spouse shall inherit one-half of the property of such person.
why_relevant: Gives Nalini one-half of Nimal's estate on his death in 2008, and gives Amali one-half of Bimal's estate on his death in 2010. It is the first deduction to be made from each estate before the remainder passes down the section 23 order.
temporal_note: Section is part of the 1876 principal Ordinance; corpus records in_force_from_year 1876 and no amendment events, so the text was in force at each death (2008, 2009, 2010) and at the matter reference date 2018-04.

relevant_excerpt: Subject to the right of the surviving spouse in the preceding section mentioned, the right of inheritance is divided in the following order as respects (a) descendants, (b) ascendants, (c) collaterals.
why_relevant: Sets the order in which the residue after the surviving spouse's half is taken: descendants first (Nimal's and Nalini's estates), and only on their failure ascendants and then collaterals (Bimal's estate).
temporal_note: Section is part of the 1876 principal Ordinance; corpus records in_force_from_year 1876 and no amendment events, so the text was in force at each death (2008, 2009, 2010) and at the matter reference date 2018-04.

relevant_excerpt: Children, grandchildren, and remoter descendants are preferent to all others in the estate of the parents; all the children take equally per capita, but the children or remoter issue of a deceased child take per stirpes or by representation.
why_relevant: Divides the residue of Nimal's estate equally among his four surviving children (Achini, Amal, Bimal, Krishni), and the whole of Nalini's estate equally among her three children (Amal, Bimal, Krishni). Achini, not being a child of Nalini, is excluded from Nalini's estate.
temporal_note: Section is part of the 1876 principal Ordinance; corpus records in_force_from_year 1876 and no amendment events, so the text was in force at each death (2008, 2009, 2010) and at the matter reference date 2018-04.

relevant_excerpt: The children and remoter descendants failing, the inheritance of the deceased goes to his father and mother in case they are both alive; but if only one of the parents be alive, the surviving parent takes half
why_relevant: Bimal died issueless, so his descendants fail and the residue after Amali's half would go to his parents. Both Nimal and Nalini had already died, so no ascendant of the first degree survives and the devolution moves on to collaterals.
temporal_note: Section is part of the 1876 principal Ordinance; corpus records in_force_from_year 1876 and no amendment events, so the text was in force at each death (2008, 2009, 2010) and at the matter reference date 2018-04.

relevant_excerpt: Father and mother both failing, the property of the intestate goes to his brothers and sisters, whether of the whole or balf-blood, and their children and other issue by representation.
why_relevant: Both of Bimal's parents having predeceased him, the residue of his estate after Amali's half goes to his brothers and sisters, expressly including half-blood siblings. This brings in Amal and Krishni (full blood) and Achini (half blood on the father's side).
temporal_note: Section is part of the 1876 principal Ordinance; corpus records in_force_from_year 1876 and no amendment events, so the text was in force at each death (2008, 2009, 2010) and at the matter reference date 2018-04.
verifier_note: Wording and role confirmed; note that the corpus body carries the OCR form "balf-blood" where the Ordinance reads "half-blood", so the excerpt reproduces a corpus artefact rather than a drafting variant.

relevant_excerpt: but if there are only half-brothers and sisters or such issue of one side, the full brothers and sisters and the issue of deceased full brothers and sisters by representation, take then in the first place one-half of the property, and divide the other half with the half-brothers and sisters and their issue by representation.
why_relevant: Achini is a half-sister on the father's side only and there is no half-sibling on the mother's side. This limb therefore governs: Amal and Krishni take one half of the sibling portion of Bimal's estate first, and share the other half with Achini.
temporal_note: Section is part of the 1876 principal Ordinance; corpus records in_force_from_year 1876 and no amendment events, so the text was in force at each death (2008, 2009, 2010) and at the matter reference date 2018-04.
verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim and the final limb is the right one for a half-sibling on one side only, but it starts mid-sentence and omits the opening words that supply the condition ("The division however in the case of half-brothers and sisters is as follows"), and s.27 does not itself say how "the other half" is shared between the full and half blood - that per capita step comes from s.30, so s.27 alone does not carry claim CL-M106-Q02-015.

relevant_excerpt: if all those who succeed to the inheritance are equally near in degree to the intestate, they take per capita, and not per stirpes.
why_relevant: Confirms per capita division among heirs of the same degree: the four children of Nimal, the three children of Nalini, and the three siblings sharing the second half of the sibling portion of Bimal's estate.
temporal_note: Section is part of the 1876 principal Ordinance; corpus records in_force_from_year 1876 and no amendment events, so the text was in force at each death (2008, 2009, 2010) and at the matter reference date 2018-04.
verifier_note: Excerpt drops the governing opening words "Except when otherwise expressly provided,", which matter here because s.27 does expressly provide otherwise for the first half of the sibling portion; s.30 supports only the per capita division of the four children, the three children of Nalini and the second half of the sibling portion.

relevant_excerpt: includes land, incorporeal tenements, and things attached to the earth or permanently fastened to anything which is attached to the earth, and any interest in land except that of a mortgagee
why_relevant: Defines 'immovable property' for the Ordinance. The divided and defined lots 6 and 7, and the undivided share interests in them, fall within this definition, which is the term on which section 21(1) turns.
temporal_note: Section is part of the 1876 principal Ordinance; corpus records in_force_from_year 1876 and no amendment events, so the text was in force at each death (2008, 2009, 2010) and at the matter reference date 2018-04.

relevant_excerpt: In all questions relating to the distribution of the property of an intestate, if the present Ordinance is silent, the rules of the Roman-Dutch law as it prevailed in North Holland are to govern and be followed.
why_relevant: Residual clause. Recorded as background to show that the Ordinance itself directs where to look if it were silent; here sections 22 to 27 and 30 cover each step, so no resort to the residual rule is required.
temporal_note: Section is part of the 1876 principal Ordinance; corpus records in_force_from_year 1876 and no amendment events, so the text was in force at each death (2008, 2009, 2010) and at the matter reference date 2018-04.

relevant_excerpt: the relevant deed or instrument shall be in writing, signed by every executant or by any person duly authorised by such executant and the witnesses in the presence of a licenced notary public present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and the same shall be attested by such notary
why_relevant: Background only: it explains why the 1998 notarially attested Deed of Transfer No. 346 was effective to move Aruni's 1/12 share to Nimal, which is the reason Nimal's estate is 6/12 and not 5/12. The share is taken from the facts, not from this section.

That wording was not in force in June 1998 when Deed No. 346 was executed, nor at the matter reference date 2018-04. It is recorded as background context only and no claim rests on it.

relevant_excerpt: There shall be no community of goods between husband and wife, married after the proclamation of this Ordinance, as a consequence of marriage, either in respect of movable or immovable property.
why_relevant: Added by the verifier. The map takes the whole of Nimal's 6/12 as his estate at death and gives Nalini one-half of it under s.22. That step assumes Nalini held nothing in the land already by virtue of the marriage. Section 7 is the provision that says so: there is no community of goods between spouses married after the 1876 proclamation. Without it the estate on which s.22 operates is not fixed.
temporal_note: Section is part of the 1876 principal Ordinance; corpus records in_force_from_year 1876 and no amendment events, so the text was in force at each death (2008, 2009, 2010) and at the matter reference date 2018-04.

relevant_excerpt: Illegitimate children inherit the property of their intestate mother, but not that of their father or that of the relatives of their mother.

The research notes rejected s.33 outside the map, but the map's central move - admitting Achini as one of four children of Nimal under s.24 - only holds because s.33 is disapplied by the scenario's description of Malini as Nimal's first wife. It is recorded as background so that the exception the answer relies on being switched off is visible on the face of the map.
temporal_note: Section is part of the 1876 principal Ordinance; corpus records in_force_from_year 1876 and no amendment events, so the text was in force at each death (2008, 2009, 2010) and at the matter reference date 2018-04.

relevant_excerpt: Every instrument (except a will) presented for registration shall contain embodied therein, or in a schedule annexed thereto, an accurate and clear description of the land affected thereby, its boundaries, extent, and situation specifying the district and the village, pattu, korale, or other division of the district in which the land is situated; and in case the land is situated in any town, the name, if any, of the street in which it is situated.
why_relevant: This is the provision the question names. It fixes the particulars any schedule to Deed No. 429 must carry: an accurate and clear description of the land, its boundaries, its extent, its situation with the district and the village/pattu/korale or other division, and, the land being at Akuregoda Road, Pelawatta, Battaramulla, the name of the street.
temporal_note: In force from 1927; the section was amended by Ordinance No. 50 of 1982, well before both the 2001 deed and the April 2018 reference date. The consolidated corpus text is the text in force at the matter date.
verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim, but the corpus text is the 1990 consolidation: subsection (1) was repealed and substituted by the Registration of Documents (Amendment) Act, No. 48 of 2011, s.2, so this wording was not the law at the April 2018 reference date; the text in force is recorded at PROV-M107-901 and this entry is kept as the historical pre-2011 wording, moved from indispensable to supporting.

relevant_excerpt: If the land consists of a divided portion of a land or allotment, such portion shall be clearly and accurately defined by its particular boundaries and extent.
why_relevant: Lot C4 is a divided portion of Lot C carved out by a sub-division. Subsection (2) is therefore engaged and adds a requirement over and above subsection (1): the divided portion itself must be defined by its own particular boundaries and its own extent, not merely by reference to the parent Lot C.
temporal_note: In force from 1927, unaffected by any amendment recorded after 1982; applicable at the April 2018 reference date.
verifier_note: Confirmed unchanged at the reference date: 50-1982 s.2 touched only subsections (5), (5A)-(5B) and (6), 48-2011 s.2 only subsection (1), and 21-2013 s.2 only subsection (6).

relevant_excerpt: If the land consists of an undivided share in a land, the proportion which the share bears to the entire land shall be staled, and a description of the entire land shall be given as required by subsection (1).
why_relevant: Records the alternative that is NOT engaged. The gift to Waruni is of a defined 10-perch lot, not of an undivided share, so the schedule does not have to state a fractional proportion. Keeping the contrast makes the choice of subsection (2) over subsection (3) explicit. The corpus text carries the obvious scanning error 'staled' for 'stated'.
temporal_note: In force from 1927; applicable at the reference date.
verifier_note: Excerpt verbatim; 'staled' is a scanning artefact in the consolidated corpus text, and subsection (3) is unamended at the reference date.

relevant_excerpt: Every Registrar shall refuse to register an instrument, other than a will, which docs not state the particulars required by the foregoing provisions of this section.
why_relevant: Supplies the consequence that makes the drafting requirement operative: a schedule that omits any of the section 13 particulars will cause the Registrar to refuse registration of Deed No. 429. The corpus text carries the scanning error 'docs' for 'does'.
temporal_note: In force from 1927; subsections (5A) and (5B) (appeal to the Registrar-General and thence to the District Court) were added by Ordinance No. 50 of 1982 and were in force at the reference date.
verifier_note: Excerpt verbatim; 50-1982/s2 in the corpus confirms both the researcher's temporal note (it inserted (5A) and (5B)) and that the true word is 'does', the corpus 'docs' being a scanning artefact.

relevant_excerpt: There shall be typewritten or written in ink at the head of every instrument (except a will) presented for registration a reference to the volume and folio in which some earlier instrument relating to the same land is registered
why_relevant: Completes the section 13 obligations for Deed No. 429. Deed of Gift No. 409 is an earlier instrument relating to the same land, so its volume and folio reference has to be written at the head of Deed No. 429. It is recorded as supporting rather than indispensable because it is a requirement on the face of the deed, not a requirement of the schedule itself.
temporal_note: In force from 1927; applicable at the reference date.
verifier_note: Excerpt stops at 'is registered' and omits the qualifier that follows in the corpus body, that the reference is required only 'if such reference is known to the notary who prepared the instrument, or, if the instrument was not prepared by a notary, if such reference is known to the person presenting the instrument for registration'; the duty is conditional, not absolute.

relevant_excerpt: " land " includes things attached to the earth or permanently fastened to anything attached to the earth and any estate or interest in land
why_relevant: Defines 'land' for the whole Ordinance, including for the description requirement in section 13 and the registration provisions in sections 7, 8 and 14. Buildings standing on an allotment are things attached to the earth, so the description of a lot for section 13 purposes extends to the buildings on it, and a schedule should say what stands on the lot.
temporal_note: In force from 1927; applicable at the reference date.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument, other than a will or codicil, affecting land or other immovable property, unless the deed or instrument embodies therin or in a Schedule annexed therto an accurate and clear description of the said land or other property affected thereby, showing its boundaries, extent, situation specifying the district, pattu, korale, Divisional Secretary's Division, local authority division and the Grama Niladari Division, and the village within the District in which the land is situated
why_relevant: The parallel duty on the attesting notary. It reinforces the same content requirement from the notarial side and, in its present form, lists further administrative divisions (Divisional Secretary's Division, local authority division, Grama Niladhari Division) that a practitioner would in fact insert. Supporting only, because the question is expressly confined to section 13 of the Registration of Documents Ordinance and because the corpus wording postdates the matter.
temporal_note: The corpus text of section 31 is a consolidation whose recorded amendment events run to Act No. 31 of 2022 and Act No. 6 of 2024, both after the April 2018 reference date. Rule (16) itself was substituted by Act No. 47 of 2011, which was in force in 2018, but the corpus does not expose the 2011-to-2022 wording separately, so the exact 2018 text of this rule cannot be confirmed from the corpus and this provision is not treated as indispensable.
verifier_note: Excerpt verbatim, but the temporal reasoning is wrong: the corpus does expose the April 2018 wording of rule (16)(a), as enacted by the Notaries (Amendment) Act, No. 47 of 2011, s.2, added here as PROV-M107-902. The consolidated wording quoted here carries later additions (the assessment number, the reference to the Pradeshiya Sabha Act, No. 15 of 1987, and the condominium limb) that were not in force in April 2018.

relevant_excerpt: if such property consist of a share of a land or other property, the deed shall state whether it is a divided or undivided share, and the fractional part which it is of the whole. If it be a divided share, such share shall be clearly and accurately defined by its particular boundaries and extent
why_relevant: The notarial counterpart of section 13(2). It confirms that where, as here, a divided share of Lot C is being gifted, the schedule must say that the share is divided and must define it by its own particular boundaries and extent.
temporal_note: Same temporal caveat as PROV-M107-007: the corpus carries the section 31 text as consolidated after the 2022 and 2024 amending Acts, later than the April 2018 reference date. Supporting only.
verifier_note: Excerpt verbatim, but 47-2011 s.2 replaced only paragraph (a) of rule (16), so paragraph (b) was not touched in 2011, and the corpus gives no way to attribute the 2022 and 2024 amendment events on section 31 to particular paragraphs; the April 2018 wording of paragraph (b) cannot be confirmed and it stays supporting only.

relevant_excerpt: be void as against all parties claiming an adverse interest thereto on valuable consideration by virtue of any subsequent instrument which is duly registered under this Chapter
why_relevant: The only statutory priority rule in the corpus that could arbitrate between the competing deeds of 4th June 2001. It shows why it cannot arbitrate here: the protection of prior registration runs only in favour of a party claiming an adverse interest on valuable consideration, and both Deed No. 409 and Deed No. 429 are deeds of gift. Neither donee can invoke section 7 against the other on the facts given.
temporal_note: In force from 1927 with no later change recorded in the corpus; applicable both when the deeds were executed in 2001 and at the April 2018 reference date.
verifier_note: Excerpt is a verbatim mid-sentence fragment of subsection (1); read in full the subsection bears the reading given, that the priority runs only in favour of a party claiming an adverse interest on valuable consideration.

relevant_excerpt: Registration of an instrument under this Chapter shall not cure any defect in the instrument or confer upon it any effect or validity which it would not otherwise have except the priority conferred on it by this section.
why_relevant: Directly answers the temptation to resolve Waruni's claim by pointing to the register. Registering Deed No. 429 gives it no operative effect it would not otherwise have. If Nimal had already divested himself of the whole of Lot C by Deed No. 409, registration of Deed No. 429 cannot supply the title he no longer had.
temporal_note: In force from 1927 with no later change recorded in the corpus; applicable at the reference date.

relevant_excerpt: all instruments, including wills, decrees and orders of any court or authority, and awards, which purport or operate to create, confer, declare, limit, assign, transfer, charge, incumber, release, or extinguish any right, title, or interest, whether vested or contingent, past, present, or future, to, in or over land
why_relevant: Establishes that both deeds of gift are instruments affecting land for the purposes of the Ordinance, so that the registration Chapter, and with it sections 7, 13 and 14, applies to Deed No. 409 and Deed No. 429 alike.
temporal_note: In force from 1927 with no later change recorded in the corpus; applicable at the reference date.

relevant_excerpt: An instrument, whether registered before or after the commencement of this Ordinance, shall not be deemed to be duly registered under this Chapter unless it is registered in accordance with the foregoing provisions of this section.
why_relevant: Background on what 'duly registered' means for section 7 purposes: registration in the correct folio for the land affected. It matters to the sub-division because Lot C4 has to be traced through the folio in which Lot C is registered.
temporal_note: In force from 1927, last changed by Act No. 14 of 1974, well before the reference date.

relevant_excerpt: Every instrument (other than a will) presented for registration shall embody therein or in a Schedule annexed thereto, an accurate and clear description of the land or immovable property affected thereby, its boundaries, extent and situation specifying the District, Pattu, Korale, Divisional Secretary's Division, local authority division and the Grama Niladari Division and the village, of the District in which the land is situated and in case the land or immovable property affected by this instrument is situated in within any municipality, town or developed area, declared under section 2 of the Municipal Councils Ordinance (Chapter 252), section 2 of the Urban Councils Ordinance (Chapter 255) and section 2 of the Pradeshiya Sabha number and the name, if any, of the street, in which such land or immovable property is situated.

Act No. 48 of 2011 repealed the subsection quoted at PROV-M107-001 and substituted this wider list, which adds the Divisional Secretary's Division, the local authority division and the Grama Niladari Division to the district, pattu and korale, and, for land in a municipality, town or developed area, requires the number as well as the street name. The schedule to Deed No. 429 has to be drafted to this list, not to the 1927 list.
temporal_note: Enacted in 2011 and unamended in the corpus; in force at April 2018. The corpus edition of the principal Ordinance is a 1990 consolidation, which is why the consolidated section 13(1) still shows the pre-2011 wording.
verifier_note: Added by the verifier. The substituted subsection is quoted verbatim from 48-2011/s2; the run-on 'section 2 of the Pradeshiya Sabha number' is a scanning artefact in the corpus text of the amending Act.

relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument, other than a will or codicil, affecting land or other immovable property, unless the deed or instrument embodies therin or in a Schedule annexed therto an accurate and clear description of the said land or other property affected thereby, showing its boundaries, extent, situation specifying the district, pattu, korale, Divisional Secretary's Division, local authority division and the Grama Niladari Division, and the village within the District in which the land is situated

It matches the substituted section 13(1) requirement and supplies the wording the researcher recorded as unavailable, so the notarial limb of the drafting duty can be stated for the matter date without relying on the post-2022 consolidation quoted at PROV-M107-007.
